items.title: Percentage Tricks and Formulas for Bank and SSC Exams
items.description: Percentage shortcuts with fraction equivalents, base-change rules, pass-mark and election sums, worked examples and 5 practice MCQs.
items.intro: Percentage is the backbone of arithmetic in IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI PO/Clerk, RBI Grade B and SSC CGL/CHSL. Direct percentage questions are only one or two per paper, but the same skill drives profit and loss, interest, data interpretation and quantity comparison, so weak percentage speed slows down almost a third of the quant section. The aim is not formula memory but instant conversion between fractions and percentages and a clear sense of which quantity is the base.

concepts.heading: What a percentage really is
concepts.text: A percentage is a fraction with denominator 100. "x% of N" means N × x/100. The harder part in exams is identifying the base: "A is 20% more than B" uses B as the base, while "B is what percent less than A" uses A. Most wrong answers in this chapter come from using the wrong base, not from bad arithmetic.

concepts.heading: More than / less than
concepts.text: If A is r% more than B, then B is less than A by r/(100 + r) × 100 percent. If A is r% less than B, then B is more than A by r/(100 − r) × 100 percent. The same rule handles price-rise and consumption questions: when price rises by r%, consumption must fall by r/(100 + r) × 100 percent to keep spending unchanged.
concepts.formula: B less than A = r / (100 + r) × 100

concepts.heading: Marks and elections
concepts.text: Pass-mark questions give marks scored and the shortfall; add them to get the pass mark, then divide by the pass percentage. Election questions give the winning margin; the margin equals the difference of the two vote-share percentages applied to valid votes cast, not to total voters.

shortcuts: Swap trick: x% of y = y% of x. So 16% of 25 = 25% of 16 = 4.
For 15% of a number, take 10% and add half of it: 15% of 860 = 86 + 43 = 129.
Increase by r% means multiply by (100 + r)/100: a 12.5% rise is × 9/8, so ₹1,600 becomes ₹1,800.
Decrease by 20% = × 4/5 and decrease by 25% = × 3/4; recognising the fraction saves time in long chains.
If the answer must be a whole number of people or marks, eliminate options that make the base a fraction.
1% of a number is just the decimal moved two places: 1% of 3,450 = 34.5, so 7% = 241.5.

examples.question: A’s salary is 25% more than B’s. By what percent is B’s salary less than A’s?
examples.solution: Take B = 100, so A = 125. B is less than A by 25 on a base of 125, so 25/125 × 100 = 20%. Using the rule r/(100 + r) × 100 = 25/125 × 100 gives the same 20% directly.

examples.question: A candidate needs 40% marks to pass. He scores 185 marks and fails by 35 marks. Find the maximum marks.
examples.solution: Pass mark = 185 + 35 = 220. This equals 40% of the maximum, so maximum = 220 ÷ 0.40 = 550 marks.

examples.question: The price of edible oil rises by 25%. By what percent should a family reduce its consumption so that its monthly expenditure on oil stays the same?
examples.solution: Reduction = 25/(100 + 25) × 100 = 20%. Check: if the family earlier bought 10 litres at ₹100, spending ₹1,000, the new price is ₹125 and ₹1,000 now buys 8 litres, which is 20% less.

examples.question: In a municipal ward, 60% of registered voters voted. The winner got 55% of the votes cast and won by 1,800 votes. There were only two candidates. Find the number of registered voters.
examples.solution: The loser got 45% of votes cast, so the margin is 10% of votes cast = 1,800. Votes cast = 18,000. These are 60% of registered voters, so registered voters = 18,000 ÷ 0.60 = 30,000.

practice: What is 35% of 840?
35% = 30% + 5%: 30% of 840 is 252 and 5% is 42, so the total is 294.
A’s income is 20% less than B’s income. By what percent is B’s income more than A’s?
Take B = 100, so A = 80. B exceeds A by 20 on a base of 80, which is 20/80 × 100 = 25%.
A student needs 33% marks to pass. She gets 210 marks and fails by 21 marks. What are the maximum marks?
Pass mark = 210 + 21 = 231, which is 33% of the maximum, so the maximum is 231 ÷ 0.33 = 700.
If the price of rice rises by 20%, by how much must consumption fall so that expenditure is unchanged?
Required reduction = 20/(100 + 20) × 100 = 16.67%, i.e. one-sixth of the earlier consumption.
12% of a number is 54. What is 35% of the same number?
The number is 54 ÷ 0.12 = 450, and 35% of 450 equals 157.5.
faqs: How many percentage questions come in IBPS PO prelims?

Usually one to three direct arithmetic questions use percentage, but percentage calculation appears inside almost every DI set and in profit and loss, interest and quantity-comparison questions. Treat it as a core speed skill rather than a single topic to tick off.
Should I memorise fractions up to 1/20?

Yes, at least up to 1/12 plus 1/15, 1/16 and 1/20. These cover most exam percentages such as 8.33%, 6.25% and 14.28%. Knowing them turns multiplication into simple division and cuts calculation time noticeably in DI sets.

items.title: Successive Percentage Change, Population and Depreciation
items.description: Learn the a + b + ab/100 rule for successive changes, population growth and depreciation sums, with solved examples and practice MCQs.
items.intro: Successive percentage change is the idea behind back-to-back price hikes, salary cuts followed by raises, population growth and asset depreciation. IBPS and SBI prelims use it in arithmetic word problems and in quantity-comparison pairs, while SSC CGL frames it as area and volume change when dimensions change. CAT and CMAT hide it inside multi-step growth questions. One clean formula handles all of these, provided you keep signs straight for decreases.

concepts.heading: The net-change formula
concepts.text: When a quantity changes by a% and then by b%, the overall change is a + b + ab/100 percent. Use a negative sign for a decrease. For +20% and −10%, the net change is 20 − 10 − 2 = +8%. For three changes, apply the formula to the first two, then combine that result with the third.

concepts.heading: Equal rise and fall
concepts.text: A rise of x% followed by a fall of x% (or the reverse) always gives a net loss of x²/100 percent. A salary cut of 25% followed by a raise of 25% leaves the employee 6.25% poorer, not back to the start, because the raise is calculated on a smaller base.

concepts.heading: Population growth
concepts.text: If a town’s population grows at r% a year, after n years it is P(1 + r/100)ⁿ. This is the compound-interest formula with people instead of rupees. For different rates in different years, multiply the separate factors, e.g. 1.05 × 1.08.

concepts.heading: Depreciation
concepts.text: Machines, vehicles and computers lose value at a fixed percentage of their current value each year. Value after n years = P(1 − r/100)ⁿ. The amount lost in the first year is larger than in later years because each year’s fall is calculated on a lower value.

shortcuts: Area change when both sides change: use a + b + ab/100. Length +10%, breadth +10% gives area +21%.
Radius change r% in a circle: area changes by 2r + r²/100 percent. Radius +10% gives area +21%.
For three equal rises of 10%, remember 1.331: the total rise is 33.1%.
Price rises 25% then falls 20%: 25 − 20 − 5 = 0, so the price is back to the original. Watch for this pair in options.
Depreciation of 10% for two years = factor 0.81; of 20% for two years = 0.64. Learn these factors to skip multiplication.
To reverse a change, divide by the factor: if a value after a 25% rise is ₹500, the original is 500 ÷ 1.25 = ₹400.

examples.question: The price of a refrigerator is increased by 10% and then by 20%. What is the overall percentage increase?
examples.solution: Net = 10 + 20 + (10 × 20)/100 = 30 + 2 = 32%. Check with ₹100: after 10% it is ₹110; 20% more makes it ₹132, an increase of 32%.

examples.question: A town has 50,000 people and the population grows at 4% a year. What will it be after 2 years?
A printing machine costing ₹2,00,000 depreciates at 10% a year. What is its value after 3 years?
The length of a rectangular plot is increased by 20% and its breadth is decreased by 10%. Find the percentage change in area.
examples.solution: Area change = 20 + (−10) + (20 × −10)/100 = 20 − 10 − 2 = +8%. The area increases by 8%.

examples.question: An employee’s salary is cut by 25% and later increased by 25%. What is the net effect?
examples.solution: Equal rise and fall gives a loss of 25²/100 = 6.25%. On ₹40,000 the salary first becomes ₹30,000 and then ₹37,500, which is ₹2,500 or 6.25% lower.

practice: A price is increased by 30% and then decreased by 20%. The net change is:
4% increase
10% increase
4% decrease
6% increase
Net change = 30 − 20 − (30 × 20)/100 = 10 − 6 = +4%, so the price rises by 4%.
A village has 64,000 people. If its population falls by 5% every year, what will it be after 2 years?
If the radius of a circle is increased by 10%, its area increases by:
Area depends on r², so the change is 10 + 10 + (10 × 10)/100 = 21 percent.
A scooter bought for ₹80,000 depreciates at 15% a year. What is its value after 2 years?
Value = 80,000 × 0.85² = 80,000 × 0.7225 = ₹57,800 after two years of depreciation.
A price rises by 10% three years in a row. The total rise is:
The factor is 1.1³ = 1.331, so the total rise is 33.1 percent over the original price.
faqs: Is successive percentage the same as compound interest?

The arithmetic is the same: both multiply growth factors one after another. Compound interest is the special case where the rate is the same every period and is applied to money. The a + b + ab/100 rule works for any two changes, equal or different, increases or decreases.
How do I handle three successive changes quickly?

Combine the first two with a + b + ab/100, then combine that answer with the third using the same formula. Alternatively multiply the factors, for example 1.1 × 0.9 × 1.2, if the numbers are friendly. Both methods give the same result.

items.title: Profit and Loss Shortcuts with Solved Examples
items.description: Profit and loss formulas, the x²/100 loss rule, false-weight dealer sums and cost-price reversal, with worked bank and SSC style examples.
items.intro: Profit and loss gives one to three questions in IBPS PO, SBI Clerk and RBI Grade B prelims, and it is a favourite in SSC CGL and CHSL arithmetic. It also shows up in DI caselets where you must compute profit percentages for several shops. The concepts are simple; marks are lost by calculating profit percentage on selling price instead of cost price, or by mixing up per-item and total figures.

concepts.heading: Basic relations
concepts.text: Cost price (CP) is what the seller paid; selling price (SP) is what the buyer pays. Profit = SP − CP and Loss = CP − SP. Profit or loss percentage is always on CP unless the question explicitly says "on selling price".

concepts.heading: Working backwards to CP
concepts.text: When SP and the profit or loss percentage are given, divide rather than subtract. If an article sold for ₹1,104 involves an 8% loss, CP = 1,104 ÷ 0.92 = ₹1,200. Subtracting 8% of ₹1,104 is the classic mistake.

concepts.heading: Same SP, equal gain and loss
concepts.text: If two articles are sold at the same price, one at x% profit and the other at x% loss, the seller always makes an overall loss of x²/100 percent. The two cost prices are different, so the gains and losses do not cancel.

concepts.heading: Dishonest dealers
concepts.text: A dealer who claims to sell at cost price but gives less weight earns a gain equal to error ÷ (true weight − error) × 100. Giving 900 g instead of 1 kg means the error is 100 g on 900 g actually given, so gain = 11.11%.

shortcuts: Buy a items for ₹x and sell b items for ₹x: profit% = (a − b)/b × 100. Buy 12, sell 10 for the same money gives 20%.
Profit on SP of r% equals profit on CP of r/(100 − r) × 100 percent. 20% on SP is 25% on CP.
If selling at ₹S1 gives x% loss and at ₹S2 gives y% profit, CP = (S2 − S1) × 100 / (x + y).
Convert profit percentages to fractions: 25% profit means SP = 5/4 of CP, 12.5% means SP = 9/8 of CP.
When an answer comes out as an odd decimal like 5.26%, check if it is 100/19 — many dealer questions produce fractions with 19, 9 or 99.

examples.question: A shopkeeper buys 12 pens for ₹100 and sells 10 pens for ₹100. Find his profit percentage.
examples.solution: CP of one pen = 100/12 = ₹8.33 and SP of one pen = ₹10. Profit = 1.67 on 8.33, which is 20%. Shortcut: (12 − 10)/10 × 100 = 20%.

examples.question: Two mobile phones are sold for ₹9,900 each. One is sold at 10% profit and the other at 10% loss. Find the overall result.
examples.solution: CP of first = 9,900 ÷ 1.1 = ₹9,000; CP of second = 9,900 ÷ 0.9 = ₹11,000. Total CP = ₹20,000, total SP = ₹19,800, so there is a loss of ₹200, which is 1%. Formula check: 10²/100 = 1% loss.

examples.question: A grocer claims to sell rice at cost price but uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg. Find his gain percentage.
examples.solution: Error = 100 g, actual quantity given = 900 g. Gain = 100/900 × 100 = 11.11%.

examples.question: By selling a fan for ₹1,104, a trader loses 8%. At what price should he sell it to gain 10%?

practice: An article costing ₹640 is sold at a profit of 15%. Find the selling price.
An article sold for ₹1,350 results in a loss of 10%. What was its cost price?
CP = 1,350 ÷ 0.90 = ₹1,500. Subtracting 10% of 1,350 would wrongly give ₹1,215.
A vendor buys bananas at 6 for ₹10 and sells them at 4 for ₹10. His profit percentage is:
Using (a − b)/b × 100 with a = 6 and b = 4 gives 2/4 × 100 = 50 percent profit.
Two cycles are sold at ₹4,800 each, one at 20% profit and the other at 20% loss. The overall result is:
4% loss
No profit, no loss
2% loss
4% profit
Same SP with equal profit and loss percentages always gives a loss of 20²/100 = 4 percent.
A dealer sells goods at cost price but uses 950 g instead of 1 kg. His gain is about:
Gain = 50/950 × 100 = 5.26 percent, because the error of 50 g is measured against the 950 g actually given.
faqs: Is profit percentage calculated on cost price or selling price?

On cost price, unless the question clearly says "profit on selling price". Bank and SSC questions follow this convention. If a question mentions margin on selling price, convert it: a 20% margin on SP equals a 25% profit on CP.
Why is there a loss when profit and loss percentages are equal?

Because the two cost prices differ. The article sold at a loss had a higher cost price, so the rupee loss on it is larger than the rupee gain on the other. The net effect is always a loss of x²/100 percent when the selling prices are equal.

items.title: Discount and Marked Price: Formulas and Tricks
items.description: Marked price, successive discounts, buy-x-get-y-free offers and markup-to-profit links explained with solved examples and practice questions.
items.intro: Discount questions extend profit and loss by adding a third price, the marked price (MP) or list price. IBPS Clerk and SBI Clerk ask one question regularly, SSC CGL and CHSL ask two or three, and DI caselets about shops often include marked price and discount. Festive sales in India, with offers such as "flat 20% + extra 10%" or "buy 2 get 1 free", are exactly the situations these questions model.

concepts.heading: Three prices
concepts.text: Marked price is the printed price, selling price is what the customer pays after discount, and cost price is what the seller paid. Discount is always calculated on the marked price, while profit is always calculated on cost price. Mixing the two bases is the main source of errors.

concepts.heading: Successive discounts
concepts.text: Two discounts of a% and b% are not equal to a single discount of (a + b)%. The single equivalent discount is a + b − ab/100. Flat 20% plus extra 10% equals 28%, not 30%. For three discounts, combine two first and then the third.

concepts.heading: Linking markup, discount and profit
concepts.text: If the seller marks the item m% above cost and then gives d% discount, SP = CP × (1 + m/100)(1 − d/100). The ratio MP : CP equals (100 + profit%) : (100 − discount%), which answers "how much above cost should he mark" questions in one line.

concepts.heading: Free-item offers
concepts.text: In "buy x get y free", the customer pays for x items but takes x + y. The effective discount is y/(x + y) × 100. Buy 3 get 1 free is a 25% discount, not 33.33%.

shortcuts: Equivalent of 10% and 10% is 19%; of 20% and 20% is 36%; of 10% and 20% is 28%.
Marked 25% above cost and sold at 20% discount gives no profit, no loss (1.25 × 0.8 = 1).
Marked 50% above cost with a 20% discount gives 20% profit (1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2).
For "buy x get y free", the discount fraction is y/(x + y); for "buy x for the price of y" it is (x − y)/x.
If you know SP and two successive discounts, divide by both factors to get MP: SP ÷ 0.8 ÷ 0.9.

examples.question: A jacket is marked at ₹2,500 and two successive discounts of 20% and 10% are given. Find the selling price and the single equivalent discount.
A trader marks goods 40% above cost price and allows a discount of 25%. Find his profit percentage.
A store offers "buy 3 shirts, get 1 free". What is the effective discount?
examples.solution: The customer pays for 3 but takes 4. Discount = 1/4 × 100 = 25%.

examples.question: A shopkeeper wants a profit of 20% after allowing a 10% discount. By what percent above cost should he mark his goods?
examples.solution: MP/CP = 120/90 = 4/3, so the marked price must be 33.33% above cost price.

examples.question: A washing machine is marked at ₹5,000. After a 15% discount the dealer still earns a profit of 6.25%. Find the cost price.
examples.solution: SP = 5,000 × 0.85 = ₹4,250. Since this includes a 6.25% profit, CP = 4,250 ÷ 1.0625 = ₹4,000. Note that 6.25% = 1/16, so CP = 4,250 × 16/17, which is quicker to compute mentally.

practice: A bag is marked at ₹1,200 and sold at a discount of 15%. Find the selling price.
SP = 1,200 × 0.85 = ₹1,020, since 15% of 1,200 is ₹180 off the marked price.
Two successive discounts of 20% and 5% are equivalent to a single discount of:
Equivalent discount = 20 + 5 − (20 × 5)/100 = 25 − 1 = 24 percent overall.
An item is marked 50% above cost and sold at 20% discount. The profit percentage is:
Taking CP as 100, MP is 150 and SP is 150 × 0.8 = 120, so the profit is 20 percent.
An offer says "buy 4, get 1 free". The effective discount is:
The buyer pays for 4 but receives 5 items, so the discount is 1/5 × 100 = 20 percent.
An article costs ₹800. The seller wants 25% profit after giving a 20% discount. What should the marked price be?
faqs: Is discount calculated on cost price?

No. Discount is always on the marked price, because that is the price shown to the customer. Profit or loss is on cost price. Keeping these two bases separate solves most discount questions correctly.
Why is 20% plus 10% not 30%?

The second discount applies to the already reduced price. After 20% off ₹100 the price is ₹80, and 10% of ₹80 is only ₹8, so the total discount is ₹28 or 28%. The formula a + b − ab/100 captures this.

items.title: Simple Interest Formulas and Tricks for Competitive Exams
items.description: Simple interest formula, doubling-time rule, two-amount method and split-investment sums explained with worked examples and five practice MCQs.
items.intro: Simple interest (SI) is one of the most scoring arithmetic topics in IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk, SSC CHSL and SSC CGL. Expect one question on its own and another combined with compound interest. Because interest is earned only on the original principal, every year adds the same rupee amount, which makes most SI questions solvable with a straight-line, "per-year" way of thinking rather than heavy formulas.

concepts.heading: The formula
concepts.text: SI = P × R × T / 100, where P is the principal in rupees, R the rate per cent per annum and T the time in years. Amount A = P + SI. Months must be converted to years: 9 months = 0.75 year, 3 years 6 months = 3.5 years. For days, divide by 365.

concepts.heading: Interest per year is constant
concepts.text: Since interest is on the principal only, the amount grows by the same figure each year. If a sum amounts to ₹8,960 after 3 years and ₹9,600 after 5 years, the 2-year gap shows ₹640 of interest, so ₹320 a year. Subtract 3 × 320 from ₹8,960 to get the principal.

concepts.heading: Multiples of the principal
concepts.text: A sum becomes n times itself when the interest equals (n − 1) × P. So the time needed is (n − 1) × 100 / R. If a sum doubles in 8 years, R = 12.5%, and it becomes four times (interest = 3P) in 24 years.

concepts.heading: Splitting a sum
concepts.text: When a total is lent in two parts at different rates and the combined interest is known, set one part as x and write a single equation. Alligation also works: the overall rate sits between the two rates, and the distances give the ratio of the parts.

shortcuts: Work in "per cent of principal": at 8% for 3.5 years, the interest is 28% of P.
If the time and rate are interchanged, SI stays the same: P at 5% for 8 years = P at 8% for 5 years.
When two amounts are given for two times, the difference ÷ time gap = yearly interest.
Rate × time = 100 means the sum has doubled; = 200 means it has tripled.
For a rate like 6.25% (1/16), think in fractions: SI for 4 years is 1/4 of the principal.

examples.question: Find the simple interest on ₹12,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years 6 months.
A sum amounts to ₹8,960 in 3 years and ₹9,600 in 5 years at simple interest. Find the principal and the rate.
examples.solution: Interest for 2 years = 9,600 − 8,960 = ₹640, so ₹320 per year. Interest for 3 years = ₹960, principal = 8,960 − 960 = ₹8,000. Rate = 320/8,000 × 100 = 4% per annum.

examples.question: A sum doubles in 8 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become four times?
examples.solution: Doubling means interest = P in 8 years, so R = 100/8 = 12.5%. Four times needs interest = 3P, which takes 3 × 8 = 24 years.

examples.question: Rohit lends ₹10,000 in two parts, one at 6% and the other at 9% simple interest. The total yearly interest is ₹750. How much did he lend at 6%?
examples.solution: Let x be lent at 6%. Then 0.06x + 0.09(10,000 − x) = 750, so 900 − 0.03x = 750 and x = ₹5,000. The other part is also ₹5,000, which makes sense because 7.5% is exactly halfway between 6% and 9%.

practice: Find the simple interest on ₹6,500 at 7% per annum for 4 years.
A sum becomes 1.5 times itself in 5 years at simple interest. The rate of interest is:
Interest equals 0.5 P in 5 years, so the rate is 50/5 = 10 percent per annum.
The simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 9% per annum is ₹2,430. The sum is:
A sum amounts to ₹5,600 in 2 years and ₹6,200 in 4 years at simple interest. The principal is:
Yearly interest is (6,200 − 5,600)/2 = ₹300, so principal = 5,600 − 600 = ₹5,000.
A sum triples itself in 20 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become five times?
35 years
30 years
50 years
40 years
Tripling means interest 2P in 20 years, so 10% a year; five times needs 4P, which takes 40 years.
faqs: Is simple interest used in real Indian banking?

Most bank deposits compound interest quarterly, but simple interest concepts are used for short-term loans, some gold loans and interest on overdue amounts. In exams, SI is tested mainly as a calculation skill and as a base for comparing with compound interest.
How do I convert days into years for SI questions?

Divide the number of days by 365. Count days carefully between dates: usually the day of deposit is excluded and the day of withdrawal included. Exam questions mostly use friendly numbers like 73 days, which is exactly 1/5 of a year.

items.title: Compound Interest Shortcuts: Annual, Half-Yearly, Quarterly
items.description: Compound interest formula with annual, half-yearly and quarterly compounding, fractional years and doubling rules, plus worked bank-exam examples.
items.intro: Compound interest (CI) appears in almost every IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B prelims paper, either as a stand-alone question or inside quantity comparison. SSC CGL also asks one or two. Indian fixed deposits compound quarterly, so the idea is practical as well. The exam challenge is speed: handling 2–3 year powers, changing the rate for half-yearly compounding and dealing with fractional years without a calculator.

concepts.heading: Basic formula
concepts.text: Amount A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ and CI = A − P. Each year, interest is earned on the previous year’s amount, so the interest grows every year. For 2 years at 10%, the factor is 1.21; for 3 years, 1.331.

concepts.heading: Half-yearly and quarterly
concepts.text: For half-yearly compounding, halve the rate and double the number of periods. For quarterly, divide the rate by 4 and multiply the periods by 4. ₹16,000 at 10% p.a. compounded half-yearly for 1 year uses 5% for 2 periods.

concepts.heading: Fractional years
concepts.text: For 2.5 years at R%, compound for 2 full years and then apply simple interest at R/2 for the last half year: A = P(1 + R/100)² × (1 + R/200). This is the convention used in exam questions.

concepts.heading: Different rates in different years
concepts.text: When the rate changes from year to year, multiply the separate growth factors: A = P(1 + R1/100)(1 + R2/100)(1 + R3/100). The order of the rates does not change the final amount, which is a useful check when options look close.

concepts.heading: Multiplying rule
concepts.text: If a sum becomes k times in n years at CI, it becomes k² times in 2n years and k³ times in 3n years. Doubling in 5 years means 8 times in 15 years. This works because growth factors multiply, unlike simple interest where they add.

shortcuts: Year-wise CI at 10% on ₹1,000: 100, 110, 121. Each year adds 10% of the previous year’s interest on top.
Effective annual rate for R% compounded half-yearly = R + R²/400. At 12%, it is 12.36%.
For a rate like 12.5% (1/8), write factor 9/8: two years gives 81/64, so pick principals that are multiples of 64.
If the amount for year n and year n + 1 is known, the rate = (difference ÷ earlier amount) × 100.

examples.question: Find the compound interest on ₹20,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years, compounded annually.
Find the CI on ₹16,000 for 1 year at 10% per annum compounded half-yearly.
examples.solution: Rate per half year = 5%, periods = 2. A = 16,000 × 1.05² = 16,000 × 1.1025 = ₹17,640. CI = ₹1,640, which is ₹40 more than annual compounding would give.

examples.question: A sum doubles in 5 years at compound interest. In how many years will it become 8 times?
examples.solution: 8 = 2³, so the time is 3 × 5 = 15 years.

examples.question: Find the amount on ₹10,000 for 2½ years at 10% per annum compound interest.
Find the compound interest on ₹12,800 for 2 years at 12.5% per annum, compounded annually.
examples.solution: 12.5% = 1/8, so the yearly factor is 9/8. A = 12,800 × 81/64 = 200 × 81 = ₹16,200. CI = ₹3,400. Choosing the fraction route avoids squaring 1.125, and 12,800 was picked by the setter precisely because it is divisible by 64.

examples.question: A deposit earns 5% in the first year and 10% in the second year, compounded annually. What is the amount on ₹40,000 after 2 years?
examples.solution: Multiply the separate factors: 40,000 × 1.05 × 1.10 = 42,000 × 1.10 = ₹46,200. The total interest is ₹6,200, which is 15.5%, slightly more than the 15% that simple interest at the same rates would give.

practice: Find the compound interest on ₹5,000 at 8% per annum for 2 years.
A = 5,000 × 1.1664 = ₹5,832, so CI = ₹832, which is ₹32 more than simple interest.
Find the CI on ₹8,000 for 1 year at 20% per annum compounded half-yearly.
Use 10% per half year for 2 periods: 8,000 × 1.21 = ₹9,680, so CI = ₹1,680.
A sum doubles in 4 years at compound interest. It will become 16 times in:
12 years
32 years
16 years
8 years
16 = 2⁴, so the time needed is 4 × 4 = 16 years when the sum doubles every 4 years.
A sum amounts to ₹8,820 in 2 years at 5% per annum compound interest. The principal is:
P = 8,820 ÷ 1.05² = 8,820 ÷ 1.1025 = ₹8,000, the original principal.
What is the effective annual rate for 12% per annum compounded half-yearly?
Effective rate = 1.06² − 1 = 0.1236, i.e. 12.36 percent per year when compounding twice.
faqs: Why do bank exams prefer rates like 10%, 20% and 12.5%?

Because the growth factors become friendly fractions such as 11/10, 6/5 and 9/8, allowing mental calculation without a calculator. When you see such rates, convert them to fractions and choose principal values that cancel cleanly. This speeds up two- and three-year questions considerably.
How does quarterly compounding compare with annual compounding?

For the same nominal rate, quarterly compounding always gives a slightly higher amount because interest is added more often. At 8% p.a., quarterly compounding gives an effective annual rate of about 8.24%. The difference grows with higher rates and longer periods.

items.title: Difference Between Compound and Simple Interest Tricks
items.description: Two-year and three-year formulas for the gap between compound and simple interest, rate-finding from SI and CI pairs, with solved questions.
items.intro: Questions on the difference between compound and simple interest are a favourite of IBPS PO, SBI Clerk and SSC CGL setters because they test whether you understand why CI grows faster. The difference has neat closed formulas for two and three years, so a question that looks like it needs two full calculations can be finished in one line. Expect one such question in many bank prelims papers, often in quantity comparison form.

concepts.heading: Why the gap appears
concepts.text: In the first year, CI and SI are equal. From the second year on, CI also earns interest on the first year’s interest. For two years, the extra is just the interest on year-1 interest, which equals P(R/100)².

concepts.heading: Three-year gap
concepts.text: Over three years, the extra includes interest on two years of interest plus interest on interest. The closed form is P(R/100)² × (300 + R)/100. At 10% on ₹8,000 this gives 8,000 × 0.01 × 3.1 = ₹248.
concepts.formula: Three years: CI − SI = P(R/100)²(300 + R)/100

concepts.heading: Finding the rate from SI and CI
concepts.text: If two-year SI and CI on the same sum are given, the one-year SI is half the two-year SI. The extra (CI − SI) is interest on that one-year SI for one year, so R = (CI − SI) / (SI/2) × 100. Then P follows from the one-year SI.

concepts.heading: Using the gap in quantity comparison
concepts.text: Since the two-year gap depends only on P and R², you can compare two scenarios without computing either interest fully. Doubling the rate quadruples the gap, while doubling the principal only doubles it. This makes comparison questions very quick.

concepts.heading: Reverse questions
concepts.text: Given the difference, rate and time 2 years, the principal is D ÷ (R/100)². A ₹25 difference at 5% means P = 25 ÷ 0.0025 = ₹10,000. Always check whether the question says 2 or 3 years before choosing the formula.

shortcuts: At 10%, the two-year difference is 1% of P; at 5% it is 0.25% of P; at 20% it is 4% of P.
Three-year difference ÷ two-year difference = (300 + R)/100. At 10% this ratio is 3.1.
For half-yearly compounding over 1 year, the gap from SI is P(R/200)².
If SI for 2 years is S and CI is C, the rate is 200(C − S)/S percent.

examples.question: Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹15,000 for 2 years at 6% per annum.
The difference between CI and SI on a sum for 2 years at 5% per annum is ₹25. Find the sum.
Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹8,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum.
On a certain sum, the SI for 2 years is ₹1,200 and the CI for 2 years is ₹1,290. Find the rate and the sum.
examples.solution: SI for one year = ₹600. The extra ₹90 is interest on ₹600 for one year, so R = 90/600 × 100 = 15%. Principal = 600 ÷ 0.15 = ₹4,000.

examples.question: The difference between CI and SI on a sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹31. Find the sum.
examples.solution: Three-year difference = P × 0.01 × 3.1 = 0.031P. So 0.031P = 31 and P = ₹1,000. Check: CI = 1,000 × 0.331 = ₹331 and SI = ₹300.

examples.question: Quantity I: CI − SI on ₹6,400 for 2 years at 12.5%. Quantity II: CI − SI on ₹10,000 for 2 years at 10%. Which is greater?
examples.solution: Quantity I = 6,400 × (1/8)² = 6,400/64 = ₹100. Quantity II = 10,000 × (1/10)² = ₹100. The two quantities are equal. Such pairs are common in IBPS quantity comparison, so do not assume the larger principal wins.

practice: Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹20,000 for 2 years at 4% per annum.
Difference = 20,000 × (0.04)² = 20,000 × 0.0016 = ₹32 for the two-year period.
The difference between CI and SI for 2 years at 8% per annum is ₹48. The principal is:
P = 48 ÷ (0.08)² = 48 ÷ 0.0064 = ₹7,500 using the two-year difference formula.
Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹5,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum.
The SI on a sum for 2 years is ₹800 and the CI is ₹840. The rate of interest is:
One-year SI is ₹400, and the extra ₹40 is interest on ₹400 for a year, so the rate is 10 percent.
Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹12,500 for 2 years at 12% per annum.
faqs: Does the CI − SI formula work for half-yearly compounding?

Yes, with adjustment. Replace R by the rate per period and n by the number of periods. For one year at 10% compounded half-yearly, the difference from simple interest is P × (0.05)². Simple interest is still calculated at the annual rate for the full year.
Is the first-year interest always equal under CI and SI?

Yes, when compounding is annual. Both methods charge R% on the same principal in year one. The difference starts from the second year. With half-yearly or quarterly compounding, CI pulls ahead within the first year itself.

items.title: Ratio and Proportion: Rules, Tricks and Solved Questions
items.description: Combine ratios, divide money in given ratios, find mean, third and fourth proportionals, and solve coin-bag sums with worked ratio examples.
items.intro: Ratio and proportion is less a chapter than a language used across the quant section: partnership, ages, mixtures, time and work and most DI sets are ratio problems in disguise. IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and SSC CHSL ask one or two direct questions, and CAT expects you to manipulate ratios fluently in algebra. Students who think in "parts" instead of writing equations usually finish these questions in under 40 seconds.

concepts.heading: Thinking in parts
concepts.text: A ratio 3 : 5 means the quantities are 3k and 5k for some k. If their total is ₹640, then 8k = 640 and k = 80. The single unknown k turns a two-variable problem into one division. When a change happens (adding 10 to each), write the new ratio with k and cross-multiply.

concepts.heading: Combining ratios
concepts.text: To merge A : B and B : C, make the common term B equal. For A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, scale the first by 4 and the second by 3: A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15. The value of A : C alone is the product of the two ratios: (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15.

concepts.heading: Proportionals
concepts.text: If a : b = c : d, then d is the fourth proportional = bc/a. The third proportional to a and b is b²/a, and the mean proportional between a and b is √(ab). These three definitions are asked directly in SSC papers.

concepts.heading: Inverse ratios
concepts.text: Dividing ₹5,200 in the ratio 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4 means first converting fractions to whole numbers using the LCM of the denominators (12): 6 : 4 : 3. Shares go in proportion to these numbers, not to 2 : 3 : 4.

shortcuts: If a/b = c/d, then (a + b)/(a − b) = (c + d)/(c − d) (componendo–dividendo); useful in CAT algebra.
Coin-bag questions: convert the count ratio to a value ratio first. 5 : 6 : 8 coins of ₹1, 50p, 25p have values 5 : 3 : 2.
When the same number x is added to both terms of a ratio, solve with cross-multiplication; options can often be checked faster than solving.
A share is (its ratio term ÷ sum of terms) × total. For 2 : 3 : 4 of ₹3,600, the largest share is 4/9 × 3,600 = ₹1,600.
Duplicate ratio of a : b is a² : b²; sub-duplicate is √a : √b. These terms appear in SSC questions.

examples.question: If A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, find A : B : C.
examples.solution: Make B common: multiply the first ratio by 4 and the second by 3. A : B = 8 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 15, so A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15.

examples.question: Divide ₹5,200 among A, B and C in the ratio 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4.
examples.solution: LCM of 2, 3, 4 is 12. Multiplying gives 6 : 4 : 3, total 13 parts. One part = 5,200 ÷ 13 = ₹400. Shares: A ₹2,400, B ₹1,600, C ₹1,200.

examples.question: Find the fourth proportional to 4, 9 and 12, and the mean proportional between 9 and 16.
examples.solution: Fourth proportional = 9 × 12 ÷ 4 = 27. Mean proportional = √(9 × 16) = √144 = 12.

examples.question: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5. If 10 is added to each, the ratio becomes 5 : 7. Find the numbers.
examples.solution: Let them be 3x and 5x. Then (3x + 10)/(5x + 10) = 5/7, so 21x + 70 = 25x + 50 and x = 5. The numbers are 15 and 25. Check: 25/35 = 5/7.

examples.question: A bag has ₹1, 50 paise and 25 paise coins in the ratio 5 : 6 : 8 by number. The total value is ₹210. How many coins of each kind are there?
examples.solution: Value ratio = 5 × 1 : 6 × 0.5 : 8 × 0.25 = 5 : 3 : 2, total 10 parts = ₹210, so one part = ₹21. Values: ₹105, ₹63, ₹42. Number of coins: 105 one-rupee, 126 fifty-paise and 168 twenty-five-paise coins.

practice: If A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 6 : 7, then A : C is:
A : C = (3/4) × (6/7) = 18/28 = 9/14, so the ratio of A to C is 9 : 14.
The third proportional to 8 and 12 is:
Third proportional = b²/a = 12² ÷ 8 = 144 ÷ 8 = 18, so 8 : 12 = 12 : 18.
₹3,600 is divided in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. The largest share is:
There are 9 parts of ₹400 each, so the largest share is 4 × 400 = ₹1,600.
Two numbers are in the ratio 4 : 7. If 6 is subtracted from each, the ratio becomes 1 : 2. The larger number is:
With 4x and 7x, 2(4x − 6) = 7x − 6 gives x = 6, so the numbers are 24 and 42.
The mean proportional between 0.08 and 0.18 is:
Mean proportional = √(0.08 × 0.18) = √0.0144 = 0.12, which lies between the two numbers.
faqs: Is ratio the same as fraction?

Numerically a ratio a : b can be written as a/b, but a ratio compares two quantities of the same kind, while a fraction is a part of a whole. In a ratio 3 : 5, the first quantity is 3/8 of the total, not 3/5. Confusing these is a common error.
How do I handle three-term ratios quickly?

Find the common term in the two given ratios and scale each ratio so that the common term matches, using the LCM of its two values. Write the merged ratio in a single line. Practise ten such questions and the scaling becomes automatic.

items.title: Average Shortcuts: Replacement, Cricket and Speed Questions
items.description: Average formulas and deviation tricks for replacement, new-entry, batsman-innings and wrong-entry questions, with worked examples for bank and SSC.
items.intro: Averages give at least one question in most IBPS, SBI and SSC papers and form the hidden logic behind DI questions that ask for "average sales per year". The chapter rewards a deviation mindset: instead of adding everything up, track how far each new value sits from the existing average. This approach turns teacher-joins-the-class, batsman-innings and replacement questions into one-line calculations.

concepts.heading: Definition and total
concepts.text: Average = sum of observations ÷ number of observations. Most questions are easier if you convert averages into totals: an average of 52 for 40 students means a total of 2,080 marks. Work with totals when people join or leave the group, then divide at the end.

concepts.heading: Deviation method
concepts.text: When a new value joins, the change in average equals (new value − old average) ÷ new count. A new person who is 30 kg heavier than the existing average of 9 people raises the average by 30/10 = 3 kg. This avoids computing totals altogether.

concepts.heading: Replacement
concepts.text: If one member of a group of n is replaced and the average rises by d, the newcomer is n × d heavier (or older) than the person who left. For 8 people and an increase of 2.5 kg, the newcomer weighs 20 kg more than the person replaced.
concepts.formula: New − Old = n × change in average

concepts.heading: Average speed
concepts.text: For equal distances at speeds x and y, the average speed is 2xy/(x + y), the harmonic mean, not (x + y)/2. For equal times, it is the simple mean. Going at 40 km/h and returning at 60 km/h gives 48 km/h, not 50.

shortcuts: Average of consecutive numbers is the middle number (or the mean of the two middle numbers).
Average of the first n natural numbers = (n + 1)/2; of the first n even numbers = n + 1; of the first n odd numbers = n.
Wrong entry: corrected average = old average ± (difference ÷ count). Reading 75 instead of 45 among 50 numbers lowers the true average by 30/50 = 0.6.
Overlapping groups: if the first six and last six of eleven numbers share the sixth, that number = sum of both groups − total of all eleven.
In cricket questions, the run scored in the new innings = new average + (old innings × increase).

examples.question: The average age of 30 students is 14 years. When the teacher’s age is included, the average becomes 15 years. Find the teacher’s age.
examples.solution: Total with teacher = 31 × 15 = 465; total of students = 30 × 14 = 420. Teacher’s age = 45 years. Deviation view: the teacher adds 1 year to each of 31 people, so she is 31 years above 14, i.e. 45.

examples.question: A batsman scores 87 runs in his 17th innings and thereby raises his average by 3. Find his average after the 17th innings.
examples.solution: Let the old average be a. Then 16a + 87 = 17(a + 3), so a = 87 − 51 = 36. New average = 39. Shortcut: new average = 87 − 16 × 3 = 39.

examples.question: The average of 50 numbers is 38. Later it is found that 45 was wrongly read as 75. Find the correct average.
examples.solution: The total was overstated by 30, so the average was overstated by 30/50 = 0.6. Correct average = 38 − 0.6 = 37.4.

examples.question: A cyclist rides from Pune to Lonavala at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. Find the average speed for the round trip.
examples.solution: Distances are equal, so average speed = 2 × 40 × 60/(40 + 60) = 4,800/100 = 48 km/h.

practice: The average of the first 20 even natural numbers is:
The first n even numbers average n + 1, so for n = 20 the average is 21 (sum 420 ÷ 20).
The average weight of 8 people rises by 2.5 kg when a person weighing 65 kg is replaced by a new person. The new person weighs:
80 kg
90 kg
85 kg
The newcomer is 8 × 2.5 = 20 kg heavier than the person replaced, so the weight is 65 + 20 = 85 kg.
The average of 11 numbers is 50. The average of the first six is 49 and of the last six is 52. The sixth number is:
Sixth number = 6 × 49 + 6 × 52 − 11 × 50 = 294 + 312 − 550 = 56, as it is counted twice.
A batsman scores 90 runs in his 12th innings and his average increases by 4. His new average is:
New average = 90 − 11 × 4 = 46, because the extra runs above the new average lift the 11 earlier innings by 4 each.
The average of three numbers is 20. When a fourth number is added, the average becomes 22. The fourth number is:
The new total is 4 × 22 = 88 and the old total is 60, so the fourth number is 28.
faqs: When should I use the deviation method instead of totals?

Use deviations when one value joins, leaves or is replaced and the change in average is small and given. It saves multiplication of large totals. When several groups merge, such as two sections of a class, totals are usually clearer and less error-prone.
Why is average speed not the simple mean of two speeds?

Because you spend more time at the slower speed when distances are equal. Average speed is total distance divided by total time, which gives the harmonic mean 2xy/(x + y). The simple mean applies only when equal time is spent at each speed.

items.title: Problems on Ages: Ratio Method and Solved Questions
items.description: Solve age problems with the ratio-of-differences method, one-variable equations and option checking, with worked father–son and family examples.
items.intro: Problems on ages are a steady single question in IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk, SSC CHSL and SSC MTS papers, and they occasionally appear as statements in data sufficiency. They are pure linear-equation questions dressed in family language. The fastest approach combines one key fact — the age gap between two people never changes — with option elimination, so many questions can be solved without writing an equation at all.

concepts.heading: The constant gap
concepts.text: Two people age at the same rate, so the difference in their ages is fixed forever. If a father is 30 years older than his son today, he was 30 years older ten years ago and will be 30 years older in twenty years. Many ratio-change questions are solved by matching this gap across two ratios.

concepts.heading: Ratio-difference method
concepts.text: If present ages are 4 : 5 and after 6 years they become 5 : 6, both ratios have a difference of 1 part. Hence 1 part in the first ratio equals 1 part in the second, and the change of 1 part (from 4 to 5) equals the 6 years. So 1 part = 6 years and present ages are 24 and 30.

concepts.heading: Writing equations
concepts.text: Let the unknown present age be x. "n years ago" means subtract n from each person, "after n years" means add n to each. Always shift every person in the question, not just one. Then form the equation from the statement and solve.
concepts.formula: Age t years ago = present age − t

concepts.heading: Average-age questions
concepts.text: When a family’s average age is given at one time and asked at another, multiply by the number of members, add the years passed for each member, and handle newborns separately because a child born later contributes only its own age.

shortcuts: Check options against both conditions — most age questions have one option that fits quickly.
If A is k times B now, the gap = (k − 1) × B’s age. Use it to cross-check.
For n children born at equal intervals of d years with sum S, the youngest = (S − d × n(n − 1)/2) ÷ n.
Present ages in ratio a : b with sum S give ages aS/(a + b) and bS/(a + b).
A ratio can only increase towards 1 as time passes; if a future ratio is further from 1, re-read the question.

examples.question: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 4 : 5. After 6 years, the ratio will be 5 : 6. Find their present ages.
examples.solution: Both ratios have a difference of 1 part, so the parts are directly comparable. A moves from 4 parts to 5 parts in 6 years, so 1 part = 6 years. Present ages: 24 and 30. Check: 30/36 = 5/6.

examples.question: A father is three times as old as his son. After 15 years, he will be twice as old as his son. Find their present ages.
examples.solution: Let the son be s. Then 3s + 15 = 2(s + 15), so s = 15 and the father is 45. The gap of 30 years stays constant: after 15 years they are 30 and 60.

examples.question: The sum of the ages of 5 children born at intervals of 3 years each is 50 years. Find the age of the youngest.
examples.solution: Ages are x, x + 3, x + 6, x + 9, x + 12, so 5x + 30 = 50 and x = 4 years.

examples.question: Ten years ago, A was half of B in age. The ratio of their present ages is 3 : 4. What are their present ages?
examples.solution: Present ages 3x and 4x. Ten years ago: 3x − 10 = (4x − 10)/2, so 6x − 20 = 4x − 10 and x = 5. Present ages: 15 and 20 years. Check: ten years ago they were 5 and 10.

practice: The present ages of two brothers are in the ratio 5 : 7 and their sum is 48 years. What will be the elder brother’s age after 5 years?
28 years
33 years
25 years
35 years
The ages are 20 and 28 years, so the elder brother will be 28 + 5 = 33 years old.
A mother is four times as old as her daughter. In 5 years she will be three times as old. The mother’s present age is:
36 years
44 years
40 years
32 years
With daughter d, 4d + 5 = 3(d + 5) gives d = 10, so the mother is 40 years old.
Eight years ago, A was three times as old as B. Now A is twice as old as B. A’s present age is:
24 years
16 years
36 years
32 years
With A = 2B, 2B − 8 = 3(B − 8) gives B = 16, so A is 32 years old today.
At their marriage, the average age of a husband and wife was 23 years. Five years later, with a 1-year-old child, the family’s average age is:
18 years
20 years
19 years
21 years
The couple total 46 + 10 = 56 after five years, plus the child’s 1 gives 57, and 57 ÷ 3 = 19.
The sum of the present ages of a father and son is 60 years. Six years ago, the father was five times as old as the son. The son’s present age is:
14 years
12 years
16 years
10 years
From F + S = 60 and F − 6 = 5(S − 6), we get 6S = 84, so the son is 14 years old.
faqs: Can age problems be solved without algebra?

Often yes. The ratio-difference method and option checking handle most bank-exam age questions. Algebra is still the safest fallback when the statement involves three people or both past and future conditions. Use whichever is faster for the specific wording.
Why do age problems appear in data sufficiency?

Because each statement gives one relation, and setters can test whether two relations are independent. For example, a ratio and a sum together fix the ages, while two ratios at the same moment may not. Practising equations helps you judge sufficiency quickly.

items.title: Partnership Problems: Profit Sharing by Capital and Time
items.description: Share business profit by capital × time, handle late joiners, withdrawals and working-partner salaries, with solved partnership questions.
items.intro: Partnership questions ask how a business profit is shared when partners invest different amounts for different periods. IBPS PO, SBI Clerk and RBI Grade B prelims usually include one, and they are common in DI caselets where several partners join or withdraw during a year. The whole chapter rests on a single rule — profit is shared in the ratio of capital multiplied by time — plus careful book-keeping for changes during the year.

concepts.heading: Capital × time
concepts.text: Each partner’s share of profit is proportional to the product of capital and the number of months it was invested. ₹50,000 for 12 months has weight 6,00,000; ₹40,000 for 9 months has weight 3,60,000. The ratio 5 : 3 decides how profit is split.
concepts.formula: Profit ratio = C1 × T1 : C2 × T2

concepts.heading: Changes during the year
concepts.text: If a partner adds or withdraws capital mid-year, split their investment into periods. A partner who starts with ₹20,000 and withdraws ₹5,000 after 6 months has an effective weight of 20,000 × 6 + 15,000 × 6. Add the pieces for each partner before forming the ratio.

concepts.heading: Working partners
concepts.text: Sometimes one partner gets a salary or a fixed percentage of profit for managing the business. Deduct that amount first, then divide the remainder in the capital-time ratio, and finally add the salary back to the working partner’s share.

concepts.heading: Finding time or capital
concepts.text: If the profit ratio and capital ratio are given, the time ratio = profit ratio ÷ capital ratio term by term. Capitals 3 : 5 with profits 9 : 10 give times (9/3) : (10/5) = 3 : 2.

shortcuts: Drop common zeros: ₹45,000 and ₹30,000 become 45 and 30 before multiplying by months.
If everyone invests for the same period, ignore time and use capitals alone.
Late joiner: a partner joining after k months invests for (12 − k) months in a one-year business.
Check: the shares must add to the total profit — a fast way to catch a slip.
If two partners have equal capital × time, they share equally, even with very different capitals.

examples.question: A invests ₹50,000 for 12 months and B invests ₹40,000 for 9 months. The profit is ₹24,000. Find B’s share.
A starts a business with ₹30,000. After 4 months B joins with ₹45,000. At the end of the year the profit is ₹17,000. How is it shared?
examples.solution: A: 30 × 12 = 360; B: 45 × 8 = 360. The ratio is 1 : 1, so each gets ₹8,500 despite B’s larger capital.

examples.question: A and B invest in the ratio 2 : 3. A, the working partner, gets 10% of the profit as salary. If the total profit is ₹50,000, find each partner’s total receipt.
examples.solution: Salary = ₹5,000. Remaining ₹45,000 is divided 2 : 3, giving ₹18,000 and ₹27,000. A receives 5,000 + 18,000 = ₹23,000 and B receives ₹27,000.

examples.question: A invests ₹20,000 and withdraws ₹5,000 after 6 months. B invests ₹15,000 for the whole year. Share a profit of ₹39,000.
A, B and C start a business with ₹20,000, ₹30,000 and ₹40,000. After 6 months, A doubles his capital. Find C’s share of a yearly profit of ₹54,000.

practice: A and B invest ₹15,000 and ₹25,000 for the same period. Out of a profit of ₹16,000, B gets:
The ratio is 15 : 25 = 3 : 5, so B receives 5/8 × 16,000 = ₹10,000 of the profit.
A invests ₹40,000 for 12 months and B invests ₹60,000 for 6 months. Out of a profit of ₹14,000, A gets:
Capitals of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 5 and their profits are in the ratio 9 : 10. The ratio of their investment periods is:
Time ratio = (9/3) : (10/5) = 3 : 2, since profit equals capital multiplied by time.
A starts with ₹24,000. B joins after 3 months with ₹32,000. Out of a yearly profit of ₹13,200, B gets:
A has 24 × 12 = 288 and B has 32 × 9 = 288, so they share equally: ₹6,600 each.
A, B and C invest in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5 for the same period. Out of a profit of ₹45,000, C gets:
C’s share is 5/10 of the total profit, which is half of ₹45,000, or ₹22,500.
faqs: Do partnership questions use months or years?

Either works as long as all partners use the same unit. Months are more convenient because partners often join or leave mid-year. If the business runs for more than a year, count the total months each capital was in use.
What if interest on capital is also given?

Treat interest on capital like a salary: calculate it for each partner first, deduct the total from profit, and then share the remainder in the agreed ratio. Each partner finally receives interest plus their share of the remaining profit.

items.title: Mixtures and Alligation Rule with Solved Examples
items.description: Use the alligation cross to mix two prices or concentrations, adjust milk–water ratios and combine vessels, with worked bank and SSC questions.
items.intro: Mixtures and alligation is a high-value topic in IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B, where it often carries one or two questions, and in SSC CGL. Alligation is really a weighted-average shortcut, so the same cross diagram solves problems on grocery prices, milk and water, alloys, average marks of boys and girls, and even interest rates on split investments. Learning to spot the "two groups and one mean" structure is the key skill.

concepts.heading: The alligation rule
concepts.text: When two ingredients with values c (cheaper) and d (dearer) are mixed to get a mean value m, they must be in the ratio (d − m) : (m − c). The value can be price per kg, percentage of milk, marks or speed — anything that averages by weight.

concepts.heading: Adding a pure component
concepts.text: If water is added to a milk–water mixture, the quantity of milk does not change. Find milk first, use the target ratio to find the required water, and subtract the water already present. This avoids setting up an equation.

concepts.heading: Mixing with a profit
concepts.text: When a mixture is sold at a price that includes profit, first remove the profit to get the mixture’s cost price. Only then apply alligation. Selling at ₹60 with 20% profit means the mixture costs ₹50 per kg.

concepts.heading: Combining vessels
concepts.text: For two vessels with different ratios mixed in equal quantity, convert each ratio to a fraction of milk (3 : 1 means 3/4 milk) and average the fractions. For unequal quantities, use weighted averages of these fractions.

shortcuts: Write the cross: c and d on top, m in the middle, (d − m) and (m − c) below — the bottom numbers give the ratio.
The mean must lie between the two values; if it does not, re-read the question.
Alligation works for averages of groups too: class averages 60 (boys) and 75 (girls) with overall 66 give boys : girls = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2.
To mix equal quantities, the mean is the simple average of the two values.
Convert ratios to fractions of the whole (e.g. 7 : 3 → 70% milk) to apply alligation directly.

examples.question: In what ratio must rice at ₹40 per kg be mixed with rice at ₹55 per kg to get a mixture worth ₹50 per kg?
A 40-litre mixture has milk and water in the ratio 5 : 3. How much water must be added to make the ratio 1 : 1?
examples.solution: Milk = 25 L, water = 15 L. For 1 : 1, water must equal 25 L, so add 10 litres.

examples.question: A shopkeeper mixes tea costing ₹45 per kg and ₹60 per kg and sells the mixture at ₹60 per kg, gaining 20%. Find the mixing ratio.
examples.solution: Cost of mixture = 60 ÷ 1.2 = ₹50 per kg. Ratio = (60 − 50) : (50 − 45) = 10 : 5 = 2 : 1, cheaper to dearer.

examples.question: Two vessels contain milk and water in ratios 3 : 1 and 5 : 3. Equal quantities are mixed. Find the ratio of milk to water in the new mixture.
examples.solution: Milk fractions are 3/4 = 6/8 and 5/8. Average = (6/8 + 5/8)/2 = 11/16. So milk : water = 11 : 5.

practice: In what ratio must sugar at ₹30 per kg be mixed with sugar at ₹45 per kg to get a mixture worth ₹36 per kg?
Cheaper : dearer = (45 − 36) : (36 − 30) = 9 : 6, which simplifies to 3 : 2.
60 litres of a mixture contain milk and water in the ratio 7 : 3. How much water must be added to make the ratio 7 : 5?
10 litres
15 litres
12 litres
8 litres
Milk is 42 L, so water must become 30 L; it is 18 L now, so 12 L of water is added.
Sugar at ₹60 per kg and ₹80 per kg is mixed in the ratio 2 : 3. The cost of the mixture per kg is:
Vessel A has milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1 and vessel B in the ratio 4 : 1. Equal quantities are mixed. The milk-to-water ratio is:
Milk fractions are 2/3 and 4/5; their average is 11/15, so milk : water = 11 : 4.
In a class of 50, boys average 60 marks and girls average 75 marks. The class average is 66. How many boys are there?
Boys : girls = (75 − 66) : (66 − 60) = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2, so boys are 3/5 of 50, which is 30.
faqs: Can alligation be used for simple interest problems?

Yes. If a sum is lent partly at 6% and partly at 9% and the overall rate is 7.5%, alligation gives the ratio of the two parts directly: (9 − 7.5) : (7.5 − 6) = 1 : 1. Any problem with two groups and one weighted average fits.
Which value goes on which side of the alligation cross?

Put the lower value on the left and the higher on the right with the mean in the middle. The difference on the left of the bottom row belongs to the cheaper item. If you swap them, you get the inverse ratio, which is a common trap answer.

items.title: Replacement Problems in Mixtures: Repeated Dilution Formula
items.description: Repeated removal and replacement of liquid explained with the (1 − x/V)ⁿ formula, reverse questions and partial-concentration swaps, with examples.
items.intro: Replacement questions — where some liquid is drawn out and replaced with water again and again — are a distinct sub-type of mixtures that IBPS PO, SBI PO and SSC CGL setters like because the naive approach (subtracting the same amount each time) gives a wrong answer that always appears among the options. One compact formula handles every version, and the reverse form helps find how much was drawn each time.

concepts.heading: Why repeated removal is multiplicative
concepts.text: Each time x litres are drawn from a vessel of V litres, the same fraction x/V of every component leaves. So the pure liquid remaining is multiplied by (1 − x/V) every round. After three rounds of removing 4 L from 40 L, milk = 40 × 0.9³ = 29.16 L, not 40 − 12 = 28 L.

concepts.heading: Ratio after replacement
concepts.text: Once the remaining pure liquid is known, the rest of the vessel is water (or the replacing liquid), because the volume stays at V. With 80 L of wine and 8 L replaced twice, wine = 64.8 L and water = 15.2 L, giving a ratio 81 : 19.

concepts.heading: Finding the quantity drawn
concepts.text: If the final amount is given, take the n-th root: (1 − x/V)ⁿ = final/initial. From 50 L of pure milk, two rounds leaving 32 L give (1 − x/50)² = 0.64, so 1 − x/50 = 0.8 and x = 10 L.

concepts.heading: Replacing with another mixture
concepts.text: If part of a 30% solution is replaced by a 15% solution to get 25%, use alligation on concentrations: replaced part : kept part = (30 − 25) : (25 − 15) = 1 : 2, so one-third was replaced.

shortcuts: Fraction left after n rounds is (1 − x/V)ⁿ; for x/V = 1/10, 1/5, 1/4 use 0.9, 0.8, 0.75 powers.
Exam numbers are chosen so that the root is clean: 0.64 → 0.8, 0.729 → 0.9, 0.5625 → 0.75.
If the replacing liquid is water, the ratio of milk to water after n rounds is (V − x)ⁿ : Vⁿ − (V − x)ⁿ.
The option equal to V − n × x is almost always the trap answer.

examples.question: A vessel has 40 litres of milk. 4 litres are taken out and replaced with water. This is done three times. How much milk is left?
From 80 litres of pure wine, 8 litres are drawn and replaced with water. The process is repeated once more. Find the ratio of wine to water.
A container has 50 litres of pure milk. A certain quantity is removed and replaced with water twice, leaving 32 litres of milk. How much was removed each time?
A jar is full of a 30% acid solution. Part of it is replaced by a 15% solution, and the strength becomes 25%. What fraction was replaced?
examples.solution: Replaced : kept = (30 − 25) : (25 − 15) = 5 : 10 = 1 : 2. So 1/3 of the solution was replaced.

examples.question: A 50-litre can holds milk and water in the ratio 4 : 1. Ten litres of the mixture are taken out and replaced with water. Find the new ratio.
examples.solution: Milk at the start = 40 L. Removing 10 of 50 litres takes away one-fifth of each component, so milk left = 40 × 0.8 = 32 L. Total volume is back to 50 L, so water = 18 L. New ratio = 32 : 18 = 16 : 9. The formula works on the milk component even when the starting liquid is already a mixture.

practice: A tank has 60 litres of milk. 6 litres are removed and replaced with water, twice. Milk left is:
48 litres
48.6 litres
49.2 litres
50.4 litres
Milk = 60 × 0.9² = 60 × 0.81 = 48.6 litres; subtracting 12 litres directly would be wrong.
From 100 litres of milk, 20 litres are replaced with water twice. The milk-to-water ratio becomes:
Milk = 100 × 0.8² = 64 L and water = 36 L, so the ratio is 64 : 36 = 16 : 9.
A 40-litre vessel of milk has x litres replaced with water twice, leaving 22.5 litres of milk. Find x.
10 litres
8 litres
12 litres
15 litres
Part of a 50% solution is replaced by a 20% solution, giving 30%. The fraction replaced is:
Replaced : kept = (50 − 30) : (30 − 20) = 2 : 1, so two-thirds of the solution was replaced.
From 25 litres of pure juice, 5 litres are replaced with water three times. Juice left is:
12.8 litres
10 litres
13.5 litres
12 litres
Juice = 25 × (1 − 5/25)³ = 25 × 0.512 = 12.8 litres after three rounds.
faqs: Why can’t I just subtract the quantity removed each time?

Because after the first round the vessel contains a mixture, so each later draw removes some water too. Only part of the drawn quantity is milk. The multiplicative formula accounts for this; simple subtraction overstates the milk removed.
Does the formula work if the vessel is not full?

It works as long as the total volume stays the same before each draw, because the fraction removed is x/V each time. If the volume changes between rounds, compute each round separately using that round’s volume.

items.title: Time and Work: LCM Method, Formulas and Solved Questions
items.description: Solve time and work questions with the LCM (total units) method, man-days formula and leaving-midway cases, plus five practice MCQs with answers.
items.intro: Time and work is one of the most predictable arithmetic topics: IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B prelims ask one or two questions, and SSC CGL and CHSL ask two or three. CAT uses the same ideas inside harder multi-stage problems. The fastest approach is to assume the total work as a convenient number of units (the LCM of the given days), which turns fractions into simple whole-number division.

concepts.heading: Work rate
concepts.text: If A finishes a job in 12 days, A does 1/12 of it per day. Rates add when people work together: A (12 days) and B (18 days) do 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 per day, so they finish in 36/5 = 7.2 days. Time taken = 1 ÷ combined rate.

concepts.heading: LCM or total-units method
concepts.text: Take the total work as the LCM of the individual days. For A = 20 days and B = 30 days, total = 60 units; A does 3 units a day and B does 2. Together they do 5 units, so the job takes 12 days. This avoids fractions entirely and makes leaving-midway questions easy.

concepts.heading: Man-days formula
concepts.text: Work is proportional to men × days × hours. If 12 men finish a job in 18 days, the job is 216 man-days, so 8 men need 27 days. When the amount of work also changes, divide each side by its work.

concepts.heading: Someone leaves or joins
concepts.text: Compute the work done in the joint period with the combined rate, subtract from total units, and let the remaining workers finish the rest at their rate. Always add the two time periods if total time is asked.

shortcuts: Two people: together time = ab/(a + b). For 10 and 15 days, 150/25 = 6 days.
If A + B take T days and A alone takes a days, B alone takes aT/(a − T) days.
Efficiency is the inverse of time: A twice as efficient as B means A takes half B’s time.
Three people with times a, b, c: use LCM units rather than the product formula; it is quicker and safer.
If the answer must be in days and hours, convert the fractional part: 0.2 of an 8-hour day is 1.6 hours.

examples.question: A can finish a task in 12 days and B in 18 days. How long will they take together?
examples.solution: Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days. LCM method: total 36 units, A does 3 and B does 2 per day, so 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2 days.

examples.question: A and B together can do a job in 8 days. A alone can do it in 12 days. How long would B take alone?
examples.solution: B’s rate = 1/8 − 1/12 = 1/24, so B alone takes 24 days. Using total 24 units: together 3 units a day, A 2 units, so B does 1 unit a day.

examples.question: A can do a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. They start together, but A leaves after 4 days. In how many days is the job finished?
examples.solution: Total = 30 units; A does 3, B does 2 per day. In 4 days together they do 20 units. B finishes the remaining 10 units in 5 days. Total time = 9 days.

examples.question: 12 men can build a wall in 18 days. How many days will 8 men take to build the same wall?
examples.solution: Work = 12 × 18 = 216 man-days. Days for 8 men = 216 ÷ 8 = 27 days.

practice: A can complete a work in 10 days and B in 15 days. Working together, they finish in:
5 days
7.5 days
6 days
12.5 days
Using 30 units, A does 3 and B does 2 per day, so together 5 units a day finish 30 units in 6 days.
A and B together finish a job in 6 days. A alone takes 10 days. B alone takes:
12 days
16 days
4 days
15 days
B’s rate is 1/6 − 1/10 = 2/30 = 1/15, so B alone needs 15 days for the job.
15 men can finish a work in 16 days. How many days will 20 men take?
10 days
12 days
14 days
21 days
The work is 15 × 16 = 240 man-days, and 240 ÷ 20 = 12 days for twenty men.
A, B and C can do a job in 24, 36 and 72 days respectively. Working together, they finish in:
10 days
15 days
12 days
18 days
Total 72 units; daily output is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 units, so the job takes 72 ÷ 6 = 12 days.
A is twice as efficient as B. Together they finish a job in 14 days. B alone would take:
42 days
28 days
21 days
36 days
Efficiencies are 2 : 1, so total work = 3 × 14 = 42 units and B at 1 unit a day needs 42 days.
faqs: Is the LCM method allowed in exams?

Yes — the exam only checks the final answer. The LCM method is simply a way of choosing a convenient size for the total work so that daily outputs are whole numbers. It gives the same answer as the fraction method, usually faster and with fewer errors.
How are pipes and cisterns related to time and work?

They use exactly the same logic. A filling pipe is like a worker adding work, and an outlet or leak is like a worker undoing work, so its rate is subtracted. Practising one topic automatically builds speed in the other.

items.title: Work Efficiency, Wages and Alternate-Day Work Problems
items.description: Share wages in proportion to work done, compare men and women efficiency, and solve alternate-day and percentage-efficiency work questions.
items.intro: Once basic time and work is comfortable, bank and SSC papers add a twist: payment shared among workers, men and women of different efficiency, or people who work on alternate days. These variants regularly appear in IBPS PO, SBI PO, RBI Grade B and SSC CGL, and they are also good quantity-comparison material. All of them reduce to one idea — measure everything in units of work per day.

concepts.heading: Wages follow work, not time
concepts.text: When workers are paid jointly for a job, each person’s share is proportional to the work they did. If everyone worked for the same number of days, the share is proportional to efficiency, which is the inverse of their individual time. A (10 days) and B (15 days) working together share in the ratio 3 : 2.

concepts.heading: Helper problems
concepts.text: When a third person C helps A and B finish in fewer days, compute what fraction of the job A and B did in those days; the rest was C’s work, and C’s wage is that fraction of the total payment.

concepts.heading: Men, women and children
concepts.text: Convert everyone to one unit. "2 men or 3 women can finish a job in 12 days" means 1 man = 1.5 women. Then 4 men + 6 women = 12 women-equivalents, and since 3 women need 12 days (36 woman-days), 12 women need 3 days.

concepts.heading: Percentage efficiency
concepts.text: If A is 40% more efficient than B, A’s efficiency : B’s = 140 : 100 = 7 : 5, so time is in the ratio 5 : 7. If B takes 21 days, A takes 15 days.
concepts.formula: Time ratio = inverse of efficiency ratio

concepts.heading: Alternate days
concepts.text: When A and B work on alternate days starting with A, treat a two-day block as one cycle and count full cycles, then handle the final day carefully: the last person may need only part of a day.

shortcuts: Share of wages = (days worked ÷ individual time) × total wage.
For "x% more efficient", time of the efficient worker = original time × 100/(100 + x).
In alternate-day questions, stop the cycle count before the work overshoots and finish with a partial day.
If the units fit exactly after an odd number of days, the person who started also finishes.

examples.question: A can do a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. Working together they earn ₹5,000. How much does A get?
examples.solution: Efficiencies are 3 : 2 on 30 units. A’s share = 3/5 × 5,000 = ₹3,000.

examples.question: A can finish a job in 6 days and B in 8 days. With C’s help they finish in 3 days and are paid ₹6,400. Find each person’s share.
examples.solution: A does 3/6 = 1/2 of the job and B does 3/8. C does 1 − 1/2 − 3/8 = 1/8. Shares: A ₹3,200, B ₹2,400, C ₹800.

examples.question: 2 men or 3 women can complete a job in 12 days. How long will 4 men and 6 women take?
examples.solution: 1 man = 1.5 women, so 4 men + 6 women = 12 women. The job is 3 × 12 = 36 woman-days, so 12 women need 3 days.

examples.question: A is 40% more efficient than B. If B takes 21 days to finish a job, how long does A take?
examples.solution: Efficiency ratio 7 : 5 means time ratio 5 : 7. A’s time = 21 × 5/7 = 15 days.

examples.question: A can do a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. When will the job be completed?
examples.solution: Total 36 units; A does 3, B does 2. Each 2-day cycle gives 5 units. After 7 cycles (14 days), 35 units are done. On day 15, A needs only 1 unit, i.e. 1/3 of a day. Total = 14⅓ days.

practice: A can do a work in 12 days and B in 24 days. Working together, they are paid ₹1,800. A’s share is:
Efficiencies are 2 : 1 for 12 and 24 days, so A gets 2/3 × 1,800 = ₹1,200 of the payment.
A is 50% more efficient than B. If B takes 30 days to finish a job, A alone takes:
15 days
20 days
45 days
25 days
Efficiency 3 : 2 means time 2 : 3, so A takes 30 × 2/3 = 20 days for the job.
3 men or 5 women can finish a job in 30 days. How many days will 6 men and 5 women take?
10 days
12 days
9 days
15 days
5 women equal 3 men, so the team is 9 men; the job is 90 man-days, so 9 men need 10 days.
A can do a job in 6 days and B in 9 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. The job is finished in:
7.5 days
7 days
8 days
6.5 days
On 18 units, A does 3 and B does 2; three cycles give 15 units in 6 days and A finishes 3 units on day 7.
A and B can finish a job in 10 and 15 days. With C they finish it in 4 days and receive ₹3,000. C’s share is:
A does 4/10 and B does 4/15 of the job, worth ₹1,200 and ₹800, so C earns the remaining ₹1,000.
faqs: Why are wages not shared by days worked?

Because two people working the same days may produce very different amounts of work. Fair payment is for output. Only when all workers are equally efficient do days worked and work done give the same ratio. Exams always intend payment by work done unless stated otherwise.
Does the starting person matter in alternate-day problems?

Yes, it can change the answer when the job does not finish at the end of a full cycle. If the faster worker starts, the job may finish sooner. Always check which worker is on duty on the final day and use their rate for the partial day.

items.title: Pipes and Cisterns: Inlet, Outlet and Leak Problems
items.description: Pipes and cisterns tricks for filling and emptying pipes, leaks and pipes closed midway, using the capacity-units method, with solved examples.
items.intro: Pipes and cisterns is the time-and-work chapter with water tanks. IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and SSC CHSL ask it as a single question, while IBPS PO and RBI Grade B use it in quantity comparison and occasionally in caselet form. The only new idea is negative work: an outlet pipe or a leak empties the tank, so its rate is subtracted from the filling pipes.

concepts.heading: Rates and signs
concepts.text: A pipe that fills a tank in 20 hours adds 1/20 of the tank per hour; a pipe that empties it in 30 hours removes 1/30 per hour. When pipes run together, add inlet rates and subtract outlet rates. If the net rate is negative, the tank empties.
concepts.formula: Net rate = Σ inlet rates − Σ outlet rates

concepts.heading: Capacity-units method
concepts.text: Assume the tank capacity as the LCM of the given times. For pipes of 10 and 15 hours with an outlet of 30 hours, take 30 units: the inlets add 3 and 2 units per hour, the outlet removes 1. Net 4 units an hour fills 30 units in 7.5 hours.

concepts.heading: Leaks
concepts.text: If a pipe alone fills a tank in 8 hours but takes 10 hours because of a leak, the leak’s rate is 1/8 − 1/10 = 1/40. The leak alone would empty a full tank in 40 hours.

concepts.heading: Pipes closed or opened later
concepts.text: Split the time into phases. Find how much is filled in the first phase with all open pipes, subtract from capacity, and let the remaining pipes complete the rest. Add the phases for the total time.

shortcuts: Two inlets with times a and b fill together in ab/(a + b); an inlet a with outlet b (b > a) fills in ab/(b − a).
If a tank is half full, only half the capacity units need filling — a common trap.
When an outlet is faster than the inlets, the answer is the time to empty, not to fill.
Use capacity in litres only if the question gives litres; otherwise units are enough.
For "cistern fills in x hours with leak", leak rate = 1/(normal time) − 1/x.

examples.question: Pipe A fills a tank in 20 hours and pipe B in 30 hours. How long will both together take?
examples.solution: Capacity 60 units; A adds 3, B adds 2 per hour. Together 5 units an hour, so 60 ÷ 5 = 12 hours.

examples.question: A pipe fills a tank in 12 hours and another empties it in 18 hours. If both are opened, when will the tank be full?
examples.solution: Net rate = 1/12 − 1/18 = 1/36. The tank fills in 36 hours.

examples.question: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 10 and 15 hours; pipe C empties it in 30 hours. All three are opened together. Find the time to fill.
examples.solution: Capacity 30 units: 3 + 2 − 1 = 4 units per hour, so 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5 hours.

examples.question: A pipe normally fills a tank in 8 hours, but because of a leak it takes 10 hours. How long would the leak take to empty a full tank?
examples.solution: Leak rate = 1/8 − 1/10 = 1/40, so the leak empties the tank in 40 hours.

examples.question: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 16 and 24 minutes. Both are opened, and B is closed after 6 minutes. How long does it take in all to fill the tank?
examples.solution: Capacity 48 units; A adds 3, B adds 2 per minute. In 6 minutes both fill 30 units. A fills the remaining 18 units in 6 minutes. Total = 12 minutes.

practice: Two pipes fill a tank in 15 hours and 10 hours. Together they fill it in:
12.5 hours
5 hours
7.5 hours
6 hours
Capacity 30 units; the pipes add 2 and 3 units an hour, so 30 ÷ 5 = 6 hours together.
An inlet fills a tank in 6 hours and an outlet empties it in 9 hours. With both open, the tank fills in:
15 hours
3 hours
12 hours
18 hours
Net rate = 1/6 − 1/9 = 1/18 of the tank per hour, so it fills in 18 hours.
A pipe fills a tank in 5 hours, but a leak makes it take 6 hours. The leak alone empties the full tank in:
11 hours
25 hours
30 hours
36 hours
Leak rate = 1/5 − 1/6 = 1/30, so the leak alone needs 30 hours to empty the full tank.
Pipes A and B fill a tank in 12 and 15 hours, and pipe C empties it in 20 hours. With all three open, the tank fills in:
8 hours
10 hours
12 hours
9 hours
On 60 units, the net hourly rate is 5 + 4 − 3 = 6 units, so the tank fills in 10 hours.
Pipes A and B fill a tank in 20 and 30 minutes. Both are opened and A is closed after 5 minutes. The total time to fill the tank is:
22.5 minutes
20 minutes
25 minutes
17.5 minutes
On 60 units, both fill 25 units in 5 minutes; B then fills 35 units at 2 per minute in 17.5 minutes.
faqs: Is a leak the same as an outlet pipe?

Mathematically, yes: both remove water at a fixed rate and their rates are subtracted. The wording differs only in how the information is given. A leak is usually described indirectly, through the extra time it causes, so you have to compute its rate first.
What if the net rate comes out negative?

Then the tank cannot be filled; it will empty instead. If the tank starts full, the time to empty is capacity divided by the net outflow rate. Some questions deliberately set this up to test whether you notice the sign.

items.title: Speed, Time and Distance Formulas and Shortcut Tricks
items.description: Speed, time and distance basics: unit conversion, late-and-early problems, relative speed, meeting points and average speed with worked examples.
items.intro: Speed, time and distance (STD) is the parent chapter for trains, boats and races, so mastering it pays off several times over. IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B include one or two STD-family questions in prelims, SSC CGL includes two or three, and CAT tests the ideas in tougher multi-stage problems.
