Most questions need just three tools: the D = S × T relation, inverse proportion between speed and time, and relative speed.

concepts.heading: The core relation
concepts.text: Distance = Speed × Time. Keep units consistent: convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18 and m/s to km/h by multiplying by 18/5. So 72 km/h = 20 m/s and 15 m/s = 54 km/h. Minutes must be converted to hours (15 minutes = 1/4 hour) when speed is in km/h.

concepts.heading: Speed and time are inversely proportional
concepts.text: For a fixed distance, if speed becomes a/b of the usual, time becomes b/a of the usual. If a person walks at 3/4 of usual speed and is 20 minutes late, the time becomes 4/3 of usual, so the extra 1/3 equals 20 minutes and the usual time is 60 minutes.

concepts.heading: Relative speed
concepts.text: Two objects moving towards each other close the gap at the sum of their speeds; moving in the same direction, at the difference. Cars starting 200 km apart at 45 and 55 km/h towards each other meet after 200 ÷ 100 = 2 hours.
concepts.formula: Opposite: S1 + S2;  Same: S1 − S2

concepts.heading: Average speed
concepts.text: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. For equal distances at speeds x, y and z, it is the harmonic mean 3/(1/x + 1/y + 1/z). For two equal distances it reduces to 2xy/(x + y).

shortcuts: Late-and-early problems: distance = (product of speeds ÷ difference of speeds) × total time difference.
If two people start together and one reaches t hours early, compare their times, not speeds.
For meeting problems, the ratio of distances covered equals the ratio of speeds.
Average speed is always closer to the lower speed when distances are equal.

examples.question: A man walking at 5 km/h reaches his office 10 minutes late. Walking at 6 km/h, he reaches 5 minutes early. Find the distance.
examples.solution: The time difference is 15 minutes = 1/4 hour. d/5 − d/6 = 1/4 gives d/30 = 1/4, so d = 7.5 km. Shortcut: (5 × 6 ÷ 1) × 1/4 = 7.5 km.

examples.question: Delhi and Agra are about 200 km apart. Two cars leave the two cities towards each other at 45 km/h and 55 km/h. When do they meet?
examples.solution: Relative speed = 100 km/h, so they meet after 2 hours. The first car covers 90 km and the second 110 km.

examples.question: Walking at 3/4 of his usual speed, a man is 20 minutes late. What is his usual time?
examples.solution: New time = 4/3 of usual, so the extra 1/3 of usual time = 20 minutes. Usual time = 60 minutes.

examples.question: A cyclist covers three equal stretches at 30, 40 and 60 km/h. Find the average speed.
examples.solution: Take each stretch as 120 km (LCM). Times are 4, 3 and 2 hours. Total 360 km in 9 hours gives 40 km/h.

examples.question: Asha leaves home on a scooter at 10 km/h. Two hours later her brother follows on a bike at 15 km/h along the same road. When and where does he catch her?
examples.solution: In 2 hours Asha has a 20 km head start. The gap closes at the relative speed 15 − 10 = 5 km/h, so it takes 20 ÷ 5 = 4 hours after the brother starts. He catches her 15 × 4 = 60 km from home. Check: Asha has ridden 6 hours × 10 km/h = 60 km.

practice: A speed of 54 km/h equals:
12 m/s
15 m/s
18 m/s
Multiply by 5/18: 54 × 5/18 = 15 metres per second, a standard conversion worth memorising.
A bus covers 360 km in 4 hours 30 minutes. Its average speed is:
75 km/h
90 km/h
72 km/h
80 km/h
Speed = 360 ÷ 4.5 = 80 km/h, after converting 30 minutes to half an hour.
Walking at 4 km/h a student is 10 minutes late; at 5 km/h he is 5 minutes early. The distance is:
4 km
6 km
5 km
7.5 km
d/4 − d/5 = 15/60 hour, so d/20 = 1/4 and the distance is 5 km.
Two cars start 300 km apart and drive towards each other at 70 km/h and 80 km/h. They meet after:
2 hours
2.5 hours
1.5 hours
3 hours
Relative speed is 70 + 80 = 150 km/h, so the gap of 300 km closes in 2 hours.
Travelling at 4/5 of his usual speed, a man is 15 minutes late. His usual time is:
45 minutes
60 minutes
75 minutes
50 minutes
Time becomes 5/4 of usual, so the extra 1/4 equals 15 minutes and the usual time is 60 minutes.
faqs: Should I always convert to m/s?

Only when lengths are in metres and time in seconds, as in train problems. If distances are in km and times in hours, stay in km/h. Converting unnecessarily adds steps and errors. Choose the unit system of the answer options.
What is the quickest way to solve meeting-point questions?

Use relative speed for the meeting time, then multiply each speed by that time for the distances. Alternatively, split the total distance in the ratio of speeds. Both methods avoid setting up two equations.

items.title: Problems on Trains: Crossing Poles, Platforms and Trains
items.description: Train problems explained: crossing a pole, platform, man or another train, same and opposite direction, with km/h to m/s conversions and examples.
items.intro: Train questions are a special case of speed and distance where the moving object has length. IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and SSC CHSL/CGL nearly always include one, and Indian Railways settings — a Rajdhani crossing a platform, two trains on parallel tracks — make them easy to picture. The trick is to decide what distance is covered (train length alone, or train plus something else) and which speed applies (actual or relative).

concepts.heading: Crossing a point object
concepts.text: When a train passes a pole, a signal post or a standing man, it covers its own length. A 240 m train at 72 km/h (20 m/s) passes a pole in 240 ÷ 20 = 12 seconds.

concepts.heading: Crossing a platform or bridge
concepts.text: The train must cover its own length plus the platform’s length. The same 240 m train crosses a 360 m platform in (240 + 360) ÷ 20 = 30 seconds.

concepts.heading: Two trains
concepts.text: Two trains crossing each other cover the sum of their lengths. Use the sum of speeds if they move in opposite directions and the difference if they move in the same direction (overtaking).

concepts.heading: Moving man or car
concepts.text: A man walking or a car has negligible length, so the distance is the train’s length, but the speed is relative: train speed minus man’s speed if they move in the same direction, plus if opposite.

shortcuts: If a train passes a pole in t1 and a platform of length P in t2, its speed = P/(t2 − t1) and its length = speed × t1.
Two trains of the same length crossing in opposite directions: each covers one length in the crossing time at half the relative speed.
A man sitting in a train sees the other train pass in (length of the other train) ÷ relative speed — his own train’s length is irrelevant.

examples.question: A 240 m long train runs at 72 km/h. How long does it take to pass a pole and to cross a 360 m platform?
Two trains, 150 m and 100 m long, run in opposite directions at 50 km/h and 40 km/h. How long do they take to cross each other?
examples.solution: Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Distance = 250 m. Time = 10 seconds.

examples.question: A 120 m train at 72 km/h overtakes a 130 m train running at 54 km/h on a parallel track. How long does overtaking take?
examples.solution: Relative speed = 72 − 54 = 18 km/h = 5 m/s. Distance = 250 m. Time = 50 seconds.

examples.question: A train at 60 km/h passes a man walking at 6 km/h in the same direction in 9 seconds. Find the train’s length.
examples.solution: Relative speed = 54 km/h = 15 m/s. Length = 15 × 9 = 135 m.

examples.question: A train passes a pole in 15 seconds and a 100 m platform in 25 seconds. Find its speed and length.
examples.solution: The extra 10 seconds are needed for the 100 m platform, so speed = 10 m/s (36 km/h). Length = 10 × 15 = 150 m.

examples.question: Two trains, each 120 m long, run in opposite directions on parallel tracks and cross each other in 8 seconds. One train runs at 54 km/h. Find the speed of the other.
examples.solution: Total length 240 m in 8 s gives a relative speed of 30 m/s. One train runs at 15 m/s, so the other also runs at 15 m/s, i.e. 54 km/h. When the lengths and crossing time are given, always find the relative speed first and then split it.

practice: A 180 m long train running at 54 km/h passes a pole in:
10 seconds
15 seconds
12 seconds
9 seconds
54 km/h equals 15 m/s, so the train covers its 180 m length in 12 seconds.
A 300 m train at 90 km/h crosses a 200 m bridge in:
12 seconds
18 seconds
25 seconds
20 seconds
Distance is 300 + 200 = 500 m at 25 m/s, which takes 20 seconds to cover.
Two trains 140 m and 160 m long run in opposite directions at 60 km/h and 48 km/h. They cross each other in:
10 seconds
12 seconds
9 seconds
15 seconds
Relative speed is 108 km/h = 30 m/s, and 300 m ÷ 30 = 10 seconds to cross.
A train passes a pole in 12 seconds and a 180 m platform in 24 seconds. Its length is:
The platform adds 12 seconds, so speed = 180/12 = 15 m/s and length = 15 × 12 = 180 m.
A 200 m train at 90 km/h overtakes a 160 m train at 72 km/h moving in the same direction. Overtaking takes:
20 seconds
36 seconds
72 seconds
60 seconds
Relative speed is 18 km/h = 5 m/s, and the total length of 360 m takes 72 seconds.
faqs: Why is the platform length added when a train crosses it?

Crossing is complete only when the last coach leaves the far end of the platform. From the moment the engine enters to that moment, the engine travels the platform length plus the whole train length. That total is the distance used in the formula.
Do I subtract speeds when a train passes a man walking towards it?

No. If they move towards each other, their speeds add. Subtract only when both move in the same direction. Read the direction carefully because both versions appear and the options usually include the wrong-sign answer.

items.title: Boats and Streams: Upstream and Downstream Formulas
items.description: Boats and streams formulas for upstream, downstream, speed in still water and round trips, with solved examples and practice MCQs for bank exams.
items.intro: Boats and streams questions appear in nearly every IBPS PO, SBI PO and SBI Clerk prelims paper, often as a quantity comparison or a two-part word problem. SSC CGL also asks one regularly. The setting is simple — a boat or swimmer moving with or against a river current — and all questions rest on two speeds: downstream and upstream. Once those are written down, most problems become simple speed–time calculations.

concepts.heading: Downstream and upstream speeds
concepts.text: If a boat’s speed in still water is b and the stream’s speed is s, then downstream speed D = b + s and upstream speed U = b − s. The current helps going down and opposes going up.
concepts.formula: D = b + s;  U = b − s

concepts.heading: Recovering b and s
concepts.text: Adding and subtracting the two equations gives b = (D + U)/2 and s = (D − U)/2. If a boat covers 30 km downstream in 2 hours (15 km/h) and 18 km upstream in 3 hours (6 km/h), then b = 10.5 km/h and s = 4.5 km/h.

concepts.heading: Round trips
concepts.text: For a trip of d km downstream and back, total time = d/(b + s) + d/(b − s). Because more time is spent going slowly upstream, the average speed for the round trip is less than b.

concepts.heading: Time-ratio questions
concepts.text: If going upstream takes k times as long as going downstream over the same distance, then (b + s) = k(b − s), so b : s = (k + 1) : (k − 1).

shortcuts: Write D and U first — every question becomes clear once both are known.
If upstream time is twice the downstream time, b : s = 3 : 1; if three times, 2 : 1.
Round-trip average speed = (b + s)(b − s)/b.
A floating object moves at the stream’s speed; a man rowing in still water moves at b.

examples.question: A boat’s speed in still water is 12 km/h and the stream flows at 3 km/h. How long does it take to go 45 km downstream and to come back?
examples.solution: D = 15 km/h, U = 9 km/h. Downstream 45 ÷ 15 = 3 hours; upstream 45 ÷ 9 = 5 hours.

examples.question: A boat covers 30 km downstream in 2 hours and 18 km upstream in 3 hours. Find the speed of the boat and of the stream.
A boat at 10 km/h in still water goes some distance downstream and returns in 5 hours in all. The stream speed is 2 km/h. Find the one-way distance.
examples.solution: D = 12 and U = 8 km/h. d/12 + d/8 = 5, so 5d/24 = 5 and d = 24 km.

examples.question: A man takes twice as long to row upstream as to row the same distance downstream. Find the ratio of the boat’s speed to the stream’s speed.
examples.solution: (b + s) = 2(b − s) gives b = 3s, so b : s = 3 : 1.

examples.question: A swimmer covers 4 km against the current in 1 hour and the same 4 km with the current in 40 minutes. Find her speed in still water and the speed of the current.
examples.solution: Upstream speed U = 4 km/h. Downstream speed D = 4 ÷ (40/60) = 6 km/h. So b = (6 + 4)/2 = 5 km/h and s = (6 − 4)/2 = 1 km/h. Converting 40 minutes into 2/3 hour before dividing is the step most students rush.

examples.question: A ferry goes 40 km downstream in 4 hours and returns 24 km upstream in the same time. How long would it take to cover 32 km in still water?
examples.solution: D = 40/4 = 10 km/h and U = 24/4 = 6 km/h, so b = 8 km/h. In still water 32 km takes 32 ÷ 8 = 4 hours. The stream speed of 2 km/h is not needed for this part, though setters often ask it as a follow-up.

practice: A boat’s speed in still water is 15 km/h and the stream flows at 3 km/h. Time to travel 72 km downstream is:
5 hours
6 hours
4.8 hours
4 hours
Downstream speed is 15 + 3 = 18 km/h, and 72 ÷ 18 = 4 hours for the trip.
A boat’s downstream speed is 16 km/h and upstream speed is 10 km/h. The speed of the stream is:
6 km/h
3 km/h
13 km/h
2 km/h
Stream speed = (D − U)/2 = (16 − 10)/2 = 3 km/h, half the gap between the two speeds.
A boat runs at 9 km/h in still water; the stream flows at 3 km/h. A round trip takes 6 hours. The one-way distance is:
18 km
24 km
27 km
30 km
D = 12 and U = 6, so d/12 + d/6 = d/4 = 6 hours, giving a one-way distance of 24 km.
Rowing upstream takes three times as long as rowing the same distance downstream. The ratio of boat speed to stream speed is:
b + s = 3(b − s) gives 2b = 4s, so b = 2s and the ratio is 2 : 1.
A man rows at 5 km/h in still water and takes twice as long to go upstream as downstream. The stream’s speed is:
2 km/h
5/2 km/h
1 km/h
5/3 km/h
From 5 + s = 2(5 − s), we get 3s = 5, so the stream flows at 5/3 km/h.
faqs: Why is the round-trip time not equal to the time in still water?

Because the boat spends more time going upstream at the slower speed than it saves going downstream. The losses and gains in speed are equal, but the time effect is not. So any current makes a round trip longer than the same trip in still water.
Do boats-and-streams questions appear in quantity comparison?

Yes, frequently in IBPS PO and SBI PO. A typical pair asks for the stream speed in one quantity and the time for a trip in the other. Writing D and U first lets you evaluate both quantities quickly and compare them.

items.title: Races and Circular Track Problems: Relative Speed Tricks
items.description: Solve linear race questions on beats-by and head starts, plus circular track meeting times in same and opposite directions, with worked examples.
items.intro: Races and circular-track problems apply relative speed to sport-like settings. SSC CGL and CAT ask them most, while IBPS PO and RBI Grade B use them occasionally as a harder speed question. Phrases like "A beats B by 40 m" or "they meet at the starting point" have precise meanings that are easy to misread, so learning the standard interpretations is more valuable here than learning new formulas.

concepts.heading: Reading "beats by"
concepts.text: "In a 1 km race A beats B by 100 m" means that when A crosses the finish line, B has run 900 m. Since they ran for the same time, their speeds are in the ratio 1000 : 900 = 10 : 9. "Beats by t seconds" means B reaches the finish t seconds after A.

concepts.heading: Chaining races
concepts.text: If A beats B and B beats C over the same distance, combine the speed ratios. When A finishes, B has run a known distance; at that moment C has covered B’s distance multiplied by the C : B ratio. This avoids comparing times.

concepts.heading: Circular track meetings
concepts.text: Two runners starting together on a track of length L meet for the first time after L ÷ (sum of speeds) if they run in opposite directions, and L ÷ (difference of speeds) if they run in the same direction, because the faster runner must gain a full lap.

concepts.heading: Meeting at the start
concepts.text: Both runners are back at the starting point together after the LCM of their individual lap times. For lap times of 120 s and 600/7 s, the LCM is 600 s, when one has run 5 laps and the other 7.

shortcuts: Head start for a dead heat = the distance by which A beats B.
If A beats B by x m in a race of d m, B runs (d − x) m in A’s time; B’s speed = A’s speed × (d − x)/d.
LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators ÷ HCF of denominators — handy for lap times.
On a circular track, the number of distinct meeting points (opposite directions) equals the sum of the speeds in lowest ratio terms; (same direction) equals their difference.

examples.question: In a 1 km race, A beats B by 100 m. Find the ratio of their speeds and the start A can give B for a dead heat.
examples.solution: When A runs 1,000 m, B runs 900 m, so speeds are 10 : 9. If B starts 100 m ahead, B needs only 900 m and both finish together, so the start is 100 m.

examples.question: In a 500 m race, A beats B by 40 m and B beats C by 50 m. By how much does A beat C?
examples.solution: When A finishes, B has run 460 m. B : C = 500 : 450, so C has run 460 × 450/500 = 414 m. A beats C by 86 m, not 90 m.

examples.question: Two runners on a 600 m circular track run at 5 m/s and 7 m/s. When do they first meet if they run in opposite directions, and in the same direction?
examples.solution: Opposite: 600 ÷ 12 = 50 s. Same direction: the faster one must gain 600 m at 2 m/s, which takes 300 s.

examples.question: For the runners above, when do they first meet again at the starting point?
examples.solution: Lap times are 120 s and 600/7 s. The LCM is 600 s: the first runner completes 5 laps and the second 7 laps.

examples.question: A runs 200 m in 40 seconds and beats B by 10 seconds. By how many metres does A beat B?
examples.solution: B takes 50 s for 200 m, so B’s speed is 4 m/s. In A’s 40 s, B runs 160 m. A beats B by 40 m.

practice: In a 100 m race, A beats B by 20 m. The ratio of their speeds is:
When A runs 100 m, B runs 80 m in the same time, so speeds are 100 : 80 = 5 : 4.
In a 1,000 m race, A beats B by 100 m and B beats C by 100 m. By how much does A beat C?
When A finishes, B has run 900 m and C has run 900 × 0.9 = 810 m, so A beats C by 190 m.
Two runners on a 400 m circular track run at 6 m/s and 4 m/s in opposite directions. They first meet after:
200 seconds
40 seconds
50 seconds
100 seconds
Their relative speed is 10 m/s when running towards each other, so they meet after 400 ÷ 10 = 40 seconds.
The same two runners (6 m/s and 4 m/s, 400 m track) run in the same direction. They first meet after:
200 seconds
40 seconds
100 seconds
160 seconds
The faster runner must gain one full lap of 400 m at 2 m/s, which takes 200 seconds.
In a 400 m race, A finishes in 50 seconds and B in 64 seconds. By how many metres does A beat B?
B runs at 400/64 = 6.25 m/s, covering 312.5 m in 50 seconds, so A wins by 87.5 m.
faqs: Is "A beats B by 40 m" the same as "A gives B a 40 m start"?

They describe the same speed ratio but different races. In the first, both start together and B is 40 m short at the end. In the second, B starts 40 m ahead; if B’s speed ratio matches, the race ends in a dead heat. Questions mix these to test careful reading.
Why does the meeting time on a circular track use relative speed?

Because the meeting depends only on how fast the gap between the runners changes. Running towards each other, the gap of one lap closes at the sum of speeds. Running the same way, the faster runner must lap the slower one, gaining at the difference of speeds.

items.title: Mensuration 2D: Triangle, Rectangle, Rhombus, Trapezium
items.description: Area and perimeter formulas for triangles, rectangles, squares, rhombus and trapezium, Heron’s formula and path-around-field questions with examples.
items.intro: Two-dimensional mensuration covers the area and perimeter of plane figures. SSC CGL and CHSL test it heavily, often three or four questions with geometry, and IBPS PO and SBI PO include one mensuration question in many prelims papers, frequently in quantity comparison. Questions are formula-driven, so a clean formula sheet and recognition of common Pythagorean triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17) matter more than clever tricks.

concepts.heading: Rectangles and squares
concepts.text: Rectangle: area = l × b, perimeter = 2(l + b), diagonal = √(l² + b²). Square: area = a², perimeter = 4a, diagonal = a√2, so area also equals diagonal²/2. Fencing cost uses perimeter; flooring or tiling uses area.

concepts.heading: Triangles
concepts.text: Area = ½ × base × height. When only the three sides are known, use Heron’s formula with s = (a + b + c)/2. For an equilateral triangle of side a, area = (√3/4)a² and height = (√3/2)a.

concepts.heading: Rhombus, parallelogram and trapezium
concepts.text: Rhombus area = ½ × d1 × d2; its diagonals bisect at right angles, so side = √((d1/2)² + (d2/2)²). Parallelogram area = base × height. Trapezium area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height.

concepts.heading: Paths around or inside a field
concepts.text: For a path of width w outside an l × b rectangle, path area = (l + 2w)(b + 2w) − lb = 2w(l + b + 2w). For a path inside, use (l × b) − (l − 2w)(b − 2w). Cross roads through the middle are l × w + b × w − w².

shortcuts: Learn triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 9-40-41 and their multiples like 6-8-10.
Heron’s formula with 13-14-15 gives 84 and with 9-10-17 gives 36 — common exam triangles.
If every side of a figure is scaled by k, its area scales by k² and perimeter by k.
Among rectangles of fixed perimeter, the square has the largest area.
Cross roads: two 3 m roads through a 50 m × 30 m park cover 50 × 3 + 30 × 3 − 3 × 3 = 231 m², because the central square is counted twice.

examples.question: A rectangular field is 60 m long and 40 m wide. A path 2.5 m wide runs around it on the outside. Find the area of the path.
examples.solution: Outer dimensions are 65 m × 45 m = 2,925 m². Field = 2,400 m². Path = 525 m². Formula check: 2 × 2.5 × (60 + 40 + 5) = 525 m².

examples.question: Find the area of a triangle with sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm.
Find the area of an equilateral triangle of side 12 cm.
The diagonals of a rhombus are 24 cm and 10 cm. Find its area and side.
examples.solution: Area = ½ × 24 × 10 = 120 cm². Half-diagonals are 12 and 5, so side = 13 cm.

examples.question: A square plot has an area of 1,600 m². Find the cost of fencing it at ₹25 per metre.
examples.solution: Side = 40 m, perimeter = 160 m. Cost = 160 × 25 = ₹4,000. Note that the rate is per metre, so it applies to the perimeter, not to the area of 1,600 m².

examples.question: The parallel sides of a trapezium-shaped plot are 18 m and 12 m and the distance between them is 8 m. Find its area and the cost of levelling it at ₹15 per m².
examples.solution: Area = ½ × (18 + 12) × 8 = 15 × 8 = 120 m². Cost = 120 × 15 = ₹1,800. Here the rate is per square metre, so it multiplies the area. Always match the unit of the rate before multiplying.

practice: A rectangle has perimeter 78 m and length 24 m. Its area is:
336 m²
384 m²
360 m²
390 m²
Breadth = 78/2 − 24 = 15 m, so the area is 24 × 15 = 360 square metres.
The area of a triangle with sides 9 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm is:
36 cm²
45 cm²
42 cm²
30 cm²
With s = 18, Heron’s formula gives √(18 × 9 × 8 × 1) = √1,296 = 36 square centimetres.
The diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 30 cm. Its side is:
15 cm
23 cm
19 cm
17 cm
Half-diagonals are 8 and 15 cm, which form an 8-15-17 right triangle, so the side is 17 cm.
A garden is 30 m × 20 m. A path 2 m wide runs inside along its edges. The area of the path is:
200 m²
184 m²
216 m²
176 m²
Inner area is 26 × 16 = 416 m², so the path covers 600 − 416 = 184 square metres.
The diagonal of a square is 12√2 m. Its area is:
144 m²
288 m²
72 m²
169 m²
Area = diagonal²/2 = 288/2 = 144 m², equivalently a side of 12 m squared.
faqs: Do I need Heron’s formula for bank exams?

Occasionally. Most bank questions give base and height or a right triangle, but Heron’s formula is useful when three sides are given, especially in SSC. Memorise the standard triangles 13-14-15 (area 84) and 5-12-13 (area 30) to save time.
How do I avoid unit mistakes in mensuration?

Convert all lengths to the same unit before calculating, and remember that area units are squared: 1 m² = 10,000 cm² and 1 hectare = 10,000 m². Cost questions usually give a rate per metre or per square metre; match it to perimeter or area accordingly.

items.title: Circle Mensuration: Area, Circumference, Sector and Ring
items.description: Circle formulas for area, circumference, wheel revolutions, sectors, arcs and circular paths using π = 22/7, with solved bank and SSC examples.
items.intro: Circle-based mensuration questions — wheels, circular parks, tracks and sectors — appear regularly in SSC CGL and CHSL and in bank quantity-comparison questions. Exam setters choose radii that are multiples of 7 so that π = 22/7 cancels neatly, which is a strong hint about how to calculate. The key formulas are few; most errors come from mixing radius and diameter or from forgetting the straight edges of semicircles and sectors.

concepts.heading: Basic formulas
concepts.text: Circumference = 2πr and area = πr². With r = 7, the circumference is 44 and the area 154; with r = 14, they are 88 and 616; with r = 21, 132 and 1,386. These values recur across exams.

concepts.heading: Wheels and revolutions
concepts.text: In one revolution a wheel covers its circumference. Distance = number of revolutions × 2πr. Convert km to cm or m carefully: 1.1 km = 1,10,000 cm.

concepts.heading: Sectors and arcs
concepts.text: A sector with central angle θ is θ/360 of the circle. Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr and sector area = (θ/360) × πr². The perimeter of a sector adds two radii to the arc; a semicircle’s perimeter is πr + 2r.

concepts.heading: Rings and circular paths
concepts.text: The area of a ring between radii R and r is π(R² − r²) = π(R + r)(R − r). For a path of width w around a circular park of radius r, use R = r + w.

shortcuts: Use π = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7, and 3.14 otherwise, unless the question specifies.
If the radius doubles, area becomes 4 times (a 300% increase) while circumference doubles.
The largest circle inside a square of side a has radius a/2; the leftover area is a² − πa²/4.
Area from circumference: A = C²/(4π). For C = 88, area = 616.
Semicircle perimeter = r(π + 2) = 36r/7 with π = 22/7.
Widening a circular track by w adds 2πw to its circumference whatever the original size: an inner circumference of 440 m with a 14 m wide track gives an outer circumference of 440 + 88 = 528 m.

examples.question: A wheel of radius 35 cm rolls 1.1 km. How many revolutions does it make?
examples.solution: Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm. Distance = 1,10,000 cm. Revolutions = 1,10,000 ÷ 220 = 500.

examples.question: A circular park of radius 21 m has a 3.5 m wide path around it on the outside. Find the area of the path.
examples.solution: R = 24.5 m. Area = 22/7 × (24.5² − 21²) = 22/7 × 159.25 = 500.5 m². Using (R + r)(R − r) = 45.5 × 3.5 makes the arithmetic easier.

examples.question: Find the area and arc length of a sector with radius 14 cm and angle 60°.
The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. Find its area.
The largest possible circle is cut from a square sheet of side 14 cm. How much sheet is wasted?
examples.solution: Radius = 7 cm, circle area = 154 cm². Square = 196 cm². Waste = 42 cm², which is about 21% of the sheet whatever the size of the square, since 1 − π/4 ≈ 0.215.

examples.question: The minute hand of a clock is 21 cm long. What area does it sweep in 20 minutes, and how far does its tip travel?
examples.solution: In 20 minutes the hand turns 20/60 of a full circle, i.e. 120°. Area swept = (120/360) × 22/7 × 441 = 462 cm². Distance moved by the tip = (1/3) × 2 × 22/7 × 21 = 44 cm. Clock-hand questions are just sector questions in disguise.

practice: The circumference of a circle is 132 cm. Its area is:
r = 132 ÷ (44/7) = 21 cm, so the area is 22/7 × 441 = 1,386 square centimetres.
A wheel of diameter 70 cm makes 400 revolutions. The distance covered is:
Circumference is 22/7 × 70 = 220 cm, so 400 revolutions cover 88,000 cm, which is 880 metres.
The area of a quadrant (90° sector) of a circle of radius 14 cm is:
616 cm²
308 cm²
44 cm²
154 cm²
A quadrant is one-fourth of the circle, so its area is 616/4 = 154 square centimetres.
If the radius of a circle increases from 7 cm to 14 cm, the area increases by:
Doubling the radius makes the area four times as large, which is an increase of 300 percent.
The perimeter of a semicircle of radius 7 cm is:
36 cm
22 cm
29 cm
44 cm
Perimeter = πr + 2r = 22 + 14 = 36 cm, including the diameter as the straight edge.
faqs: Should I use π = 22/7 or 3.14?

Use whatever the question specifies. If it is silent, check the radius: multiples of 7 suggest 22/7, while radii like 10 or 5 suggest 3.14. Options are usually designed around one of them, so compute with the value that makes an option match exactly.
Why does a semicircle’s perimeter include the diameter?

Because the perimeter is the full boundary of the shape, and a semicircle is closed by its straight edge. Only the curved length is πr; the diameter 2r must be added. Questions on fencing semicircular plots test this point.

items.title: Volume and Surface Area of Cube, Cuboid and Cylinder
items.description: Volume, surface area and diagonal formulas for cubes, cuboids and cylinders, with tank-capacity, melting and recasting examples for bank and SSC.
items.intro: Solid mensuration starts with the three shapes that have flat or straight sides: cubes, cuboids and cylinders. IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B include a 3D question in many prelims papers, usually a tank, a box or a pipe, and SSC CGL asks several. These shapes also appear in quantity comparison, where you must compute two volumes quickly. Knowing which formula answers which practical phrase — paint, capacity, cloth, sheet — is half the job.

concepts.heading: Cuboid
concepts.text: For length l, breadth b and height h: volume = lbh, total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl), lateral (four walls) area = 2h(l + b), and the longest rod that fits = √(l² + b² + h²). Painting the four walls of a room uses lateral area; the floor and ceiling are extra.

concepts.heading: Cube
concepts.text: All edges equal a: volume = a³, total surface area = 6a², lateral area = 4a² and diagonal = a√3. If the edge doubles, surface area becomes 4 times and volume 8 times.

concepts.heading: Cylinder
concepts.text: For radius r and height h: volume = πr²h, curved surface area = 2πrh, total surface area = 2πr(r + h). A closed tank needs total surface; an open drum needs curved surface plus one base; a pipe or a roller uses only the curved surface.

concepts.heading: Capacity and recasting
concepts.text: Capacity conversions: 1 m³ = 1,000 litres and 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre. When one solid is melted and recast into others, volume is conserved: number of new solids = volume of original ÷ volume of one new solid. Surface area is not conserved.

shortcuts: Pythagorean quadruples like 12-4-3 (13), 12-9-8 (17) and 2-3-6 (7) give clean cuboid diagonals.
For a cube, TSA ÷ 6 = a²; for volume, take the cube root — memorise cubes up to 15.
If a cylinder’s radius doubles and height halves, its volume doubles.
Number of small cubes of edge b from a cube of edge a is (a/b)³.
Rain or water-level problems: rise in level = volume added ÷ base area.

examples.question: A cuboid measures 12 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm. Find its volume, total surface area and diagonal.
A cube has a volume of 343 cm³. Find its total surface area.
examples.solution: Edge = ∛343 = 7 cm. TSA = 6 × 49 = 294 cm².

examples.question: A closed cylindrical drum has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume, curved surface area and total surface area.
examples.solution: Volume = 22/7 × 49 × 10 = 1,540 cm³. CSA = 2 × 22/7 × 7 × 10 = 440 cm². Each base is 154 cm², so TSA = 440 + 308 = 748 cm².

examples.question: An overhead tank measures 2 m × 1.5 m × 1 m. How many litres can it hold?
examples.solution: Volume = 3 m³. Since 1 m³ = 1,000 litres, capacity = 3,000 litres.

examples.question: A metal cube of edge 12 cm is melted and recast into small cubes of edge 3 cm. How many small cubes are formed?
examples.solution: Number = (12/3)³ = 4³ = 64 cubes. Volume is conserved: 1,728 cm³ ÷ 27 cm³ = 64.

examples.question: A rectangular water tank has a base of 8 m × 5 m. If 20,000 litres of water are pumped into it, by how much does the water level rise?
examples.solution: 20,000 litres = 20 m³. Rise in level = volume ÷ base area = 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5 m, i.e. 50 cm. The same logic answers rainfall questions: rain of 2 cm on a 1,000 m² roof gives 20 m³ of water.

practice: The volume of a cuboid measuring 10 cm × 6 cm × 4 cm is:
200 cm³
248 cm³
120 cm³
240 cm³
Volume = length × breadth × height = 10 × 6 × 4 = 240 cubic centimetres.
The total surface area of a cube is 486 cm². Its volume is:
512 cm³
729 cm³
648 cm³
Each face is 486/6 = 81 cm², so the edge is 9 cm and the volume is 9³ = 729 cm³.
The volume of a cylinder with radius 14 cm and height 20 cm is:
Volume = 22/7 × 196 × 20 = 616 × 20 = 12,320 cubic centimetres.
A hall is 12 m long, 9 m wide and 8 m high. The longest rod that can be placed in it is:
Longest rod = √(144 + 81 + 64) = √289 = 17 metres, the space diagonal of the hall.
A cylinder of radius 14 cm has a curved surface area of 880 cm². Its height is:
12 cm
10 cm
8 cm
20 cm
faqs: When do I use curved surface area instead of total surface area?

Use curved surface area when the ends are open or not part of the job — a pipe, a roller, or the side wall of a well. Use total surface area for closed objects such as a sealed tin. An open-top tank needs curved area plus one base.
How are litres related to cubic metres?
One cubic metre holds 1,000 litres and one litre equals 1,000 cubic centimetres. Tank and water questions often give dimensions in metres but ask for litres, so multiply the volume in m³ by 1,000.

items.title: Cone, Sphere and Hemisphere: Volume and Surface Formulas
items.description: Volume and surface area of cones, spheres and hemispheres, slant height, and melting or recasting questions explained with step-by-step examples.
items.intro: Curved solids — cones, spheres and hemispheres — complete the 3D mensuration syllabus. SSC CGL asks them almost every shift, and IBPS PO and SBI PO use them in quantity comparison and in "melt and recast" word problems. Because the formulas contain fractions such as 1/3, 2/3 and 4/3, the risk is arithmetic slips rather than conceptual errors, so pick radii that cancel with 7 and 3, and check whether the answer needs curved or total surface.

concepts.heading: Cone
concepts.text: For base radius r, height h and slant height l = √(r² + h²): volume = ⅓πr²h, curved surface = πrl and total surface = πr(l + r). A cone has one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height.

concepts.heading: Sphere
concepts.text: Volume = (4/3)πr³ and surface area = 4πr². The surface of a sphere equals the curved surface of a cylinder that just encloses it, which is a neat check.

concepts.heading: Hemisphere
concepts.text: Volume = (2/3)πr³, curved surface = 2πr² and total surface (with the flat circular face) = 3πr². A solid hemisphere needs 3πr²; a hemispherical bowl without a lid uses 2πr² for the inside or outside.

concepts.heading: Melting and recasting
concepts.text: Volume stays the same when a solid is melted into another shape. Equate the two volume formulas and solve for the unknown dimension; π usually cancels. For many small spheres from one large sphere, the count is (R/r)³.

shortcuts: Slant height triples: 3-4-5, 7-24-25, 5-12-13 — r and h are often chosen to make l whole.
Cone : hemisphere : cylinder volumes with equal r and h = r are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3.
If a sphere’s radius doubles, surface area becomes 4 times and volume 8 times.
When melting, cancel π and common factors before multiplying — the answer is usually an integer.
Lead shots of radius 1 cm from a sphere of radius 4 cm: (4/1)³ = 64, since volume scales with the cube of the radius.

examples.question: A cone has radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. Find its slant height, volume and curved surface area.
Find the volume and surface area of a sphere of radius 21 cm.
Find the volume and total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm.
A metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into a cone of base radius 6 cm. Find the height of the cone.
examples.solution: Sphere volume = (4/3)π × 216 = 288π. Cone volume = ⅓π × 36 × h = 12πh. So 12h = 288 and h = 24 cm.

examples.question: A conical tent has base radius 7 m and height 24 m. How much canvas is needed, and what is the cost at ₹40 per m²?
examples.solution: Slant height = 25 m, so canvas = curved surface = 22/7 × 7 × 25 = 550 m². Cost = 550 × 40 = ₹22,000. The floor of a tent is not covered with canvas, so the base area is not added.

examples.question: An ice-cream cone has radius 3.5 cm and height 12 cm and is filled with ice-cream that forms a hemisphere on top. Find the volume of ice-cream.
examples.solution: Cone part = ⅓ × π × 12.25 × 12 = 49π. Hemisphere = ⅔ × π × 42.875 ≈ 28.58π. Total ≈ 77.58π = 22/7 × 77.58 ≈ 243.83 cm³. Combined-solid questions simply add the volumes of the parts.

practice: The curved surface area of a cone with radius 3 cm and height 4 cm is:
12π cm²
20π cm²
24π cm²
15π cm²
Slant height is √(9 + 16) = 5 cm, so the curved surface is π × 3 × 5 = 15π cm².
A sphere has surface area 616 cm². Its volume is about:
4πr² = 616 gives r² = 49 and r = 7, so volume = 4/3 × 22/7 × 343 ≈ 1,437.33 cm³.
The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 14 cm is:
616 cm²
TSA = 3πr² = 3 × 22/7 × 196 = 1,848 square centimetres including the flat face.
A cone and a cylinder have the same base radius and height. The ratio of their volumes is:
A cone’s volume is one-third of a cylinder with the same base and height, so the ratio is 1 : 3.
A sphere of radius 3 cm is melted into a cylinder of radius 2 cm. The height of the cylinder is:
9 cm
6 cm
12 cm
4.5 cm
Sphere volume 36π equals cylinder volume 4πh, so the height h is 9 cm.
faqs: Why does a hemisphere’s total surface area use 3πr²?
The curved part is half the sphere’s surface, 2πr², and the flat circular face adds πr². Together they give 3πr². If the question describes a bowl or a dome open at the base, use only 2πr².
Is slant height always needed for a cone?
Only for surface area. Volume uses the vertical height h. Many questions give the slant height and radius, so you must find h first using h = √(l² − r²) before applying the volume formula.

items.title: Permutation Tricks: Arrangements, Words and Circular Seating
items.description: Permutation formulas for arrangements, words with repeated letters, vowels together, no-two-together and circular seating, with verified examples.
items.intro: Permutations count arrangements where order matters — seating people in a row, forming numbers from digits or rearranging the letters of a word. IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B occasionally ask one question, often on word arrangements, while CAT and CMAT test permutations more deeply. Because answers are exact counts, guessing rarely works; learning a few standard patterns (repeated letters, together, never together, circular) covers most exam questions.

concepts.heading: Counting principle and nPr
concepts.text: If one task can be done in m ways and an independent second task in n ways, both together can be done in m × n ways. Choosing and arranging r items from n distinct items gives nPr = n!/(n − r)! arrangements. Three-digit numbers with distinct digits from 1 to 6: 6 × 5 × 4 = 120.

concepts.heading: Repeated items
concepts.text: When some items are identical, divide by the factorial of each repeat count. BANKING has 7 letters with N twice, so it has 7!/2! = 2,520 distinct arrangements. BALLOON has L twice and O twice, giving 7!/(2! × 2!) = 1,260.

concepts.heading: Together and never together
concepts.text: To keep certain items together, glue them into one block, arrange the blocks, then arrange items inside the block. For "no two together", first arrange the others and place the restricted items in the gaps between and around them.

concepts.heading: Circular arrangements
concepts.text: Around a round table, rotations of the same arrangement are identical, so n people can sit in (n − 1)! ways. If clockwise and anticlockwise are also the same (a necklace or garland), divide by 2.

shortcuts: Digits with 0: the first place cannot be 0, so for 4-digit numbers with distinct digits there are 9 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 4,536.
Vowels-together count = (consonants + 1)! × (vowels)! — adjust for repeated letters.
Vowels never together = total − vowels together, but "no two vowels together" needs the gap method.
For the rank of a word in dictionary order, count words starting with each smaller letter first.
If the answer seems huge, check that you have not counted rotations of a circle separately.

examples.question: How many 3-digit numbers with all different digits can be formed using the digits 1 to 6?
examples.solution: Hundreds place: 6 choices, tens: 5, units: 4. Total = 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 = 6P3.

examples.question: In how many ways can the letters of BANKING be arranged?
examples.solution: There are 7 letters with N repeated twice. Arrangements = 7!/2! = 5,040/2 = 2,520.

examples.question: In how many arrangements of LEADER do the vowels come together?
examples.solution: Vowels E, A, E form one block; with L, D, R there are 4 units, arranged in 4! = 24 ways. Inside the block, E, A, E can be arranged in 3!/2! = 3 ways. Total = 24 × 3 = 72.

examples.question: In how many ways can 6 friends sit around a round table?
examples.solution: Circular arrangement: (6 − 1)! = 5! = 120 ways.

examples.question: In how many ways can 5 boys and 3 girls stand in a row so that no two girls are together?
examples.solution: Arrange the boys: 5! = 120. They create 6 gaps (including both ends). Place 3 girls in 3 of these gaps in order: 6P3 = 120. Total = 120 × 120 = 14,400.

examples.question: A shelf has room for 4 books. In how many ways can 4 books be chosen and arranged from 7 different books? How many arrangements have a particular book always on the extreme left?
examples.solution: Ordered selection = 7P4 = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 = 840. If one particular book is fixed on the extreme left, the remaining 3 places are filled from 6 books in 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 ways. Fixing an item reduces both the number of places and the pool by one.

practice: In how many ways can the letters of MOBILE be arranged?
MOBILE has 6 different letters, so there are 6! = 720 possible arrangements.
The number of distinct arrangements of the letters of BALLOON is:
There are 7 letters with L and O each repeated twice, so the count is 7!/(2! × 2!) = 1,260.
How many 4-digit numbers with all distinct digits can be formed using the digits 0 to 9?
The first digit has 9 choices (not 0), then 9, 8 and 7 choices remain, giving 9 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 4,536.
In how many ways can 8 people be seated around a circular table?
Circular arrangements of n people number (n − 1)!, so for 8 people the answer is 7! = 5,040.
In how many arrangements of ORANGE do all the vowels come together?
Treat O, A, E as one block with R, N, G: 4! × 3! = 24 × 6 = 144 arrangements.
faqs: What is the difference between permutation and combination?

Permutation counts arrangements, where order matters: ABC and BAC are different. Combination counts selections, where order does not matter: choosing A, B, C is one committee. If a question involves seating, ranking, numbers or words, think permutation; for committees and teams, think combination.
Why divide by factorials for repeated letters?

Swapping two identical letters does not create a new word, but the n! formula counts each swap as different. Dividing by 2! for a pair of identical letters removes these duplicates. For a letter repeated three times, divide by 3!.

items.title: Combination Problems: Committees, Handshakes and Diagonals
items.description: Learn nCr for committees, at-least conditions, handshakes, polygon diagonals and triangles from points, with worked examples and practice MCQs.
items.intro: Combinations count selections where order does not matter: picking a committee, choosing questions in an exam or drawing balls from a bag. They feed directly into probability, so IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B effectively test them every year, and CAT relies on them heavily. SSC CGL asks occasional direct questions on handshakes and diagonals. A handful of patterns — conditional committees, "at least", geometric counts — cover nearly all questions.

concepts.heading: The nCr formula
concepts.text: The number of ways to choose r items from n distinct items is nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Useful identities: nC0 = nCn = 1, nC1 = n and nCr = nC(n − r), so 10C8 = 10C2 = 45.

concepts.heading: Committees with conditions
concepts.text: Choose each group separately and multiply. A committee of 3 men and 2 women from 6 men and 5 women: 6C3 × 5C2 = 20 × 10 = 200. If a person must be included, remove them and choose the rest; if excluded, remove them from the pool.

concepts.heading: "At least" questions
concepts.text: Count the complement: total selections minus those that violate the condition. At least one woman = all committees − all-men committees. This is faster than adding the cases one woman, two women and so on.

concepts.heading: Geometry counts
concepts.text: Handshakes among n people = nC2. Lines through n points (no three collinear) = nC2; triangles = nC3. Diagonals of an n-sided polygon = nC2 − n = n(n − 3)/2. If k points are collinear, subtract kC3 from triangles because those points form no triangle.

shortcuts: Compute nCr by cancelling: 9C4 = (9 × 8 × 7 × 6)/(4 × 3 × 2 × 1) = 126.
Pick the smaller of r and n − r before calculating.
Total subsets of n items = 2ⁿ; non-empty subsets = 2ⁿ − 1.
Selection then arrangement: choose with nCr, then multiply by r! if the chosen items are ordered.
Pentagon has 5 diagonals, hexagon 9, octagon 20, decagon 35.
Decagon diagonals: n(n − 3)/2 = 10 × 7/2 = 35, which is also 10C2 − 10 sides = 45 − 10.

examples.question: A committee of 3 men and 2 women is to be formed from 6 men and 5 women. In how many ways can this be done?
From 5 men and 4 women, a committee of 4 is chosen with at least one woman. How many ways?
examples.solution: Total committees = 9C4 = 126. All-men committees = 5C4 = 5. Required = 126 − 5 = 121.

examples.question: At a meeting of 12 branch managers, each shakes hands with every other once. How many handshakes take place?
examples.solution: 12C2 = 12 × 11/2 = 66 handshakes.

examples.question: There are 10 points in a plane, of which 4 are collinear and no other three are. How many triangles can be formed?
examples.solution: All triangles = 10C3 = 120. The 4 collinear points give 4C3 = 4 "triangles" that do not exist. Answer = 116.

examples.question: A cricket team of 11 is to be picked from 15 players. The captain must be included and one injured player must be left out. In how many ways can the team be chosen?
examples.solution: Remove the captain (already in) and the injured player (out). We now choose 10 more players from the remaining 13: 13C10 = 13C3 = (13 × 12 × 11)/6 = 286 ways.

examples.question: A bag has 4 red and 5 green balls. In how many ways can 3 balls be drawn so that at least 2 are red?
examples.solution: Exactly 2 red: 4C2 × 5C1 = 6 × 5 = 30. Exactly 3 red: 4C3 = 4. Total = 34. Here the complement (0 or 1 red) has two cases as well, so direct counting is just as quick; choose whichever side has fewer cases.

practice: The value of 8C3 is:
8C3 = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 336/6 = 56 possible selections.
If 15 people shake hands with each other exactly once, the number of handshakes is:
Each handshake is a pair, so the count is 15C2 = 15 × 14/2 = 105.
The number of diagonals of a hexagon is:
Diagonals = n(n − 3)/2 = 6 × 3/2 = 9, which is 15 lines minus the 6 sides.
A team of 4 is selected from 7 men and 3 women. In how many ways can it include exactly 2 women?
Choose 2 women in 3C2 = 3 ways and 2 men in 7C2 = 21 ways, giving 3 × 21 = 63.
A student must answer 5 of 10 questions, and question 1 is compulsory. In how many ways can he choose?
With question 1 fixed, he chooses 4 more from the remaining 9: 9C4 = 126 ways.
faqs: How do I know whether a question needs combination or permutation?

Ask whether swapping two chosen items gives a different outcome. If choosing Ravi then Meena is the same as Meena then Ravi, it is a combination. If positions, ranks or orders differ, it is a permutation. Some questions need both: select first, then arrange.
Why use the complement for "at least" questions?

Because "at least one" includes many cases, while its opposite, "none", is a single case. Subtracting the single bad case from the total is shorter and less error-prone than adding several good cases separately.

items.title: Probability Basics with Coins and Dice for Bank Exams
items.description: Probability fundamentals using coin tosses and dice: sample spaces, sum-of-dice tables, at-least-one rule and addition rule, with verified examples.
items.intro: Probability has become a regular feature of IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B prelims and mains, usually one or two questions, and SSC CGL Tier 2 and CAT test it as well. Coin and dice questions are the entry point: their sample spaces are small enough to list, so they build the counting habits needed for harder card and ball problems. Accuracy here depends on writing the sample space correctly before counting.

concepts.heading: Classical probability
concepts.text: Probability of an event = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. It always lies between 0 and 1. A coin has 2 outcomes, a die 6, two dice 36 and three coins 8. With n coins there are 2ⁿ outcomes; with n dice, 6ⁿ.

concepts.heading: Two-dice sums
concepts.text: For two dice, the number of ways to get each sum is: 2→1, 3→2, 4→3, 5→4, 6→5, 7→6, 8→5, 9→4, 10→3, 11→2, 12→1. The distribution is symmetric around 7, the most likely sum. Memorising this table removes the need to list pairs every time.

concepts.heading: Complement rule
concepts.text: P(not E) = 1 − P(E). For "at least one" questions, compute the chance of none and subtract from 1. The chance of at least one head in 4 tosses is 1 − (1/2)⁴ = 15/16.

concepts.heading: Addition rule
concepts.text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Subtract the overlap so that outcomes in both events are not counted twice. For two dice, "a doublet or a sum of 4" overlaps at (2, 2).
concepts.formula: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

shortcuts: Exactly k heads in n coins = nCk / 2ⁿ. Exactly 2 heads in 4 coins = 6/16 = 3/8.
Product of two dice is odd only when both are odd: 9/36 = 1/4, so even product = 3/4.
Doublets on two dice: 6 of 36 = 1/6.
Sum ≥ 10 has 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 outcomes, so 1/6.
Always reduce the fraction — options are usually in lowest terms.
For a sum of s on two dice (s from 2 to 7), the number of ways is s − 1; for s from 8 to 12 it is 13 − s. So sum 5 has 4 ways and sum 10 has 3 ways.
Probability can never exceed 1. If your count of favourable outcomes is larger than the sample space, you have double-counted somewhere.

examples.question: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is 8?
examples.solution: Favourable pairs: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) — 5 outcomes out of 36. P = 5/36.

examples.question: Three coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting at least two heads.
examples.solution: Outcomes with 2 heads: HHT, HTH, THH; with 3 heads: HHH. That is 4 out of 8, so P = 1/2.

examples.question: Two dice are thrown. Find the probability of getting a doublet or a sum of 4.
examples.solution: Doublets: 6 outcomes. Sum 4: (1,3), (2,2), (3,1) — 3 outcomes. (2,2) is in both. Favourable = 6 + 3 − 1 = 8, so P = 8/36 = 2/9.

examples.question: A die is thrown twice. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is even?
examples.solution: Product is odd only when both throws are odd: (3/6) × (3/6) = 1/4. So P(even) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

examples.question: Four coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
examples.solution: P(no head) = (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. P(at least one head) = 15/16.

examples.question: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the two numbers differ by exactly 1?

practice: Two dice are thrown. The probability that the sum is 9 is:
Sum 9 comes from (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3), which is 4 of 36 outcomes, i.e. 1/9.
Three coins are tossed. The probability of exactly one head is:
The outcomes HTT, THT and TTH give exactly one head, which is 3 out of 8 outcomes.
A die is thrown once. The probability of getting a prime number is:
The primes on a die are 2, 3 and 5, so three of six faces are favourable, giving 1/2.
Two dice are thrown. The probability that the sum is at least 10 is:
Sums of 10, 11 and 12 occur in 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 ways out of 36, which equals 1/6.
Three coins are tossed. The probability of getting at least one tail is:
Only HHH has no tail, with probability 1/8, so at least one tail has probability 7/8.
faqs: Are the outcomes (2, 6) and (6, 2) different when two dice are thrown?

Yes. Treat the dice as distinguishable, for example a red die and a blue die. That gives 36 equally likely outcomes. Counting (2, 6) and (6, 2) as one would make the outcomes unequal in probability and give wrong answers.
When should I use the complement rule?

Use it whenever the question says "at least one" or when the favourable cases are many but the unfavourable cases are few. Computing the probability of the opposite event and subtracting from 1 is usually shorter and reduces counting errors.

items.title: Probability with Cards, Balls and Independent Events
items.description: Card and ball probability using combinations, with and without replacement, plus independent events like two people solving a problem, all verified.
items.intro: Card, ball and "two people attempt a problem" questions form the harder half of exam probability. IBPS PO mains, SBI PO, RBI Grade B and CAT use them, and they often come as a set of two or three questions on the same bag of balls. The method is consistent: count favourable selections with combinations, divide by total selections, and be clear about whether items are replaced between draws.

concepts.heading: The 52-card deck
concepts.text: A standard deck has 4 suits (spades and clubs are black; hearts and diamonds are red) of 13 cards each: A, 2–10, J, Q, K. There are 4 of each rank, 12 face cards (J, Q, K) and 26 red cards. For "king or heart", add 4 and 13 and subtract the king of hearts: 16/52 = 4/13.

concepts.heading: Drawing balls together
concepts.text: Drawing several balls at once is a combination: P = (ways to choose the favourable balls) ÷ (ways to choose any balls). From 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green, two reds: 5C2/12C2 = 10/66 = 5/33.

concepts.heading: With and without replacement
concepts.text: With replacement, each draw has the same probabilities and they multiply. Without replacement, the second draw depends on the first, so the denominator and counts shrink: two aces without replacement = 4/52 × 3/51 = 1/221.

concepts.heading: Independent people or events
concepts.text: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). The chance that a problem is solved by at least one of two people is 1 − P(both fail). If A solves with probability 1/3 and B with 1/4, P(solved) = 1 − (2/3)(3/4) = 1/2.

shortcuts: Exactly one of each colour from three colours: multiply single choices (a × b × c) over nC3.
Face cards = 12, honours (A, K, Q, J) = 16, red face cards = 6.
"Without replacement" draws one by one give the same answer as drawing together.
P(exactly one of A, B) = p(1 − q) + q(1 − p).
Check that all case probabilities add to 1 when a question asks several parts on the same bag.

examples.question: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck. What is the probability that it is a king or a heart?
examples.solution: Kings: 4; hearts: 13; king of hearts counted twice. Favourable = 16. P = 16/52 = 4/13.

examples.question: A bag has 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green balls. Two balls are drawn at random. Find the probability that both are red.
examples.solution: Total ways = 12C2 = 66. Favourable = 5C2 = 10. P = 10/66 = 5/33.

examples.question: From the same bag, 3 balls are drawn. What is the probability that they are of different colours?
Two cards are drawn one after another without replacement. What is the probability that both are aces?
A can solve a problem with probability 1/3 and B with probability 1/4, independently. What is the probability that the problem is solved?
Two cards are drawn together from a deck. What is the probability that exactly one is a king?
examples.solution: Choose 1 king from 4 and 1 non-king from 48: 4 × 48 = 192. Total = 52C2 = 1,326. P = 192/1,326 = 32/221.

practice: A card is drawn from a deck of 52. The probability that it is a face card is:
There are 12 face cards (J, Q, K in four suits), so the probability is 12/52 = 3/13.
A bag has 6 white and 4 black balls. Two are drawn at random. The probability that both are black is:
Favourable = 4C2 = 6 and total = 10C2 = 45, so the probability is 6/45 = 2/15.
From the same bag (6 white, 4 black), two balls are drawn. The probability of one white and one black is:
Favourable = 6 × 4 = 24 out of 45 selections, which reduces to 8/15.
A card is drawn from a deck. The probability that it is red or a queen is:
Red cards 26 plus queens 4 minus 2 red queens gives 28 cards, so 28/52 = 7/13.
A hits a target with probability 2/5 and B with probability 1/2. If both shoot once, the probability that the target is hit is:
P(both miss) = 3/5 × 1/2 = 3/10, so P(target hit) = 1 − 3/10 = 7/10.
faqs: Is drawing two balls together the same as drawing them one after another?

Yes, provided the first ball is not replaced. Drawing together counts unordered pairs (nC2), while one-by-one counts ordered pairs, but both numerator and denominator change by the same factor, so the probability is identical.
What does "independent" mean in probability questions?

Two events are independent if one happening does not change the chance of the other. Two people solving a problem separately or two separate coin tosses are independent, so their probabilities multiply. Drawing cards without replacement is not independent.

items.title: Number Series Tricks: Find the Missing Number Fast
items.description: Spot difference, multiplication, square-cube and alternating patterns in missing-number series, with a step-by-step checking order and solved examples.
items.intro: Number series is one of the highest-yield topics in bank prelims: IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI PO and SBI Clerk usually set a block of five series questions, either missing-number or wrong-number. RBI Assistant and LIC exams follow the same pattern. Each question can be solved in 20–30 seconds once you check patterns in a fixed order, which makes this block a reliable place to gain marks and save time for DI.

concepts.heading: Check order
concepts.text: Look at how fast the series grows. Slow, steady growth suggests differences (first or second level). Roughly doubling or tripling suggests multiplication with an add-on (×2 + 1, ×3 − 2). Fast irregular growth suggests ×1 + 1, ×2 + 2, ×3 + 3 type patterns. Values near perfect squares or cubes suggest n² ± k or n³ ± k.

concepts.heading: Difference patterns
concepts.text: Write the differences between consecutive terms. If they are not constant, check the differences of differences, or whether the differences themselves form a familiar sequence: squares (1, 4, 9, 16), cubes, primes or powers of 2. In 7, 9, 13, 21, 37 the differences 2, 4, 8, 16 double each time, so the next term is 37 + 32 = 69.

concepts.heading: Multiplicative patterns
concepts.text: Divide each term by the previous one. If the ratio is near a constant, test "× k ± c": 5, 11, 23, 47, 95 follows ×2 + 1. If the ratio itself changes steadily (×0.5, ×1, ×1.5, ×2), the multiplier is growing by a fixed step.

concepts.heading: Alternating and mixed series
concepts.text: If odd and even positions behave differently, split them into two series, or look for two operations alternating, such as +2 then ×2. These are common in IBPS Clerk. When nothing fits, compare each term with n², n³ or n! for its position n.

shortcuts: Know squares to 30, cubes to 20 and powers of 2 to 2¹² — they appear in nearly every set.
If differences are 1, 4, 9, 16…, the next difference is the next square; if 1, 8, 27…, the next cube.
For ×n + (n + 1) patterns, the series explodes quickly — the answer will be much larger than the last term.
Use the options: the next term usually has a predictable last digit; eliminate options that cannot fit.
Spend no more than 40 seconds; if stuck, move on and return after the other four.

examples.solution: Each term is double the previous plus 1: 5 × 2 + 1 = 11, 11 × 2 + 1 = 23 and so on. Next = 95 × 2 + 1 = 191.
Terms are 2² − 1, 3² − 1, 4² − 1, 5² − 1, 6² − 1. Next = 7² − 1 = 48. The differences 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 confirm it.
Differences are 2, 4, 8, 16, which double each time. Next difference = 32, so the answer is 37 + 32 = 69.
Multipliers are ×0.5, ×1, ×1.5, ×2, rising by 0.5. Next multiplier is ×2.5, so 180 × 2.5 = 450.

practice: Each term is twice the previous one plus 1, so the next term is 111 × 2 + 1 = 223.
The terms are n³ + 1 for n = 1 to 5, so the next is 6³ + 1 = 216 + 1 = 217.
Differences are 1, 4, 9, 16 (squares), so the next difference is 25 and the term is 40 + 25 = 65.
The multipliers are ×2, ×3, ×4, ×5, so the next term is 120 × 6 = 720, which equals 6 factorial.
The operations alternate +2 and ×2: 3, 5, 10, 12, 24, 26, so next comes 26 × 2 = 52.
faqs: How many number series questions come in IBPS Clerk and PO prelims?

Typically a block of five questions, though the pattern varies by year and sometimes the block is replaced by another type such as quadratic equations. Because the block is short and scoring, regular practice of ten series a day is a common preparation strategy.
What should I do if no pattern fits within 40 seconds?

Skip the question and return later. Often a fresh look reveals an alternating or mixed pattern you missed. Spending two minutes on one series costs more marks elsewhere than the single question is worth.

items.title: Wrong Number Series: How to Find the Odd Term Quickly
items.description: Find the wrong term in a number series by locating where the pattern breaks, using difference, ratio, square and prime checks, with solved examples.
items.intro: Wrong number series (find the term that does not fit) is the twin of the missing-number type and appears as a five-question block in many IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI and RBI Assistant prelims papers. It feels harder because the error disturbs the pattern you are trying to detect. The trick is to find the pattern from the terms that agree with each other and then test each term against it, rather than staring at the whole series.

concepts.heading: Use the majority of terms
concepts.text: In a seven-term series, six terms follow the rule and one does not. Look at the first three or four terms, guess the rule, and extend it. The first term that disagrees is the likely culprit. If the rule breaks at the very beginning, start from the end of the series instead.

concepts.heading: A wrong term breaks two differences
concepts.text: In a difference-based series, one wrong term spoils the difference before it and the difference after it. If differences are 4, 9, 15, 26, 36, 49, the pair 15 and 26 should be 16 and 25, so the term between them is wrong by 1. This tells you exactly which term to replace.

concepts.heading: Ratio and power checks
concepts.text: For geometric series, check that each term is the previous one multiplied by the same factor; the wrong term often differs by a small amount (484 instead of 486). For squares, cubes and primes, check each term directly — 26 in a list of squares or 27 in a list of primes stands out immediately.

concepts.heading: Confirm before answering
concepts.text: Replace the suspected term with the correct value and verify that the entire series now follows one rule. This 5-second check prevents choosing a term that only looks odd.

shortcuts: Mark the series growth first: steady (differences), doubling (×2 ± k) or explosive (×n + n).
Wrong terms are usually off by a small amount — 1, 2 or a digit swap — rather than wildly different.
In a series of halves, look for rounding: 31 instead of 31.25 is a classic wrong term.
In a series meant to contain primes, the odd term is usually a multiple of 3 or 7 that looks prime, such as 27, 49, 51 or 91.
If two candidates seem wrong, the rule is probably different — re-test with the other terms.

examples.question: Find the wrong term: 4, 9, 19, 39, 79, 158, 319
examples.solution: Rule ×2 + 1: 4 → 9 → 19 → 39 → 79 → 159 → 319. The given 158 should be 159, so 158 is wrong.

examples.question: Find the wrong term: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 38, 50
examples.solution: Terms are n² + 1: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37, 50. The term 38 should be 37.

examples.question: Find the wrong term: 1000, 500, 250, 125, 62.5, 31, 15.625
examples.solution: Each term is half the previous one. Half of 62.5 is 31.25, not 31, and 31.25 ÷ 2 = 15.625 matches the last term. So 31 is wrong.

examples.question: Find the wrong term: 8, 12, 21, 36, 62, 98, 147
examples.solution: Expected differences are squares 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49. The given differences are 4, 9, 15, 26, 36, 49: the 15 and 26 are both off by one, so the term between them, 36, is wrong; it should be 37.

examples.question: Find the wrong term: 3, 4, 10, 32, 136, 685

practice: Find the wrong term: 5, 7, 11, 19, 35, 68, 131
Differences should be 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, giving 35 + 32 = 67, so 68 is the wrong term.
Find the wrong term: 1, 4, 9, 16, 26, 36
The series is the squares of 1 to 6, so the fifth term should be 25 and 26 is wrong.
Find the wrong term: 2, 6, 18, 54, 162, 484
Each term is three times the previous one, so after 162 the term should be 486, not 484.
Find the wrong term: 6, 12, 21, 33, 48, 66, 88
Differences should be 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, rising by 3, so the last term should be 66 + 21 = 87, not 88.
Find the wrong term: 7, 15, 31, 64, 127
The rule is ×2 + 1, so after 31 comes 63 and then 127; the given 64 is wrong.
faqs: Is the wrong term ever the first or last term?

Yes, though less often. If the rule fits from the second term onward but not the first, the first term is wrong. Always verify by checking that the rule holds for every remaining term after replacement, including both ends.
How do wrong-number questions differ from missing-number ones?

In missing-number questions you extend a clean pattern. In wrong-number questions the pattern is disturbed, so you must infer it from most terms and test each one. The pattern families are the same: differences, ratios, squares, cubes, primes and mixed operations.

items.title: Quadratic Equations for Bank Exams: Compare x and y Fast
items.description: Solve IBPS and SBI quadratic-equation comparison questions with factorisation, the sign method and root comparison rules, plus solved practice.
items.intro: In IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and RBI Assistant prelims, quadratic equations usually appear as a block of five questions: two equations are given, one in x and one in y, and you must decide whether x > y, x < y, x ≥ y, x ≤ y, x = y or no relation can be established. Each question takes 30–40 seconds once factorisation is automatic. CAT and SSC CGL test quadratics differently, through sum and product of roots.

concepts.heading: Factorisation by splitting
concepts.text: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is c and sum is b. For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is a × c and sum is b, then split the middle term. 2x² − 7x + 3: product 6, sum −7 → −6 and −1, giving (2x − 1)(x − 3) and roots 1/2 and 3.

concepts.heading: Sign method for roots
concepts.text: For x² + bx + c with integer roots: if both b and c are positive, both roots are negative; if b is negative and c positive, both roots are positive; if c is negative, the roots have opposite signs. This tells you the signs before you calculate, and often decides the relation immediately.

concepts.heading: Comparing the roots
concepts.text: Compare every value of x with every value of y. If all x values are greater, x > y. If some x equals some y and the rest are greater, x ≥ y. If the comparison goes both ways, the answer is "no relation". Placing the roots on a number line makes this visual.

concepts.heading: Sum and product of roots
concepts.text: For ax² + bx + c = 0, sum of roots = −b/a and product = c/a. A quadratic with roots p and q is x² − (p + q)x + pq = 0. These relations are tested in SSC CGL and CAT.

shortcuts: x² = k gives x = ±√k, but y = √k gives only the positive root — a favourite trap.
If both equations have the same sign pattern, compare the magnitudes of the roots directly.
Common roots between x and y equations usually produce ≥ or ≤, not > or <.
For linear equations in x and y given together, solve them simultaneously instead of factorising.
Write roots as fractions, not decimals, so equality is easy to spot.

examples.question: I. x² − 7x + 12 = 0   II. y² − 3y + 2 = 0
examples.solution: x: (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0, so x = 3, 4. y: (y − 1)(y − 2) = 0, so y = 1, 2. Every x is greater than every y: x > y.

examples.question: I. x² + 5x + 6 = 0   II. y² + 7y + 12 = 0
examples.solution: x = −2, −3 and y = −3, −4. Comparing: −2 > −3, −2 > −4, −3 = −3, −3 > −4. All comparisons give x greater or equal, so x ≥ y.

examples.question: I. 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0   II. y² − 4y + 3 = 0
examples.solution: x = 1/2, 3 and y = 1, 3. x = 1/2 is less than y = 1, but x = 3 is greater than y = 1. The relation cannot be established.

examples.question: I. x² = 81   II. y = √81
examples.solution: x = ±9, while y = +9 only (the square-root symbol means the principal root). x = −9 < 9 and x = 9 = 9, so x ≤ y.

examples.question: The roots of x² − 11x + 28 = 0 are p and q. Form the quadratic whose roots are p − 2 and q − 2.
examples.solution: p = 4 and q = 7, so the new roots are 2 and 5. Equation: x² − (2 + 5)x + 2 × 5 = x² − 7x + 10 = 0.

practice: I. x² − 9x + 20 = 0   II. y² − 5y + 6 = 0. The relation is:
x < y
x ≥ y
x > y
No relation
x = 4, 5 and y = 2, 3, so every value of x exceeds every value of y and x > y.
I. x² + 9x + 20 = 0   II. y² + 7y + 12 = 0. The relation is:
x ≤ y
x > y
x ≥ y
x < y
x = −4, −5 and y = −3, −4; the common value −4 gives equality and all others give x < y.
I. x² − x − 6 = 0   II. y² − 4 = 0. The relation is:
x > y
x ≥ y
No relation
x ≤ y
x = 3, −2 and y = 2, −2; x = 3 exceeds both y values but x = −2 is below y = 2, so no single relation holds.
The sum of the roots of 3x² − 12x + 5 = 0 is:
Sum of roots = −b/a = 12/3 = 4, without needing to find the roots themselves.
I. 3x² − 10x + 8 = 0   II. 2y² − 11y + 15 = 0. The relation is:
x < y
x > y
x ≤ y
No relation
x = 4/3, 2 and y = 5/2, 3, so the largest x (2) is still below the smallest y (2.5): x < y.
faqs: Why is y = √81 only +9 while x² = 81 gives ±9?

The radical sign √ denotes the principal (non-negative) square root by convention, so √81 = 9. The equation x² = 81 asks for every number whose square is 81, which includes −9. Bank exams use this difference deliberately to create ≤ or ≥ answers.
What if a quadratic does not factorise neatly?

In bank comparison questions the roots are almost always rational, so if splitting fails, recheck the product and sum. For general quadratics, use the formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a. A negative discriminant means no real roots.

items.title: Simplification and BODMAS Tricks for Bank Exams
items.description: BODMAS order, percentage–fraction swaps, square and cube roots and decimal handling for simplification questions, with step-by-step solved sums.
items.intro: Simplification questions — evaluate an expression or find the value of "?" — form a block of five in IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk and RBI Assistant prelims and appear in IBPS PO as well. SSC papers include similar arithmetic. These are pure speed questions: the concepts are school-level, so marks depend on applying BODMAS correctly and on mental shortcuts for percentages, fractions, squares and cube roots.

concepts.heading: BODMAS order
concepts.text: Brackets first, then Orders (powers and roots), then Division and Multiplication from left to right, then Addition and Subtraction from left to right. Division and multiplication have equal priority, so 48 ÷ 6 × 4 = 8 × 4 = 32, not 48 ÷ 24 = 2.
concepts.formula: B → O → D/M (left to right) → A/S (left to right)

concepts.heading: Percentages and fractions
concepts.text: Convert percentages to fractions where possible: 25% of 480 = 480/4 = 120; 37.5% = 3/8; 12.5% = 1/8; 16.67% = 1/6. A mixed expression like "25% of 480 + 3/8 of 640" becomes 120 + 240 = 360 without long multiplication.

concepts.heading: Squares, cubes and roots
concepts.text: Memorise squares to 50 and cubes to 25. For square roots of perfect squares, use the last digit and the range: √1764 ends in 2 or 8 and lies between 40 and 50; 42² = 1,764. For cube roots, the last digit of the cube fixes the last digit of the root (2197 ends in 7, so the root ends in 3).

concepts.heading: Mixed fractions
concepts.text: Split mixed numbers into whole and fractional parts and add them separately, using the LCM of the denominators for the fractions. This keeps numbers small and is usually faster than converting everything into improper fractions, especially when three or more mixed numbers appear in one expression.

concepts.heading: Decimals
concepts.text: Convert decimals to fractions or scale them up: 0.25 × 0.4 ÷ 0.05 = (25 × 4 ÷ 5) × (10⁻² × 10⁻¹ ÷ 10⁻²) = 20 × 0.1 = 2. Counting decimal places separately avoids misplaced points.

shortcuts: "Find ?" questions: move known terms to one side first — 126 + ? = 195 gives ? = 69 instantly.
Squares ending in 5: 65² = 6 × 7 followed by 25 = 4,225.
Multiply by 25 by dividing by 4 and multiplying by 100: 25 × 36 = 900.

examples.solution: Division and multiplication left to right: 48 ÷ 6 = 8, 8 × 4 = 32, 5 × 3 = 15. Then 32 + 18 − 15 = 35.

examples.question: 15% of 840 + ? = 30% of 650
examples.solution: 15% of 840 = 126 and 30% of 650 = 195. So ? = 195 − 126 = 69. Check by substituting: 126 + 69 = 195, which matches the right-hand side.

examples.question: 2¾ + 3⅙ − 1 5/12 = ?
examples.solution: Convert to improper fractions with the common denominator 12: 11/4 = 33/12, 19/6 = 38/12 and 17/12. So 33/12 + 38/12 − 17/12 = 54/12 = 4.5. A faster route is to handle whole numbers and fractions separately: 2 + 3 − 1 = 4, and 3/4 + 1/6 − 5/12 = (9 + 2 − 5)/12 = 1/2, giving 4½.

practice: 40% of 350 is 140 and one-sixth of 540 is 90, so the total is 140 + 90 = 230.
√2025 = 45 because 45² = 2,025, and ∛1331 = 11, so the difference is 45 − 11 = 34.
2/5 of 1,200 is 480, and 3/4 of 480 is 360, so the expression equals 360.
faqs: Do simplification questions use the "of" operator before division?

In many Indian textbooks, "of" is treated as multiplication done before division, and it often appears as "x% of y". In modern bank papers, expressions are written to avoid ambiguity, so just apply BODMAS and evaluate "of" as multiplication immediately.
How much time should a simplification question take?

Aim for 20–30 seconds each. With five questions in the block, finishing them in about two minutes leaves time for DI and arithmetic. Daily practice of squares, cubes and fraction conversions is the main way to reach that speed.

items.title: Approximation Questions: Rounding Tricks for Bank Prelims
items.description: How to round decimals, percentages, square roots and divisions in approximation questions, with error-control tips and fully worked examples.
items.intro: Approximation is the sibling of simplification: the numbers are deliberately awkward (39.97% of 601.02), and the options are spaced far enough apart that sensible rounding gives the answer. IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI PO and SBI Clerk prelims often carry a five-question approximation block, and the same skill is essential for DI, where exact calculation wastes time. The aim is not precision but choosing the right option in under 25 seconds.

concepts.heading: Round to the nearest friendly number
concepts.text: Round each number to the nearest integer or to a value that makes the operation easy: 39.97% becomes 40%, 601.02 becomes 600, 24.97 becomes 25. Because the options are usually 10% or more apart, these small changes do not affect which option is closest.

concepts.heading: Keep errors balanced
concepts.text: When you round one factor up in a product, round the other down if possible, so the errors partly cancel. In division, rounding the numerator and denominator in the same direction keeps the quotient close to the true value.

concepts.heading: Square roots and powers
concepts.text: Round inside the root to the nearest perfect square: √1599 ≈ √1600 = 40 and √624.8 ≈ √625 = 25. For squares like 29.97², use 30² = 900; the error is about 2 × 30 × 0.03 ≈ 1.8, negligible against options.

concepts.heading: Approximation inside DI
concepts.text: In data interpretation, you often need values like 1,847 as a percentage of 6,112. Round to 1,850 ÷ 6,100 ≈ 0.303, i.e. about 30%. Using fraction benchmarks (1/3 ≈ 33.3%, 3/10 = 30%) lets you place the answer between two options without long division, which is where most DI time is saved.

concepts.heading: Finding "?" approximately
concepts.text: Rearrange first, then approximate: 44.89% of 799.9 − ? = 15.01² becomes 360 − ? ≈ 225, so ? ≈ 135. If an option is very close to your estimate and the next is far away, choose without further checking.

shortcuts: Treat x.97 to x.99 as x + 1 and x.01 to x.03 as x.
Percentages near 25, 50, 75, 20, 12.5 convert to fractions: 24.98% ≈ 1/4.
Look at the gap between options before calculating — wide gaps allow rougher rounding.
For a ÷ b × c, compute the division first if b divides a neatly after rounding.
Write intermediate results; a slip in a mental chain is the main source of error, not rounding.

examples.question: 39.97% of 601.02 + 19.98 × 15.01 ≈ ?
examples.solution: ≈ 40% of 600 + 20 × 15 = 240 + 300 = 540. The exact value is about 540.1.

examples.question: 1/7 of 3,499.88 ≈ ?
examples.solution: 3,500 ÷ 7 = 500. Rounding 3,499.88 to 3,500 is natural here because 3,500 is a multiple of 7, which turns the division into a one-step answer.

examples.question: (7.98)³ ÷ 15.97 + 63.02% of 299.8 ≈ ?
examples.solution: Round to 8³ ÷ 16 + 63% of 300 = 512 ÷ 16 + 189 = 32 + 189 = 221. The exact value is about 220.7, so 221 or the nearest option is safe. Notice that 8³ and 16 were chosen so that the division is exact once rounded.

practice: Round to 25% of 1,600 = 400 and 11 × 10 = 110, which add up to about 510.
√625 = 25 and 25 × 8 = 200; the small rounding errors do not change the nearest option.
Round to 4,800 ÷ 40 = 120; both numbers rounded up slightly, so the quotient barely changes.
