Use 30² − 20² = 900 − 400 = 500, or (30 + 20)(30 − 20) = 500 by the difference of squares.
60% of 450 is 270, so the missing value is about 400 − 270 = 130.
faqs: How far apart are options in approximation questions?
Typically 5–15% apart, so rounding errors of 1–2% do not matter. If two options are very close, round more carefully, keeping one decimal place, or check the direction of your rounding errors.
Should I approximate in DI questions too?

Yes, whenever the options are reasonably spaced. DI questions often ask for a percentage or ratio where two-significant-figure accuracy is enough. Exact calculation should be reserved for cases where options differ by less than about 2%.

items.title: Divisibility Rules and Number System Basics
items.description: Divisibility tests for 2 to 11, number of factors, sums of natural numbers and missing-digit questions explained with verified worked examples.
items.intro: The number system chapter is a staple of SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS, where three or four questions on divisibility, factors and remainders are common. Bank exams test it indirectly through simplification and data sufficiency, and CAT uses it heavily in harder forms. Divisibility rules are the foundation: they let you fill missing digits, check answers and factorise quickly without long division.

concepts.heading: Core divisibility rules
concepts.text: By 2: last digit even. By 3: digit sum divisible by 3. By 4: last two digits divisible by 4. By 5: last digit 0 or 5. By 8: last three digits divisible by 8. By 9: digit sum divisible by 9. By 11: difference between sums of digits in odd and even places is 0 or a multiple of 11.

concepts.heading: Composite divisors
concepts.text: For 6, 12, 15, 18 and similar numbers, test the co-prime factors separately: divisible by 12 means divisible by both 3 and 4; by 18 means by both 2 and 9. Do not use 2 and 6 for 12, because they are not co-prime.

concepts.heading: Number of factors
concepts.text: Write n = pᵃ × qᵇ × rᶜ in prime factors. The number of factors is (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1). For 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5, it is 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 factors. The number of odd factors ignores the power of 2: 3 × 2 = 6.

concepts.heading: Useful sums
concepts.text: Sum of the first n natural numbers = n(n + 1)/2; of the first n odd numbers = n²; of the first n even numbers = n(n + 1); of squares = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6. These appear directly in SSC and inside series questions.

shortcuts: Missing digit for 9: add the known digits and choose the digit that takes the sum to the next multiple of 9.
For 8, only the last three digits matter — ignore everything before them.
A number divisible by 7, 11 and 13 is divisible by 1,001; abcabc-type numbers always are.
Every prime above 3 is of the form 6k ± 1 — a fast primality filter.
Product of any n consecutive integers is divisible by n!.

examples.question: Is 7,35,568 divisible by 8?
examples.solution: Check the last three digits: 568 ÷ 8 = 71 exactly. So 7,35,568 is divisible by 8.

examples.question: Find the digit * so that 63*472 is divisible by 9.
examples.solution: Known digit sum = 6 + 3 + 4 + 7 + 2 = 22. The next multiple of 9 is 27, so * = 5. (Using 36 would need * = 14, impossible.)

examples.question: Is 9,48,321 divisible by 11?
examples.solution: Digits from the right: 1, 2, 3, 8, 4, 9. Odd places (1st, 3rd, 5th) sum to 1 + 3 + 4 = 8; even places sum to 2 + 8 + 9 = 19. Difference = −11, a multiple of 11, so yes (9,48,321 = 11 × 86,211).

examples.question: How many factors does 360 have?
Find the sum of the first 50 odd natural numbers.
examples.solution: Sum of the first n odd numbers is n², so the sum is 50² = 2,500.

examples.question: Find the largest 4-digit number that is exactly divisible by 88.
examples.solution: Divide the largest 4-digit number by 88: 9,999 = 88 × 113 + 55. Subtract the remainder: 9,999 − 55 = 9,944. For the smallest 4-digit multiple, you would instead add (88 − remainder of 1,000) to 1,000. These two templates cover most "largest/smallest n-digit number divisible by k" questions.

practice: What is the smallest digit that can replace * in 4*57 to make it divisible by 3?
The known digits sum to 16; adding 2 gives 18, a multiple of 3, and smaller digits do not work.
How many factors does 72 have?
72 = 2³ × 3², so the number of factors is (3 + 1)(2 + 1) = 12, from 1 up to 72.
What is the smallest digit * that makes 3524*6 divisible by 8?
Only the last three digits matter: 406 is not divisible by 8 but 416 = 8 × 52, so * = 1.
Which of these numbers is divisible by 11?
For 246862 the alternate digit sums are 2 + 8 + 4 = 14 and 6 + 6 + 2 = 14; the difference is 0, so it is divisible by 11.
The sum of the natural numbers from 1 to 100 is:
Using n(n + 1)/2 with n = 100 gives 100 × 101/2 = 5,050, as in the well-known Gauss example.
faqs: Why does the rule for 11 use alternating sums?

Because 10 leaves a remainder of −1 when divided by 11, so each digit contributes alternately + and − to the remainder. If the alternating sum is a multiple of 11 (including 0), the whole number is divisible by 11.
Is 1 a prime number?
No. A prime has exactly two distinct factors, 1 and itself. The number 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite. The smallest prime is 2, which is also the only even prime.

items.title: Remainder and Unit Digit Tricks with Cyclicity
items.description: Find unit digits of large powers with cyclicity, simplify remainders of products and powers, and solve divisor-change questions, all with examples.
items.intro: Remainder and unit-digit questions are SSC CGL and CHSL favourites and appear regularly in CAT, CMAT and MAT. Bank exams use them less often, mainly in RBI Grade B and data sufficiency. They look intimidating because of huge powers like 7⁹⁵, but the work reduces to small numbers once you use cyclicity and the fact that remainders can be multiplied and reduced at every step.

concepts.heading: Cyclicity of unit digits
concepts.text: The unit digit of powers repeats in cycles: 2 → 2, 4, 8, 6; 3 → 3, 9, 7, 1; 7 → 7, 9, 3, 1; 8 → 8, 4, 2, 6 (cycle 4). Digits 0, 1, 5, 6 always repeat themselves; 4 and 9 alternate with cycle 2. Divide the power by 4 and use the remainder (a remainder of 0 means the 4th term).

concepts.heading: Remainders of products and sums
concepts.text: The remainder of a product equals the remainder of the product of remainders. For (17 × 23 × 29) ÷ 12, use 5 × 11 × 5 = 275, which leaves 11. The same works for sums. Negative remainders can simplify further: 11 ≡ −1 (mod 12).
concepts.formula: (a × b) mod n = [(a mod n)(b mod n)] mod n

concepts.heading: Remainders of powers
concepts.text: Find a small power that leaves remainder 1 (or −1), then break the large power into that block. Since 2³ = 8 leaves 1 when divided by 7, 2⁵⁰ = (2³)¹⁶ × 2² leaves 4. For division by 5, 2⁴ = 16 leaves 1.

concepts.heading: Divisor-change questions
concepts.text: If a number leaves remainder r when divided by D, and d is a factor of D, the remainder on division by d is r mod d. A number that leaves 75 on division by 296 leaves 75 mod 37 = 1 on division by 37, because 296 = 8 × 37.

shortcuts: Unit digit of a product depends only on the unit digits of the factors.
An even base not ending in 0, raised to a multiple of 4, ends in 6 (2¹⁰⁰, 8⁴⁰); powers of 4 end in 6 for any even exponent, such as 4¹⁰².
From 5! onward, factorials end in 0, so the unit digit of 1! + 2! + … + n! (n ≥ 4) is 3.
(aⁿ − bⁿ) is divisible by (a − b) always and by (a + b) when n is even.
Remainder of xⁿ ÷ (x − 1) is always 1; of xⁿ ÷ (x + 1) is 1 if n is even and x if n is odd.

examples.question: Find the unit digit of 7⁹⁵.
examples.solution: Cycle of 7: 7, 9, 3, 1. 95 ÷ 4 leaves remainder 3, so the unit digit is the 3rd term, 3.

examples.question: Find the unit digit of 2⁴³ × 3²².
examples.solution: 2⁴³: 43 mod 4 = 3, unit digit 8. 3²²: 22 mod 4 = 2, unit digit 9. 8 × 9 = 72, so the unit digit is 2.

examples.question: Find the remainder when 2³¹ is divided by 5.
examples.solution: 2⁴ = 16 leaves 1. 2³¹ = (2⁴)⁷ × 2³, so the remainder is 1 × 8 = 8, which leaves 3 on division by 5.

examples.question: A number leaves a remainder of 75 when divided by 296. What remainder will it leave when divided by 37?
examples.solution: 296 = 8 × 37, so the remainder is 75 mod 37 = 1.

examples.question: Find the remainder when 17 × 23 × 29 is divided by 12.
examples.solution: Remainders are 5, 11, 5. 5 × 11 × 5 = 275 and 275 = 22 × 12 + 11, so the remainder is 11.

practice: The unit digit of 3⁶⁵ is:
The cycle of 3 is 3, 9, 7, 1; 65 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 4, so the unit digit is 3.
The unit digit of 4¹⁰² is:
Powers of 4 end in 4 for odd exponents and 6 for even exponents, and 102 is even, so the unit digit is 6.
The remainder when 2⁵⁰ is divided by 7 is:
2³ leaves 1 on division by 7, and 2⁵⁰ = (2³)¹⁶ × 2², so the remainder is 4.
A number leaves remainder 39 when divided by 357. What is the remainder when it is divided by 17?
Since 357 = 21 × 17, the remainder is 39 mod 17 = 5, as 39 = 2 × 17 + 5.
The unit digit of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 50! is:
Factorials from 5! end in 0, so only 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33 matters, giving a unit digit of 3.
faqs: Why is the cycle length 4 for most digits?

Because multiplying the last digit repeatedly by the same digit can produce at most four different endings before repeating, for digits 2, 3, 7 and 8. Some digits repeat faster: 4 and 9 have cycle 2, and 0, 1, 5, 6 have cycle 1.
Can I use negative remainders?

Yes, they often simplify work. A remainder of 11 when dividing by 12 can be treated as −1, so 11⁵⁰ divided by 12 leaves (−1)⁵⁰ = 1. Convert back to a positive remainder at the end if the result is negative.

items.title: HCF and LCM Shortcuts with Real-Life Word Problems
items.description: HCF and LCM by prime factorisation, the product rule, remainder-based questions, bells and lights, and tile-cutting problems with worked solutions.
items.intro: HCF (highest common factor) and LCM (least common multiple) questions are standard in SSC CGL, CHSL and MTS, usually two questions per paper, and they support many bank-exam topics such as time and work (LCM of days) and circular-track meetings. The concepts are simple, but word problems hide them: bells ringing together point to LCM, while cutting the largest equal pieces points to HCF.

concepts.heading: Finding HCF and LCM
concepts.text: Write each number in prime factors. HCF takes the lowest power of each common prime; LCM takes the highest power of every prime present. 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5, so HCF = 2³ × 3 = 24 and LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.

concepts.heading: Product rule
concepts.text: For two numbers only, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers. If HCF = 12, LCM = 336 and one number is 48, the other is 12 × 336 ÷ 48 = 84. This rule does not hold for three or more numbers.

concepts.heading: HCF word problems
concepts.text: Use HCF when the question asks for the largest size, the greatest number dividing several numbers, or cutting things into the biggest equal pieces. If remainders are given, subtract them first: the largest number dividing 245 and 1029 leaving 5 is HCF(240, 1024) = 16.

concepts.heading: LCM word problems
concepts.text: Use LCM when events repeat and you want them to coincide (bells, traffic lights, runners) or for the smallest number divisible by several numbers. For "leaves remainder r in each case", answer = LCM + r.

concepts.heading: Fractions
concepts.text: HCF of fractions = HCF of numerators ÷ LCM of denominators; LCM of fractions = LCM of numerators ÷ HCF of denominators.
concepts.formula: LCM(a/b, c/d) = LCM(a, c) / HCF(b, d)

shortcuts: HCF always divides LCM, and HCF ≤ smaller number ≤ LCM — use this to reject options.
Co-prime numbers have HCF 1, so their LCM is their product.
For different remainders with a constant difference (divisor − remainder same), answer = LCM − that difference.
Tiles question: number of square tiles = area ÷ (HCF side)².

examples.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 120.
Three bells toll at intervals of 6, 8 and 12 minutes. If they toll together at 9:00 a.m., when will they next toll together?
examples.solution: LCM(6, 8, 12) = 24 minutes, so at 9:24 a.m.

examples.question: Find the largest number that divides 245 and 1029 leaving a remainder of 5 in each case.
examples.solution: Subtract the remainder: 240 and 1,024. HCF(240, 1024) = 16. Answer: 16.

examples.question: Find the smallest number that leaves a remainder of 4 when divided by 12, 15 and 20.
A hall floor is 6.24 m by 4.32 m. Find the largest square tile that fits exactly and the number of tiles needed.
examples.solution: In cm: 624 and 432. HCF = 48 cm. Tiles = (624/48) × (432/48) = 13 × 9 = 117. Converting to centimetres first matters, because the HCF of decimals is awkward to find directly.

examples.question: Find the HCF and LCM of the fractions 2/3, 4/9 and 8/15.
examples.solution: HCF = HCF(2, 4, 8) ÷ LCM(3, 9, 15) = 2 ÷ 45 = 2/45. LCM = LCM(2, 4, 8) ÷ HCF(3, 9, 15) = 8 ÷ 3 = 8/3. Check that 8/3 ÷ 4/9 = 6, a whole number, so 8/3 is indeed a multiple of 4/9.

practice: The LCM of 18, 24 and 36 is:
18 = 2 × 3², 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3², so the LCM is 2³ × 3² = 72.
The HCF of 84 and 126 is:
The HCF of two numbers is 16 and their LCM is 480. If one number is 96, the other is:
Other number = 16 × 480 ÷ 96 = 7,680 ÷ 96 = 80, using HCF × LCM = product.
Three lights blink every 20, 30 and 45 seconds. If they blink together now, they next blink together after:
3 minutes
90 seconds
2 minutes
6 minutes
LCM(20, 30, 45) = 180 seconds, which equals 3 minutes, when all three coincide again.
The largest number that divides 410, 751 and 1,030 leaving remainder 7 in each case is:
Subtract 7 to get 403, 744 and 1,023, whose HCF is 31 (13 × 31, 24 × 31 and 33 × 31).
faqs: How do I decide between HCF and LCM in a word problem?

Ask whether the answer should be smaller or larger than the given numbers. Cutting, dividing or grouping into the largest equal parts gives a smaller answer, so use HCF. Repeating events meeting again or a number divisible by all gives a larger answer, so use LCM.
Does HCF × LCM = product work for three numbers?
No. The rule holds only for two numbers. For three numbers, compute HCF and LCM from prime factorisation directly. Applying the two-number rule to three numbers is a common trap in SSC questions.

items.title: Surds and Indices: Laws of Exponents and Simplification
items.description: Laws of indices, fractional and negative powers, simplifying and rationalising surds and comparing roots, with fully solved SSC and bank examples.
items.intro: Surds and indices are a regular part of SSC CGL and CHSL (one or two questions), feed into bank-exam simplification blocks, and form the algebraic base for CAT topics like logarithms and exponential equations. The rules are few and mechanical; the exam challenge is applying them without sign errors, especially with negative and fractional exponents, and recognising when to rationalise a denominator.

concepts.heading: Laws of indices
concepts.text: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ; a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. These apply only when the bases are the same; convert 8, 16, 32 to powers of 2 and 9, 27, 81 to powers of 3 before combining.

concepts.heading: Fractional powers
concepts.text: a^(p/q) = (q-th root of a)ᵖ. Take the root first to keep numbers small: 27^(2/3) = (∛27)² = 3² = 9; 16^(−3/4) = 1/(⁴√16)³ = 1/8.

concepts.heading: Simplifying surds
concepts.text: Take out the largest perfect-square factor: √72 = 6√2, √50 = 5√2, √18 = 3√2. Like surds (same number under the root) can then be added or subtracted like algebraic terms: 6√2 + 5√2 − 3√2 = 8√2.

concepts.heading: Rationalising
concepts.text: To remove a surd from a denominator, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate. 1/(√5 − √3) × (√5 + √3)/(√5 + √3) = (√5 + √3)/(5 − 3) = (√5 + √3)/2.

concepts.heading: Comparing surds
concepts.text: To compare roots of different orders, raise all of them to the LCM of the orders. To compare ∛4, √3 and ⁶√10, raise to the 6th power: 16, 27 and 10. So √3 is the largest and ⁶√10 the smallest.

shortcuts: Equal bases: if aˣ = aʸ then x = y — the key step in exponential equations.
Powers of 2 to 2¹⁰ and powers of 3 to 3⁶ should be instant: 1,024 and 729.
(√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b — the basis of rationalisation.
A negative base with a fractional power needs care; exam questions avoid it.
Square root of a surd sum: √(a + 2√b) = √x + √y where x + y = a and xy = b. For example, √(5 + 2√6) = √3 + √2 because 3 + 2 = 5 and 3 × 2 = 6.
When an equation has different bases such as 4ˣ = 8, rewrite both sides with a common base: 2²ˣ = 2³ gives x = 3/2.

examples.question: Simplify 2⁵ × 2⁻³ ÷ 2⁻¹.
examples.solution: All terms have base 2, so combine the exponents: multiplication adds and division subtracts. 5 + (−3) − (−1) = 5 − 3 + 1 = 3. Answer = 2³ = 8. The double negative in dividing by 2⁻¹ is where most mistakes happen.

examples.question: Find the values of 27^(2/3) and 16^(−3/4).
Simplify √72 + √50 − √18.
Rationalise 1/(√5 − √3).
examples.solution: Multiply by (√5 + √3)/(√5 + √3): numerator √5 + √3, denominator 5 − 3 = 2. Answer = (√5 + √3)/2.

examples.question: If 3ˣ⁺² = 243, find x.
examples.solution: Write 243 as a power of 3: 3⁵ = 243. Since the bases are equal, the exponents must be equal, so x + 2 = 5 and x = 3. Check: 3⁵ = 243.

examples.question: Which is the largest: ∛4, √3 or ⁶√10?
examples.solution: LCM of 3, 2 and 6 is 6. Raising each to the 6th power gives 4² = 16, 3³ = 27 and 10. The largest is √3.

practice: The exponent is 7 − 4 + (−2) = 1, so the value is 5¹ = 5 using the laws of indices.
Take the cube root first: ∛64 = 4, and then square it to get 4² = 16.
√98 = 7√2 and √32 = 4√2, so their difference is 3√2; surds cannot be subtracted under one root.
32 = 2⁵, so 2x − 1 = 5 and x = 3 by equating the exponents of the same base.
Multiplying by the conjugate gives (√3 − √2)/(3 − 2) = √3 − √2 as the rationalised form.
faqs: Why is any number to the power 0 equal to 1?

Because aⁿ ÷ aⁿ = 1, and by the division law it also equals aⁿ⁻ⁿ = a⁰. For consistency a⁰ must be 1. The only exception is 0⁰, which is left undefined in school mathematics and does not appear in exams.
When should I rationalise the denominator?

Whenever options are written without surds in the denominator, or when you need to add fractions with surd denominators. Rationalising makes the forms comparable. In comparison questions, squaring both sides is often quicker than rationalising.

items.title: Linear Equations in Two Variables: Exam Word Problems
items.description: Solve linear equations by elimination and substitution, translate word problems on coins, prices, digits and fractions, and test for consistency.
items.intro: Linear equations are the hidden engine behind ages, partnership, mixtures and many data-sufficiency statements. SSC CGL and CHSL ask direct questions on pairs of equations and word problems, IBPS PO and SBI PO use them inside arithmetic and DS, and CAT expects fast algebraic translation. The main skills are writing the right equations from words and solving them with the least arithmetic, often by adding or subtracting the equations whole.

concepts.heading: Elimination
concepts.text: Make the coefficient of one variable equal in both equations and add or subtract. For 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 2y = 16, adding eliminates y: 8x = 32, x = 4, then y = 2. Elimination is usually the fastest method in exams.

concepts.heading: Symmetric equations
concepts.text: When the equations are mirror images, such as 5p + 3n = 110 and 3p + 5n = 130, add them to get p + n and subtract them to get p − n. Then solve the two simple equations. This trick saves time in price-of-items questions.

concepts.heading: Translating word problems
concepts.text: Name each unknown, write one equation for each fact and check units. Coins: count equation and value equation. Digits: a two-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b is 10a + b; reversing gives 10b + a, so the difference is 9(a − b).

concepts.heading: Consistency
concepts.text: For a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂: a unique solution if a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂; no solution if a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ (parallel lines); infinitely many if all three ratios are equal (same line).

shortcuts: Two numbers from sum S and difference D: (S + D)/2 and (S − D)/2.
Reversing a two-digit number changes it by 9 × (difference of digits).
Substitute options back into both equations — often faster than solving in MCQs.
If the question asks for x + y, look for a combination of equations that gives it directly.
Keep fractions as fractions until the last step to avoid rounding errors.

examples.question: Solve 3x + 2y = 16 and 5x − 2y = 16.
examples.solution: Add: 8x = 32, so x = 4. Then 3(4) + 2y = 16 gives y = 2.

examples.question: The sum of two numbers is 50 and their difference is 14. Find the numbers.
A purse has 40 coins of ₹2 and ₹5, worth ₹119 in all. How many ₹5 coins are there?
examples.solution: x + y = 40 and 2x + 5y = 119. Subtract twice the first: 3y = 39, y = 13. So 13 coins of ₹5 and 27 of ₹2.

examples.question: A fraction becomes 1/2 when 1 is added to its numerator and 1/3 when 1 is added to its denominator. Find the fraction.
examples.solution: (n + 1)/d = 1/2 gives d = 2n + 2; n/(d + 1) = 1/3 gives d = 3n − 1. So 2n + 2 = 3n − 1, n = 3 and d = 8. The fraction is 3/8.

examples.question: For what value of k does kx + 2y = 5, 3x + y = 1 have no solution?
examples.solution: Need k/3 = 2/1 ≠ 5/1. So k = 6; the third ratio 5 ≠ 2 confirms the lines are parallel. Geometrically, both equations then describe lines with the same slope but different intercepts, so they never meet and no (x, y) satisfies both.

practice: If 2x + 3y = 13 and x − y = −1, then x + y = ?
From x = y − 1, 2(y − 1) + 3y = 13 gives y = 3 and x = 2, so x + y = 5.
The sum of two numbers is 75 and their difference is 15. The larger number is:
Larger number = (sum + difference)/2 = (75 + 15)/2 = 45, and the smaller is 30.
5 pens and 3 notebooks cost ₹110; 3 pens and 5 notebooks cost ₹130. The price of a notebook is:
Adding gives p + n = 30 and subtracting gives n − p = 10, so a notebook costs ₹20.
The digits of a two-digit number add up to 9. Reversing the digits increases the number by 27. The number is:
a + b = 9 and 9(b − a) = 27 give b − a = 3, so a = 3, b = 6 and the number is 36.
For what value of k do 2x + ky = 7 and 4x + 6y = 9 have no solution?
Need 2/4 = k/6, so k = 3, while 7/9 is different from 1/2, confirming parallel lines.
faqs: Which method is fastest for two linear equations in exams?

Elimination is usually fastest, especially when coefficients match or are mirror images. Substitution works well when one equation already gives a variable directly, like x = y − 1. In MCQs, substituting the options is often quickest of all.
How do linear equations appear in data sufficiency?

Each statement often gives one equation. Two independent equations in two unknowns are sufficient together; one alone usually is not. Watch for statements that are multiples of each other — they give the same line and are not independent.

items.title: Algebraic Identities for SSC: x + 1/x and Cube Tricks
items.description: Key algebraic identities for SSC and CAT: squares, cubes, x + 1/x forms, a + b + c = 0 rule and difference of squares, with verified worked examples.
items.intro: Algebra carries real weight in SSC CGL Tier 1 and Tier 2 and SSC CHSL, where three to five questions test identities such as x + 1/x, a³ + b³ and the a + b + c = 0 rule. CAT and CMAT also rely on them. Bank exams rarely ask algebra directly, but the same identities speed up simplification. Almost every question becomes a one- or two-line substitution once you know which identity to apply.

concepts.heading: Square identities
concepts.text: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). From a + b and ab you can find a² + b² = (a + b)² − 2ab and (a − b)² = (a + b)² − 4ab.

concepts.heading: Cube identities
concepts.text: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b), so a³ + b³ = (a + b)³ − 3ab(a + b). Similarly a³ − b³ = (a − b)³ + 3ab(a − b). These turn cube questions into arithmetic once a ± b and ab are known.

concepts.heading: The x + 1/x family
concepts.text: If x + 1/x = k, then x² + 1/x² = k² − 2 and x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k. If x − 1/x = k, then x² + 1/x² = k² + 2. For higher powers, square again: x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = (x² + 1/x²)² − 2.

concepts.heading: The a + b + c = 0 rule
concepts.text: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca). So if a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc. With 1, 2 and −3: 1 + 8 − 27 = −18 = 3 × 1 × 2 × (−3).
concepts.formula: If a + b + c = 0: a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc

shortcuts: Products near round numbers: 998 × 1002 = 1000² − 2² = 9,99,996.
101² − 99² = 200 × 2 = 400 — difference of squares beats squaring.
Test identity questions with simple values like x = 1 or a = 1, b = 0 to eliminate options.
If x + 1/x = 2, then x = 1 and every power sum xⁿ + 1/xⁿ = 2.
If x + 1/x = −2, x = −1; alternating signs appear for odd powers.

examples.question: If x + 1/x = 5, find x² + 1/x² and x³ + 1/x³.
If a + b = 10 and ab = 21, find a² + b² and a − b.
examples.solution: a² + b² = 100 − 42 = 58. (a − b)² = 100 − 84 = 16, so a − b = ±4 (the numbers are 7 and 3).

examples.question: Find a³ + b³ + c³ if a = 1, b = 2, c = −3.
examples.solution: a + b + c = 0, so a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc = 3 × 1 × 2 × (−3) = −18. Direct check: 1 + 8 − 27 = −18.

examples.question: Evaluate 101² − 99².
If x − 1/x = 3, find x² + 1/x².
examples.solution: Square both sides: x² − 2 + 1/x² = 9, so x² + 1/x² = 11.

practice: If x + 1/x = 4, then x² + 1/x² = ?
Square both sides: x² + 2 + 1/x² = 16, so x² + 1/x² = 14.
If a + b = 7 and ab = 12, then a² + b² = ?
a² + b² = (a + b)² − 2ab = 49 − 24 = 25, consistent with a = 3 and b = 4.
If x + 1/x = 3, then x³ + 1/x³ = ?
Use k³ − 3k with k = 3: 27 − 9 = 18 for the sum of cubes and reciprocal cubes.
If a − b = 3 and ab = 10, then a³ − b³ = ?
a³ − b³ = (a − b)³ + 3ab(a − b) = 27 + 90 = 117, matching a = 5 and b = 2.
faqs: Why do SSC exams ask so many x + 1/x questions?

Because they test whether a student can manipulate identities rather than solve for x, which is often irrational. A few standard results — k² − 2, k³ − 3k — answer most variants in seconds, so they are good discriminators of preparation.
Can I solve identity questions by picking numbers?

Often yes. If a question holds for all values satisfying a condition, choose simple values that meet it, such as a = 1, b = 2, c = −3 for a + b + c = 0, and test each option. Use this when the algebra seems long.

items.title: Logarithm Rules and Tricks for CAT and Other MBA Exams
items.description: Logarithm laws, change of base, log tables with log 2 and log 3, digit-count questions and log equations explained with verified solved examples.
items.intro: Logarithms are a core algebra topic in CAT, CMAT and MAT, typically giving one or two questions, and they also appear in SSC CGL Tier 2 and some RBI Grade B papers. Questions are usually short — evaluate an expression, solve a log equation or count the digits of a large power — but each one tests whether the basic laws are second nature. Treat a logarithm simply as an exponent and most questions become easy.

concepts.heading: Definition
concepts.text: log_a N = x means aˣ = N, with a > 0, a ≠ 1 and N > 0. So log₂ 64 = 6 because 2⁶ = 64. Common logarithms use base 10 (log 1000 = 3); natural logarithms use base e. log_a 1 = 0 and log_a a = 1 for any valid base.

concepts.heading: Laws
concepts.text: log(mn) = log m + log n; log(m/n) = log m − log n; log(mᵖ) = p log m. These let you break numbers into primes: log 72 = log(2³ × 3²) = 3 log 2 + 2 log 3. With log 2 ≈ 0.3010 and log 3 ≈ 0.4771, log 72 ≈ 1.8572.

concepts.heading: Change of base
concepts.text: log_a b = log b / log a in any common base. A useful consequence is log_a b × log_b c = log_a c, so chains of logs collapse: log₂ 3 × log₃ 32 = log₂ 32 = 5. Also log_a b = 1/log_b a.
concepts.formula: log_a b = log_c b / log_c a

concepts.heading: Equations with logs
concepts.text: To solve a log equation, combine logs on each side into a single log using the laws, then convert to exponential form. For log x + log(x − 3) = 1 (base 10), write log[x(x − 3)] = 1, so x² − 3x = 10 and x = 5 or −2. Reject −2 because log of a negative number is undefined.

concepts.heading: Number of digits
concepts.text: The number of digits in a positive integer N is ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1. For 2⁵⁰, log = 50 × 0.30103 ≈ 15.05, so 2⁵⁰ has 16 digits. This is a classic CAT-style application.

shortcuts: log 4 + log 25 = log 100 = 2 — look for pairs that multiply to powers of 10.
In log equations, always check that the arguments stay positive for your solution.
log_a b = log_{aⁿ} bⁿ — useful to match bases like 4 and 2.
If log_a x = log_a y, then x = y; equal logs with equal bases mean equal arguments.

examples.question: Evaluate log₂ 64.
examples.solution: Ask "2 to what power gives 64?" Since 2⁶ = 64, log₂ 64 = 6. Reading every logarithm as a question about exponents is the quickest way to evaluate simple logs.

examples.question: Evaluate log 8 + log 125 (base 10).
examples.solution: Adding logs multiplies the arguments: log 8 + log 125 = log(8 × 125) = log 1,000 = 3. Spotting that 8 × 125 is a power of 10 is the whole trick; computing each log separately would need tables.

examples.question: Evaluate log₃ 81 − log₃ 9.
examples.solution: Subtracting logs divides the arguments: log₃(81/9) = log₃ 9 = 2. Alternatively, 4 − 2 = 2, since log₃ 81 = 4 and log₃ 9 = 2.

examples.question: Given log 2 = 0.3010 and log 3 = 0.4771, find log 72.
How many digits does 2⁵⁰ have? (log 2 = 0.30103)
Solve log₂(x + 3) = 4.
examples.solution: x + 3 = 2⁴ = 16, so x = 13. The argument 16 is positive, so the solution is valid.

practice: log₅ 625 = ?
Since 5⁴ = 625, the logarithm of 625 to base 5 equals 4 by definition.
log 4 + log 25 (base 10) = ?
Adding logs multiplies the arguments: 4 × 25 = 100, and log 100 = 2 in base 10.
log₂ 3 × log₃ 32 = ?
The chain rule gives log₂ 32 = 5, because the intermediate base 3 cancels out.
If log 2 = 0.3010 and log 3 = 0.4771, then log 18 = ?
How many digits does 3²⁰ have? (log 3 = 0.4771)
log 3²⁰ = 20 × 0.4771 = 9.542, so the number of digits is 9 + 1 = 10.
faqs: Why can’t the logarithm of a negative number be taken?

Because a positive base raised to any real power is always positive, so no real exponent gives a negative or zero result. That is why log equations require positive arguments, and solutions that make an argument negative must be rejected.
Do I need to memorise log tables?

No full tables are needed. Knowing log 2, log 3 and log 7 to four decimal places lets you compute logs of most composite numbers used in exams, since log 5 = 1 − log 2 and others follow from the laws.

items.title: Arithmetic and Geometric Progressions: Formulas and Tricks
items.description: AP and GP nth term and sum formulas, counting multiples in a range, infinite GP sums and savings-plan word problems, with worked examples.
items.intro: Progressions appear in CAT, CMAT and MAT every year and in SSC CGL as a regular algebra topic. Bank exams use them indirectly: number series often hide an AP or GP, and data sufficiency statements may describe equally spaced values. The formulas are compact, and many questions — counting multiples of 7 between two numbers, totalling a monthly savings plan — are simple once you recognise the progression.

concepts.heading: Arithmetic progression (AP)
concepts.text: Each term increases by a constant difference d. The n-th term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of n terms is n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], or n/2 × (first + last). The average of an AP equals the average of its first and last terms.

concepts.heading: Counting terms
concepts.text: The number of terms in an AP from a to l with difference d is (l − a)/d + 1. Two-digit multiples of 7 run from 14 to 98, giving (98 − 14)/7 + 1 = 13 numbers. This formula avoids listing.

concepts.heading: Geometric progression (GP)
concepts.text: Each term is multiplied by a constant ratio r. The n-th term is a·rⁿ⁻¹ and the sum of n terms is a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1. For |r| < 1, the infinite sum converges to a/(1 − r).

concepts.heading: Means
concepts.text: The arithmetic mean of a and b is (a + b)/2; the geometric mean is √(ab). For positive numbers, AM ≥ GM, with equality only when a = b. This inequality is used in CAT to find minimum or maximum values.

shortcuts: Sum of first n natural numbers = n(n + 1)/2; of first n even numbers = n(n + 1); of first n odd numbers = n².
If three numbers are in AP, write them as a − d, a, a + d; in GP, as a/r, a, ar — the algebra simplifies.
Middle term of an AP with an odd number of terms equals the average of all terms.
A GP with ratio 2 doubles: its n-th term is larger than the sum of all previous terms.
Increase-by-fixed-amount plans (salary, savings) are APs; increase-by-percentage plans are GPs.

examples.question: Find the 20th term of 7, 11, 15, …
Find the sum of the first 25 terms of 3, 8, 13, …
How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 7?
examples.solution: The smallest two-digit multiple of 7 is 14 and the largest is 98. These form an AP with d = 7. Count = (98 − 14)/7 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13. Forgetting the "+ 1" is the most common error and gives the trap option 12.

examples.question: Find the 8th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, …
Find the sum of the infinite GP 18, 6, 2, …
Priya saves ₹500 in the first month and increases her saving by ₹100 every month. How much does she save in a year?

practice: The 15th term of the AP 5, 9, 13, … is:
The sum 2 + 4 + 6 + … + 60 equals:
There are 30 even numbers, and their sum is n(n + 1) = 30 × 31 = 930.
How many three-digit numbers are divisible by 9?
They run from 108 to 999, so the count is (999 − 108)/9 + 1 = 99 + 1 = 100.
The sum of the first 6 terms of the GP 2, 6, 18, … is:
The sum of the infinite GP 1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + … is:
S∞ = a/(1 − r) = 1 ÷ (2/3) = 3/2, since the ratio 1/3 is less than 1.
faqs: How do I identify whether a series is an AP or a GP?

Subtract consecutive terms: a constant difference means AP. Divide consecutive terms: a constant ratio means GP. If neither is constant, it may be a mixed series, such as differences forming an AP, which is common in bank number-series questions.
When does an infinite GP have a finite sum?

Only when the common ratio lies strictly between −1 and 1. Then the terms shrink towards zero and the total approaches a/(1 − r). For a ratio of 1 or more in size, the terms do not shrink and the sum grows without limit.

items.title: Trigonometry for SSC: Ratios, Values and Identities
items.description: Trigonometric ratios, standard angle values, Pythagorean identities, complementary angles and sec ± tan tricks for SSC CGL and CHSL, with examples.
items.intro: Trigonometry is an important part of SSC CGL and CHSL, contributing three to five questions per paper, and it underpins heights and distances. Bank exams do not test it. Most SSC trigonometry questions need only the standard-angle table, three identities and the complementary-angle rule. With those, questions that look like heavy algebra reduce to one or two lines.

concepts.heading: Ratios and the standard table
concepts.text: In a right triangle, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent; cosec, sec and cot are their reciprocals. Standard values: sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = 1/√2, sin 60° = √3/2, sin 90° = 1; cos reverses this order; tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3.

concepts.heading: Pythagorean identities
concepts.text: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; sec²θ − tan²θ = 1; cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1. The last two factor as (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1, so if sec θ + tan θ = 2, then sec θ − tan θ = 1/2.

concepts.heading: Complementary angles
concepts.text: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ and sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ. So sin²17° + sin²73° = sin²17° + cos²17° = 1, and tan 10° tan 80° = tan 10° cot 10° = 1.

concepts.heading: Reciprocal pairs
concepts.text: cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ and cot θ = 1/tan θ, so sin θ × cosec θ = 1 and tan θ × cot θ = 1. Many SSC simplifications end with one of these products, so rewrite every ratio in terms of sin and cos when an expression looks messy.

concepts.heading: Finding ratios from one ratio
concepts.text: Given one ratio of an acute angle, draw a right triangle with those sides and find the third side by Pythagoras. tan θ = 3/4 gives a 3-4-5 triangle, so sin θ = 3/5 and cos θ = 4/5.

shortcuts: Angles adding to 90° in a product of tans cancel in pairs.
Substitute θ = 45° or 30° to test identity-based options quickly.
1/(1 + tan²θ) = cos²θ and 1/(1 + cot²θ) = sin²θ.
Triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 give ratios like 12/13 and 8/17 directly.

examples.question: Find sin 30° + cos 60° + tan 45°.
examples.solution: From the table, sin 30° = 1/2, cos 60° = 1/2 and tan 45° = 1. The sum is 1/2 + 1/2 + 1 = 2. Note that sin 30° = cos 60° is itself an example of the complementary-angle rule.

examples.question: If tan θ = 3/4 and θ is acute, find sin θ + cos θ.
examples.solution: Draw a right triangle with opposite side 3 and adjacent side 4; the hypotenuse is √(9 + 16) = 5. Then sin θ = 3/5 and cos θ = 4/5, so the sum is 7/5. The actual angle (about 36.87°) is never needed.

examples.question: Evaluate sin²17° + sin²73°.
examples.solution: sin 73° = cos 17°, so the expression is sin²17° + cos²17° = 1.

examples.question: If sec θ + tan θ = 2, find sec θ − tan θ.
examples.solution: Since sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, (sec θ − tan θ) = 1/(sec θ + tan θ) = 1/2.

examples.question: Evaluate tan 10° × tan 20° × tan 70° × tan 80°.
examples.solution: tan 80° = cot 10° and tan 70° = cot 20°. Pairs multiply to 1, so the product is 1.

examples.question: Simplify sin²θ + 1/(1 + tan²θ).
examples.solution: Since 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, the second term is 1/sec²θ = cos²θ. The expression becomes sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every θ where it is defined. Checking with θ = 45°: 1/2 + 1/(1 + 1) = 1, which confirms the answer.

practice: sin 30° and cos 60° both equal 1/2, so 2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/2.
If cos θ = 5/13 and θ is acute, then tan θ = ?
The triangle is 5-12-13 with adjacent side 5 and opposite side 12, so tan θ = 12/5.
cos²25° + cos²65° = ?
cos 65° = sin 25°, so the expression becomes cos²25° + sin²25°, which equals 1.
If cosec θ − cot θ = 1/3, then cosec θ + cot θ = ?
Since cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1, the sum is the reciprocal of the difference, which is 3.
tan²60° − sec²45° = ?
tan²60° = 3 and sec²45° = 2, so the difference is 3 − 2 = 1.
faqs: Do bank exams ask trigonometry?

No. IBPS, SBI and RBI quantitative sections focus on arithmetic, DI and number-based topics. Trigonometry is important for SSC CGL and CHSL and for some state-level exams. Bank aspirants can skip it unless they are also preparing for SSC.
How do I remember which ratios are positive in which quadrant?

SSC questions almost always use acute angles, where all ratios are positive. If an obtuse angle appears, use the rule "All, Sin, Tan, Cos" for quadrants one to four: only the named ratios and their reciprocals are positive in each quadrant.

items.title: Heights and Distances: Angle of Elevation and Depression
items.description: Solve heights and distances questions on towers, ladders, shadows and moving observers using 30°, 45° and 60° ratios, with clear step-by-step working.
items.intro: Heights and distances is the applied side of trigonometry and a steady one- or two-question topic in SSC CGL and CHSL. The setting is always a right triangle formed by a vertical object, the ground and a line of sight, and almost every question uses 30°, 45° or 60°. Drawing a quick sketch and labelling the known side is more important than any formula.

concepts.heading: Elevation and depression
concepts.text: The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to the line of sight; the angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal at the observer’s eye. Because the horizontal lines at the top and bottom are parallel, the angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom.

concepts.heading: Choosing the ratio
concepts.text: Use tan when height and horizontal distance are involved (most questions), sin when the slant length (a ladder or a kite string) and height are involved, and cos for slant length and horizontal distance. tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3.

concepts.heading: Two-angle questions
concepts.text: When an observer walks d metres towards a tower and the elevation changes from α to β, write the two horizontal distances as h cot α and h cot β. Their difference is d. For 30° and 60°, h(√3 − 1/√3) = d, so h = d√3/2.

concepts.heading: Shadows
concepts.text: The shadow is the horizontal side and the object is the vertical side; the sun’s elevation is the angle at the tip of the shadow. When the shadow equals the height, the elevation is 45°. A shadow √3 times the height means 30°.

shortcuts: 30°–60° triangle sides are in the ratio 1 : √3 : 2; 45° triangle sides are 1 : 1 : √2.
Elevation 30° → 60° walking d towards a tower: height = (√3/2)d and the final distance = d/2.
Use √3 ≈ 1.732 only at the end; keep answers in surd form if options are in surds.
If two objects are on opposite sides of a tower, add the horizontal distances; on the same side, subtract.

examples.question: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 20 m from its foot is 60°. Find the height.
A 10 m ladder leans against a wall, making 60° with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
examples.solution: Ladder is the hypotenuse, height is opposite: h = 10 × sin 60° = 5√3 ≈ 8.66 m.

examples.question: From the top of a 50 m building, the angle of depression of a car is 30°. How far is the car from the building?
examples.solution: Angle of elevation from the car is also 30°. Distance = 50 ÷ tan 30° = 50√3 ≈ 86.6 m.

examples.question: The elevation of a tower’s top changes from 30° to 60° as an observer walks 40 m towards it. Find the height.
examples.solution: h cot 30° − h cot 60° = 40 → h(√3 − 1/√3) = 40 → h × 2/√3 = 40 → h = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m. The observer’s final distance from the tower is h/√3 = 20 m.

examples.question: A pole’s shadow is equal to its height. What is the sun’s angle of elevation?
examples.solution: tan θ = height/shadow = 1, so θ = 45°. Later in the afternoon, when the shadow becomes √3 times the height, tan θ = 1/√3 and the sun’s elevation has dropped to 30°.

practice: A pole casts a shadow of 10√3 m when the sun’s elevation is 30°. The pole’s height is:
Height = shadow × tan 30° = 10√3 × 1/√3 = 10 m, as the shadow is the horizontal side.
A kite string 100 m long makes 30° with the ground. The kite’s height is:
The string is the hypotenuse, so height = 100 × sin 30° = 100 × 1/2 = 50 m.
From a point 30√3 m from a 30 m tower, the angle of elevation of the top is:
tan θ = 30/(30√3) = 1/√3, which corresponds to an angle of elevation of 30 degrees.
Walking 20 m towards a tower changes the elevation from 30° to 60°. The tower’s height is:
Using h = d√3/2 for the 30°–60° case with d = 20 gives h = 10√3 m, about 17.32 m.
From the top of a 75 m lighthouse, the angle of depression of a boat is 45°. The boat’s distance from the lighthouse is:
At 45°, tan θ = 1, so the horizontal distance equals the height of the lighthouse, 75 m.
faqs: Is the angle of depression measured from the vertical?

No. Both elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal line through the observer’s eye. Measuring from the vertical gives the complementary angle and a wrong answer. Draw the horizontal line explicitly in your sketch.
Should I use √3 = 1.732 or keep surds?
Look at the options. If they contain √3, keep the surd form throughout. If they are decimals, substitute 1.732 at the very end to avoid rounding errors building up during the calculation.

items.title: Triangle Geometry: Angles, Similarity and Centres
items.description: Triangle properties for SSC and CAT: angle sum, exterior angles, similarity, Pythagoras, centroid, incentre and angle bisector theorem with examples.
items.intro: Geometry carries significant weight in SSC CGL (four to six questions) and CHSL, and triangles are its biggest sub-topic. CAT and CMAT also test triangle properties inside harder problems. The questions reward knowing a set of facts — angle sum, similarity ratios, properties of the centroid and incentre — and applying them quickly, rather than long constructions or proofs.

concepts.heading: Angles
concepts.text: The interior angles of a triangle add to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. The largest side is opposite the largest angle. If the angles are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4, they are 40°, 60° and 80°.
concepts.formula: Exterior angle = sum of opposite interior angles

concepts.heading: Pythagoras and triangle types
concepts.text: In a right triangle, hypotenuse² = sum of the squares of the other sides. For any triangle with sides a ≤ b ≤ c: c² = a² + b² means right-angled, c² < a² + b² acute, c² > a² + b² obtuse. Each side must be less than the sum of the other two.

concepts.heading: Similarity
concepts.text: Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides. The ratio of their areas is the square of the ratio of corresponding sides, and so is the ratio of the squares of their altitudes or medians. Sides 3 : 5 give areas 9 : 25.

concepts.heading: Centres
concepts.text: The centroid (meeting point of medians) divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1 from the vertex. The incentre (meeting point of angle bisectors) satisfies ∠BIC = 90° + A/2. The circumcentre is equidistant from the vertices; in a right triangle it is the mid-point of the hypotenuse.

concepts.heading: Angle bisector and mid-point theorems
concepts.text: The bisector of angle A divides BC in the ratio AB : AC. The segment joining the mid-points of two sides is parallel to the third side and half its length.

shortcuts: Equilateral triangle of side a: height (√3/2)a, area (√3/4)a², inradius a/(2√3), circumradius a/√3.
In a right triangle, the median to the hypotenuse equals half the hypotenuse.
Area of a triangle formed by joining mid-points is 1/4 of the original.
Medians divide a triangle into six triangles of equal area.

examples.question: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find them.
examples.solution: Total parts = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9, and these share 180°, so one part = 20°. Angles: 40°, 60°, 80°. All are less than 90°, so the triangle is acute-angled.

examples.question: An exterior angle of a triangle is 110° and one opposite interior angle is 45°. Find the other opposite interior angle.
examples.solution: Exterior angle = sum of opposite interior angles, so the other is 110° − 45° = 65°.

examples.question: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 3 : 5. Find the ratio of their areas.
examples.solution: Area ratio = 3² : 5² = 9 : 25.

examples.question: In triangle ABC, median AD = 12 cm and G is the centroid. Find AG.
examples.solution: The centroid divides the median 2 : 1 from the vertex, so AG = 2/3 × 12 = 8 cm and GD = 4 cm.

examples.question: In triangle ABC, AB = 6 cm, AC = 9 cm and BC = 10 cm. The bisector of angle A meets BC at D. Find BD.
examples.solution: By the angle bisector theorem, BD : DC = AB : AC = 6 : 9 = 2 : 3. BD = 10 × 2/5 = 4 cm and DC = 6 cm. A quick check: 4 + 6 = 10, the full length of BC.

practice: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. The largest angle is:
Six parts make 180°, so one part is 30° and the largest angle is 3 × 30° = 90°.
A right triangle has legs 9 cm and 12 cm. Its hypotenuse is:
13 cm
15 cm
16 cm
21 cm
Hypotenuse = √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15 cm, a multiple of the 3-4-5 triple.
The areas of two similar triangles are in the ratio 16 : 49. Their corresponding sides are in the ratio:
Sides are in the square-root ratio of areas, so √16 : √49 = 4 : 7.
The height of an equilateral triangle with side 6√3 cm is:
9 cm
6 cm
3√3 cm
12 cm
Height = (√3/2) × 6√3 = 3 × 3 = 9 cm, using the standard equilateral-triangle formula.
In triangle ABC, ∠A = 60° and I is the incentre. ∠BIC equals:
∠BIC = 90° + A/2 = 90° + 30° = 120°, from the incentre angle property.
faqs: Which triangle centres are most important for SSC?

The centroid (2 : 1 median ratio), the incentre (∠BIC = 90° + A/2) and the circumcentre (∠BOC = 2A for an acute triangle) cover most questions. The orthocentre property ∠BHC = 180° − A also appears occasionally. Learn all four angle results together.
How do I quickly check whether three lengths form a triangle?

Check that the sum of the two smaller lengths exceeds the largest. If it equals or is less than the largest, no triangle is possible. To classify the triangle, compare the square of the largest side with the sum of squares of the others.

items.title: Circle Theorems: Chords, Tangents and Cyclic Quadrilaterals
items.description: Circle geometry for SSC CGL and CAT: chord distance, angles at centre, cyclic quadrilaterals, tangent lengths, intersecting chords and common tangents.
items.intro: Circle geometry is the second pillar of SSC CGL geometry after triangles and often yields two questions per shift. CAT also tests circle theorems in combination with triangles. The theorems are few and visual: a perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°, and tangents meet radii at right angles.

concepts.heading: Chords
concepts.text: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it. So for a chord of length 2l at distance d from the centre of a circle with radius r, r² = l² + d². Equal chords are equidistant from the centre.

concepts.heading: Angles in a circle
concepts.text: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is twice the angle it subtends anywhere on the remaining circumference. Angles in the same segment are equal, and the angle in a semicircle is 90°.

concepts.heading: Cyclic quadrilaterals
concepts.text: If all four vertices lie on a circle, opposite angles add to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.

concepts.heading: Tangents
concepts.text: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The two tangents from an external point are equal. Tangent length from a point at distance d from the centre = √(d² − r²). For a point P outside, PT² = PA × PB for any secant PAB.

concepts.heading: Intersecting chords and common tangents
concepts.text: If chords AB and CD meet at P inside the circle, PA × PB = PC × PD. For two circles with radii r₁, r₂ and centres d apart, the direct common tangent has length √(d² − (r₁ − r₂)²) and the transverse one √(d² − (r₁ + r₂)²).

shortcuts: Triples help: radius 10 with chord 16 gives distance 6; radius 13 with chord 24 gives 5.
If an angle at the centre is reflex, the angle at the circumference is half of the reflex angle.
A parallelogram inscribed in a circle must be a rectangle.
Tangents from a point to a circle make equal angles with the line joining the point to the centre.

examples.question: A chord of length 16 cm is drawn in a circle of radius 10 cm. Find its distance from the centre.
examples.solution: Drop a perpendicular from the centre; it bisects the chord, so half chord = 8 cm. The radius, half chord and distance form a right triangle: d = √(100 − 64) = 6 cm.

examples.question: An arc subtends 140° at the centre. What angle does it subtend at a point on the remaining circumference?
examples.solution: Half of 140° = 70°.

examples.question: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = 75°. Find ∠C.
examples.solution: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°, so ∠C = 180° − 75° = 105°. The exterior angle at C would equal ∠A, i.e. 75°.

examples.question: A point is 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find the length of the tangent from the point.
Chords AB and CD intersect at P. If PA = 4 cm, PB = 6 cm and PC = 3 cm, find PD.
examples.solution: PA × PB = PC × PD → 24 = 3 × PD → PD = 8 cm.

examples.question: Two circles have radii 8 cm and 3 cm and their centres are 13 cm apart. Find the lengths of the direct and transverse common tangents.

practice: A chord of a circle of radius 13 cm is 24 cm long. Its distance from the centre is:
12 cm
7 cm
5 cm
11 cm
Half chord is 12 cm, so the distance is √(169 − 144) = √25 = 5 cm.
An arc subtends 35° at a point on the circumference. The angle it subtends at the centre is:
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so it is 70 degrees.
In a cyclic quadrilateral one angle is 112°. The angle opposite to it is:
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°, so the opposite angle is 68°.
The tangent from a point 25 cm from the centre of a circle is 24 cm long. The radius is:
7 cm
5 cm
9 cm
1 cm
Radius = √(625 − 576) = √49 = 7 cm, since the tangent meets the radius at a right angle.
From an external point P, a secant meets a circle at A and B with PA = 4 cm and PB = 9 cm. The tangent length from P is:
5 cm
13 cm
36 cm
6 cm
PT² = PA × PB = 36, so the tangent length is 6 cm by the tangent–secant theorem.
faqs: Why is the angle in a semicircle always 90°?

The diameter subtends a straight angle of 180° at the centre. By the centre-angle theorem, it subtends half of that, 90°, at any point on the circle. This fact turns many circle questions into right-triangle questions.
How do I remember direct versus transverse common tangent formulas?

Direct tangents do not cross between the circles, so the radii are on the same side and you subtract them. Transverse tangents cross between the circles, so the radii are on opposite sides and you add them. Both use d² minus the square of that result.

items.title: Mean, Median and Mode: Statistics Basics for SSC and Banks
items.description: Mean, median, mode and range with odd and even data sets, the empirical relation, effect of adding or scaling values, and weighted averages.
items.intro: Basic statistics — mean, median, mode and range — is part of the SSC CGL Tier 2 syllabus and appears in SSC CHSL and in bank DI questions that ask for "median sales" or "average production". The ideas are simple, but questions add twists: an even number of observations, a transformed data set, or the empirical relation linking the three averages. Ordering the data before anything else prevents most mistakes.

concepts.heading: Mean
concepts.text: The arithmetic mean is the sum of observations divided by their count. If every observation is multiplied by k and then increased by c, the new mean is k × old mean + c. Adding the same number to every value shifts the mean by that number but does not change the range.

concepts.heading: Median
concepts.text: Arrange the data in order. For an odd count n, the median is the ((n + 1)/2)-th value; for an even count, it is the average of the two middle values. The median is not affected by extreme values, which is why it is preferred for incomes and house prices.

concepts.heading: Mode and range
concepts.text: The mode is the most frequent value; a data set can have more than one mode or none. The range is the largest value minus the smallest and measures spread crudely.

concepts.heading: Empirical relation
concepts.text: For moderately skewed distributions, Mode ≈ 3 × Median − 2 × Mean. SSC questions use this as an exact formula: with mean 40 and median 42, mode = 126 − 80 = 46.

concepts.heading: Weighted mean
concepts.text: When values carry different weights (credits, quantities, number of students), multiply each value by its weight, add and divide by the total weight. A score of 60 with weight 2 and 75 with weight 3 gives (120 + 225)/5 = 69.

shortcuts: Always sort before finding a median — unsorted data is the most common trap.
Mean of an AP-like set equals its median.
If one value changes, the mean changes by (change ÷ count); the median may not change at all.
For grouped data in DI tables, compute totals per category first, then averages.

examples.question: Find the mean, median and range of 7, 3, 9, 5, 11.
examples.solution: Sum = 35, count = 5, mean = 7. Sorted: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, so the median is 7. Range = 11 − 3 = 8.

examples.question: Find the median of 4, 8, 6, 10, 12, 14.
examples.solution: Sorted: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. The middle values are 8 and 10, so the median is 9.

examples.question: Find the mode of 3, 5, 5, 7, 8, 5, 7.
examples.solution: Count frequencies: 3 once, 5 three times, 7 twice, 8 once. The value 5 appears most often, so the mode is 5. The mean is 40/7 ≈ 5.71, close to but different from the mode.

examples.question: In a distribution, the mean is 40 and the median is 42. Estimate the mode.
The mean of 10 observations is 25. Each is multiplied by 2 and then 5 is added. Find the new mean.
examples.solution: New mean = 2 × 25 + 5 = 55. There is no need to know the individual observations.

examples.question: A student scores 60 in a 2-credit paper and 75 in a 3-credit paper. Find the credit-weighted average.
examples.solution: (60 × 2 + 75 × 3)/5 = (120 + 225)/5 = 345/5 = 69. The simple average, 67.5, understates the weight of the bigger paper.

practice: The median of 12, 7, 15, 9, 10 is:
Sorted, the data are 7, 9, 10, 12, 15, so the middle (third) value 10 is the median.
The median of 3, 8, 5, 12, 10, 6 is:
Sorted: 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12; the two middle values 6 and 8 average to 7.
If the mean of a distribution is 22 and its median is 20, the mode by the empirical relation is:
Mode = 3 × 20 − 2 × 22 = 60 − 44 = 16 using the empirical relation.
The mean of 5 numbers is 18. If each number is increased by 4, the new mean is:
Adding 4 to every value raises the mean by exactly 4, so the new mean is 22.
The range of 23, 41, 17, 35, 29 is:
Range = largest − smallest = 41 − 17 = 24, which measures the spread of the data.
faqs: When is the median better than the mean?

When the data contain extreme values. In a small office where nine staff earn ₹30,000 and the owner earns ₹10,00,000 a month, the mean salary is misleading, while the median reflects the typical employee. DI questions sometimes test this understanding.
Is the empirical relation exact?

No, it is an approximation for moderately skewed distributions. SSC questions, however, treat it as a formula and expect you to use it directly. Outside exams, the mode should be found from the data itself.

items.title: Quantity Comparison Questions: Strategy for IBPS and SBI
items.description: Quantity I vs Quantity II questions explained: answer codes, multi-value traps, approximation and time-saving strategy, with worked arithmetic pairs.
items.intro: Quantity comparison is a newer question format in IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI PO and RBI Assistant prelims, often appearing as a block of three to five questions. Each question gives two quantities from different arithmetic topics — interest, speed, probability, mensuration or equations — and asks which is larger. It tests breadth across the syllabus and the judgement to stop calculating as soon as the comparison is clear.

concepts.heading: Answer codes
concepts.text: The options are usually: Quantity I > Quantity II, Quantity I < Quantity II, Quantity I ≥ Quantity II, Quantity I ≤ Quantity II, and Quantity I = Quantity II or no relation can be established. Read the option list once at the start of the block; it stays the same for every question.

concepts.heading: Evaluate each side independently
concepts.text: The two quantities come from unrelated mini-problems. Solve each separately, write the result, then compare. Do not carry assumptions from one side to the other, even when both mention the same numbers.

concepts.heading: Watch for multiple values
concepts.text: Quadratics, absolute values and "x² = k" produce two values. Compare every value on one side with every value on the other, exactly as in quadratic-equation questions. Equal values in some pairs lead to ≥ or ≤ instead of > or <.

concepts.heading: Stop when the order is clear
concepts.text: You do not always need exact answers. If Quantity I is clearly above 2,000 and Quantity II clearly below 1,800, the comparison is settled. Approximation and bounds save a lot of time in this block.

shortcuts: Simple interest over 3 years at 10% (30%) always beats compound interest over 2 years at 10% (21%) on the same principal.
Convert both sides to the same unit — km/h vs m/s is a classic trap.
Probabilities: compare fractions by cross-multiplying instead of converting to decimals.
If one side has a range of possible values (from a word problem with missing data), the answer is often "no relation".
Spend under a minute per pair; skip pairs needing long work on both sides.

examples.question: Quantity I: SI on ₹8,000 at 10% p.a. for 3 years. Quantity II: CI on ₹8,000 at 10% p.a. for 2 years.
Quantity I: x, where x² = 49. Quantity II: 7.
examples.solution: x = 7 or −7. Comparing with 7: equal in one case, smaller in the other. Quantity I ≤ Quantity II.

examples.question: Quantity I: speed (km/h) of a 150 m train that passes a pole in 10 seconds. Quantity II: 50 km/h.
examples.solution: I = 15 m/s = 54 km/h. 54 > 50, so Quantity I > Quantity II.

examples.question: Quantity I: probability of two heads when two coins are tossed. Quantity II: probability of a sum of 7 with two dice.
examples.solution: I: the four outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT, so P = 1/4. II: sum 7 comes from six pairs out of 36, so P = 1/6. Cross-multiplying 1 × 6 > 1 × 4 shows 1/4 > 1/6, so Quantity I > Quantity II.

examples.question: Quantity I: days taken by A (12 days) and B (18 days) together. Quantity II: 7 days.
examples.solution: I = 36/5 = 7.2 days > 7, so Quantity I > Quantity II.

examples.question: Quantity I: ways to arrange 4 people in a row. Quantity II: ways to choose 3 people from 8.
examples.solution: I = 4! = 24. II = 8C3 = 56. Quantity I < Quantity II.

practice: Quantity I: 30% of 450. Quantity II: 45% of 300. Which is true?
Quantity I > Quantity II
Quantity I < Quantity II
Quantity I = Quantity II
No relation
Both quantities equal 135: 0.30 × 450 = 135 and 0.45 × 300 = 135, so they are equal.
Quantity I: x, where x² − 5x + 6 = 0. Quantity II: 3. Which is true?
Quantity I < Quantity II
Quantity I ≤ Quantity II
Quantity I ≥ Quantity II
Quantity I = Quantity II
x = 2 or 3, so x is either smaller than or equal to 3, giving Quantity I ≤ Quantity II.
Quantity I: CI − SI on ₹10,000 at 10% for 2 years. Quantity II: ₹90. Which is true?
Quantity I > Quantity II
Quantity I < Quantity II
Quantity I = Quantity II
Quantity I ≤ Quantity II
The two-year difference is 10,000 × (0.1)² = ₹100, which is more than ₹90.
Quantity I: average of the first 10 natural numbers. Quantity II: median of 2, 4, 6, 8. Which is true?
Quantity I < Quantity II
Quantity I > Quantity II
Quantity I = Quantity II
No relation
Quantity I is 5.5 and Quantity II is (4 + 6)/2 = 5, so Quantity I is larger.
Quantity I: speed of the stream if downstream speed is 20 km/h and upstream 12 km/h. Quantity II: 16 km/h. Which is true?
Quantity I > Quantity II
Quantity I = Quantity II
Quantity I ≥ Quantity II
Quantity I < Quantity II
Stream speed = (20 − 12)/2 = 4 km/h, which is less than 16 km/h (16 km/h is the boat’s speed).
faqs: Which topics appear most in quantity comparison?

Interest, profit and loss, speed and distance, boats, probability, permutation, mensuration and quadratic equations are the usual sources. Essentially any arithmetic topic can be used, so broad coverage matters more than depth in one chapter for this block.
How do I handle a quantity that depends on unknown data?

If a word problem leaves a value undetermined, list the possible values or a range. If the range overlaps the other quantity, the answer is that no relation can be established. Setters include such questions deliberately to test this judgement.

items.title: Installment and EMI Problems: CI and SI Methods
items.description: Equal annual installments under compound and simple interest, present worth and a monthly EMI example, explained step by step with verified answers.
items.intro: Installment questions ask what equal yearly payment clears a loan, or how much was borrowed if fixed payments are made. They appear in IBPS PO mains, SBI PO and RBI Grade B as harder interest questions, and in SSC CGL Tier 2. The idea is also practical: home, car and education loans in India are repaid through EMIs. The key concept is present value — each future payment is worth less today.

concepts.heading: Present worth
concepts.text: Money due in the future is worth less today because it could earn interest meanwhile. Under compound interest at r% a year, ₹A due after n years has a present worth of A ÷ (1 + r/100)ⁿ. ₹4,840 due in 2 years at 10% is worth 4,840 ÷ 1.21 = ₹4,000 today.

concepts.heading: CI installments
concepts.text: With equal annual installments x under compound interest, the loan equals the sum of the present worths of all installments: P = x/(1 + r) + x/(1 + r)² + … (r as a decimal). At 10%, picking x as a multiple of 121 or 1,331 makes the arithmetic clean.

concepts.heading: SI installments
concepts.text: Under simple interest, compare everything at the final date. Each installment earns simple interest from its payment date to the end; the total must equal the debt due at the end. For a debt due in 3 years at 12% with annual payments x: x(1 + 0.24) + x(1 + 0.12) + x = 3.36x.

concepts.heading: Monthly EMI
concepts.text: Bank EMIs use the same present-value idea with a monthly rate. EMI = P × r × (1 + r)ⁿ / [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1], where r is the monthly rate and n the number of months. Actual loan rates and terms vary by lender; this formula only illustrates the method.

shortcuts: At 10% CI, two installments of ₹1,210 repay ₹2,100 (1,100 + 1,000).
At 10% CI, three installments of ₹1,331 repay ₹3,310 (1,210 + 1,100 + 1,000).
Total interest paid = (number of installments × installment) − principal.
For SI installments, the last installment earns no interest; the first earns interest for the longest time.

examples.question: A loan of ₹2,100 is repaid in 2 equal annual installments at 10% compound interest. Find each installment.
What equal annual installment will discharge a debt of ₹1,092 due in 3 years at 12% simple interest?
examples.solution: Value at the end of 3 years: first installment grows to 1.24x, second to 1.12x, third stays x. Total 3.36x = 1,092, so x = ₹325.

examples.question: A person borrows ₹3,310 at 10% compound interest and repays in 3 equal annual installments. Find the installment.
examples.solution: Present worths of ₹1,331 due in 1, 2 and 3 years are 1,210, 1,100 and 1,000, totalling 3,310. So each installment is ₹1,331.

examples.question: Find the present worth of ₹4,840 due in 2 years at 10% compound interest.
examples.solution: PW = 4,840 ÷ 1.21 = ₹4,000. In other words, ₹4,000 invested today at 10% compound interest grows to ₹4,840 in two years, so the two amounts are equivalent.

examples.question: Estimate the monthly EMI on a ₹1,00,000 loan for 12 months at 1% per month.
examples.solution: EMI = 1,00,000 × 0.01 × 1.01¹² ÷ (1.01¹² − 1) ≈ ₹8,885. Over 12 months the borrower pays about ₹1,06,619, so the interest is roughly ₹6,619, much less than simple interest of 12% on the full amount, because the principal reduces every month.

practice: A sum is repaid in two equal annual installments of ₹441 at 5% compound interest. The sum borrowed is:
Present worths are 441/1.05 = 420 and 441/1.1025 = 400, which add up to ₹820.
₹5,500 is borrowed at 20% CI and repaid in two equal annual installments. Each installment is:
A debt of ₹848 due in 4 years at 4% simple interest is cleared by 4 equal annual installments. Each installment is:
Values at the end are x(1.12 + 1.08 + 1.04 + 1) = 4.24x = 848, so each installment is ₹200.
The present worth of ₹6,655 due in 3 years at 10% compound interest is:
PW = 6,655 ÷ 1.331 = ₹5,000, discounting three years of 10% growth.
In the ₹5,500 loan repaid by two installments of ₹3,600 at 20% CI, the total interest paid is:
Total paid is 2 × 3,600 = ₹7,200, so the interest is 7,200 − 5,500 = ₹1,700.
faqs: Why is the installment more than the loan divided by the number of years?

Because the lender charges interest on the outstanding balance throughout the loan. Each installment covers part of the principal plus interest, so the total repaid exceeds the amount borrowed. The longer the term, the larger the total interest.
Do banks use these exact formulas for home loans?

Banks use the reducing-balance EMI formula, usually with monthly compounding, which matches the present-value approach here. Actual rates, fees and terms vary by lender and change over time, so always check the lender’s own schedule. Exam questions simply test the method.

items.title: Bar Graph Data Interpretation: Method and Practice Set
items.description: How to read and calculate from bar graph DI sets: totals, averages, percentage change, ratios and highest-growth questions with a worked data set.
items.intro: Bar graphs are the most common DI format in IBPS PO, IBPS Clerk, SBI PO and RBI Grade B prelims, where a five-question set is typical, and they appear in SSC CGL Tier 2 and CAT as well. The questions themselves are arithmetic — totals, averages, percentage change and ratios — but they reward a disciplined process: read the axis, note the units, and pull out only the bars each question needs.

concepts.heading: Read before you calculate
concepts.text: Check the title, the unit (hundreds, thousands, ₹ crore) and whether bars are simple, grouped or stacked. In a stacked bar, the height of the whole bar is the total and each segment is a part; in a grouped bar, each colour is a separate series. Misreading the unit is the most common silent error.

concepts.heading: Core calculations
concepts.text: Most questions ask for one of five things: a total, an average, a percentage change, a ratio, or one value as a percentage of another. Percentage change = (new − old)/old × 100. "A as a percentage of B" = A/B × 100. Ratios should be reduced to lowest terms.

concepts.heading: Highest growth questions
concepts.text: When asked which year had the highest percentage increase, compare (increase ÷ previous value) for each year, not the raw increase. A jump of 45 on a base of 135 (33%) beats a jump of 30 on a base of 180 (17%).

concepts.heading: Stacked and grouped bars
concepts.text: In a stacked bar, find a segment’s value by subtracting the reading at its bottom edge from the reading at its top edge; do not read the top edge alone. In grouped bars, compare bars of the same colour across groups for trend questions and bars within a group for share questions.

concepts.heading: Use approximations
concepts.text: Bank DI options are usually far enough apart that two-significant-figure accuracy is enough. Convert to fractions where possible (17.3% ≈ 1/6, 33.3% = 1/3) and compute exactly only when two options are close.

shortcuts: Write the bar values in a small table on rough paper first; it prevents re-reading the graph for every question.
For average of n bars, add and divide once; for "average of two years", just halve their sum.
If every value grows by the same percentage, ratios between them do not change.
A value doubling means a 100% increase, not 200%.
For "approximately what percent", round to the nearest option only at the end.

examples.question: Data: accounts opened (in hundreds) by five branches — A 45, B 60, C 35, D 50, E 70. Find the total and the average per branch.
examples.solution: Total = 45 + 60 + 35 + 50 + 70 = 260 hundred, i.e. 26,000 accounts. Average = 260/5 = 52 hundred = 5,200 accounts per branch.

examples.question: Using the same data, by what percent are E’s accounts more than C’s?
examples.solution: (70 − 35)/35 × 100 = 100%. E opened twice as many accounts as C.

examples.question: Find the ratio of accounts opened by B and D.
What percentage of all accounts were opened by branch A?
examples.solution: 45/260 × 100 ≈ 17.31%. Approximation: 45/260 is a little more than 1/6 (16.67%), so about 17%.

examples.question: If D’s accounts grow by 20% next year, how many will D open?
examples.solution: 50 × 1.2 = 60 hundred, i.e. 6,000 accounts — the same as B’s current level.

examples.question: Which branch’s figure is closest to the five-branch average?
examples.solution: The average is 52 hundred. Deviations: A −7, B +8, C −17, D −2, E +18. Branch D, only 2 hundred below the average, is closest. Writing deviations from the average is also a quick way to check the total: −7 + 8 − 17 − 2 + 18 = 0.

practice: Production (thousand tonnes): 2019 120, 2020 150, 2021 135, 2022 180, 2023 210. Percentage increase from 2021 to 2022 is:
Increase = 180 − 135 = 45 on a base of 135, which is one-third, i.e. 33.33 percent.
Using the same data, the average annual production over the five years is:
150 thousand tonnes
162 thousand tonnes
165 thousand tonnes
159 thousand tonnes
Using the same data, which year shows the highest percentage increase over the previous year?
Using the same data, the ratio of production in 2019 to 2023 is:
120 : 210 simplifies by dividing both by 30, giving the ratio 4 : 7.
Using the same data, production in 2023 is what percent of production in 2020?
210 ÷ 150 × 100 = 140 percent, meaning 2023 output is 1.4 times the 2020 output.
faqs: How many DI sets come in IBPS PO prelims?

Typically one or two DI sets of about five questions each, alongside arithmetic and other question types, though the pattern varies by year. Mains papers contain more and harder DI. Practising one set daily across all chart types is a common approach.
Should I skip a DI set if the first question is hard?

Look at all five questions first. Often two or three are quick (a total or a ratio) even if one needs heavy calculation. Attempt the quick ones, and skip only the questions that require long computations or ambiguous readings.

items.title: Line Graph DI: Reading Trends and Solving Questions
items.description: Solve line graph DI sets with two series, trends, gaps between lines, percentage change and averages, using a worked exports and imports example.
items.intro: Line graphs show how values change over time, and bank exams love them for that reason. IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B prelims and mains often include a line-graph set, frequently with two or three lines plotted together, such as exports and imports or sales of two products. SSC CGL Tier 2 and CAT also use them. Questions ask about trends, the gap between lines and growth rates.

concepts.heading: Slope tells the story
concepts.text: A steeper segment means a larger absolute change. However, percentage change depends on the starting level, so a gentler slope from a low base can be a bigger percentage rise. Never judge percentage growth by eye alone.

concepts.heading: Gap between two lines
concepts.text: With two series, the vertical gap at each point is their difference — a trade surplus, a profit or a shortfall. The year with the widest gap has the largest difference. When lines cross, the sign of the difference changes.

concepts.heading: Trend questions
concepts.text: Questions such as "in how many years did X fall" or "which month showed a decrease" need only the direction of each segment. Mark the up and down segments once and reuse the result for multiple questions.

concepts.heading: Reading two scales
concepts.text: Some line graphs use a second vertical axis on the right for one of the series, often for percentages. Check which line belongs to which axis before reading values, because the same height can mean very different numbers on the two scales.

concepts.heading: Averages and ratios over periods
concepts.text: For the average over several years, add the points and divide by the number of points. For ratios of totals, add each series separately first; the ratio of totals is not the average of yearly ratios.

shortcuts: Tabulate the points of each line before answering — a 30-second investment for five questions.
Percentage-point change (from 20% to 25%) is not the same as percentage change (25% rise).
If a value rises from 60 to 72, the change is 20%; from 72 back to 60 is a 16.67% fall — bases differ.
Use the steepest segment as a first guess for "largest increase" and confirm with numbers.

examples.question: Exports and imports of a firm (₹ crore), 2019–2023: exports 40, 45, 50, 60, 72; imports 30, 42, 45, 48, 54. Find the trade surplus each year and the year with the highest surplus.
examples.solution: Surplus = exports − imports for each year: 40 − 30 = 10, 45 − 42 = 3, 50 − 45 = 5, 60 − 48 = 12 and 72 − 54 = 18. The highest is ₹18 crore in 2023, where the two lines are furthest apart on the graph.

examples.question: Using the same data, find the percentage growth in exports from 2022 to 2023.
examples.solution: Increase = 72 − 60 = 12 on a base of 60, so (12/60) × 100 = 20%. Note that the same ₹12 crore rise from a base of 72 would be only 16.67%, which is why the base year matters.

examples.question: Find the average imports over the five years.
Find the ratio of total exports to total imports over the period.
examples.solution: Total exports = 267, total imports = 219. Ratio = 267 : 219 = 89 : 73 (dividing by 3).

examples.question: In which year was the surplus the smallest, and why might the graph mislead here?
examples.solution: The surplus is smallest in 2020 (₹3 crore). Both lines rose that year, but imports jumped by 12 while exports rose only 5, so the lines came close together even though exports grew.

practice: Enrolments (hundreds), Jan–Jun: 12, 15, 18, 16, 20, 24. Percentage increase from January to June is:
Enrolment doubles from 12 to 24 hundred, and a doubling is a 100 percent increase.
Using the same data, the average monthly enrolment is:
Total = 105 hundred over 6 months, so the average is 17.5 hundred, i.e. 1,750 students.
Using the same data, in which month did enrolment fall compared with the previous month?
March
May
February
April
Only April shows a decrease, from 18 hundred in March to 16 hundred.
Using the same data, the percentage decrease from March to April is about:
Decrease = 2 on a base of 18, which is 2/18 = 1/9, about 11.11 percent.
Using the same data, the ratio of February to May enrolment is:
February has 15 and May has 20 hundred, and 15 : 20 simplifies to 3 : 4.
faqs: Can I estimate values that fall between grid lines?

Bank exam line graphs usually mark exact values at each point. If a value is not labelled, estimate carefully from the grid and choose the option closest to your estimate. Avoid questions whose answer hinges on a tiny reading difference.
What is the difference between percentage change and percentage-point change?

If a pass rate moves from 20% to 25%, it rose by 5 percentage points but by 25 percent of its earlier value. DI questions use both phrasings, and options often include both numbers, so read the wording closely.

items.title: Pie Chart DI: Percentages, Degrees and Shortcut Methods
items.description: Pie chart DI with percentage and degree formats: converting angles, finding amounts, comparing sectors and handling two-pie questions, with examples.
items.intro: Pie charts show how a whole is divided into parts — a family budget, a company’s expenses or students by stream. IBPS PO, SBI PO, RBI Grade B and SSC CGL Tier 2 regularly include pie-chart sets, sometimes two pies side by side. The arithmetic is lighter than in bar or line graphs, because every value is a share of one total, so speed comes from working with percentages instead of converting everything to amounts.

concepts.heading: Two formats
