concepts.text: A pie may be labelled in percentages (adding to 100%) or in degrees (adding to 360°). Convert with: percentage = degrees × 100/360 and degrees = percentage × 3.6. A 108° sector is 30% of the whole; a 15% sector is 54°.

concepts.heading: Amounts from shares
concepts.text: Value of a sector = share × total. With a ₹60,000 monthly budget, a 25% rent share is ₹15,000. With 720 students and a 120° sector, the sector has 720 × 120/360 = 240 students.

concepts.heading: Compare shares, not amounts
concepts.text: When both sectors belong to the same pie, their ratio equals the ratio of their percentages or degrees. Education 15% and transport 10% are in the ratio 3 : 2 without computing rupee amounts. Differences can likewise be computed as (difference in %) × total.

concepts.heading: Pie linked to another chart
concepts.text: Some sets give the total in a table or bar graph and the break-up in a pie. Find the total for the relevant year from the first chart, then apply the pie’s percentage. Note which year or company the pie refers to; questions may ask you to combine figures across both charts.

concepts.heading: Two pies
concepts.text: When two pies have different totals (two years or two companies), you cannot compare percentages directly. Convert each relevant sector to an actual amount using its own total before comparing.

shortcuts: 1% of a ₹60,000 budget is ₹600; scale from there instead of multiplying each time.
If the total changes but shares stay fixed, every sector changes by the same percentage.
A sector’s central angle is never needed for amounts if percentages are given — skip the degree conversion.

examples.question: A family’s monthly income of ₹60,000 is spent as: rent 25%, food 30%, education 15%, transport 10%, savings 20%. How much is spent on rent?
examples.solution: 25% of 60,000 = 60,000 ÷ 4 = ₹15,000. Converting 25% to the fraction 1/4 makes this a one-step division.

examples.question: What is the central angle of the food sector?
examples.solution: Every 1% of the pie is 3.6°, so 30% corresponds to 30 × 3.6 = 108°. Check: the five sectors (90°, 108°, 54°, 36°, 72°) add to 360°.

examples.question: By how much do savings exceed transport spending?
examples.solution: Work with the difference in shares: (20% − 10%) × 60,000 = 10% of 60,000 = ₹6,000. Computing savings (₹12,000) and transport (₹6,000) separately and subtracting gives the same answer but takes longer.

examples.question: Find the ratio of education to transport spending.
examples.solution: 15 : 10 = 3 : 2. No rupee calculation is needed.

examples.question: If income rises by 10% and the percentages stay the same, how much will be spent on food?
examples.solution: New income = ₹66,000. Food = 30% × 66,000 = ₹19,800, which is also 10% more than the earlier ₹18,000.

examples.question: What is the combined central angle of rent and food, and what fraction of income do they take together?
examples.solution: Rent 25% + food 30% = 55% of income. Central angle = 55 × 3.6 = 198°, more than a semicircle. As an amount, 55% of ₹60,000 = ₹33,000, leaving ₹27,000 for the other three heads.

practice: 720 students are split by stream: Commerce 120°, Science 90°, Arts 60°, Management 54°, Others 36°. How many study Commerce?
Commerce students = 720 × 120/360 = 720 ÷ 3 = 240 students.
Using the same data, Science students form what percentage of the total?
90° out of 360° is one quarter of the circle, which equals 25 percent of all students.
Using the same data, how many more students are in Commerce than in Arts?
The difference is 60° of 360°, i.e. one-sixth of 720, which is 120 students.
Using the same data, Management students form what percentage of the total?
54° ÷ 360° × 100 = 15 percent, so 108 of the 720 students are in Management.
Using the same data, the ratio of Science to Others is:
90° : 36° simplifies to 5 : 2 by dividing both angles by 18°.
faqs: Do I need to convert degrees to percentages in every question?

No. For ratios and comparisons within the same pie, degrees work just as well as percentages. Convert only when you need an actual amount or when the options are in percentages. Skipping unnecessary conversions saves time across a five-question set.
How do I compare sectors from two pies with different totals?
Convert each sector to an actual value using its own pie’s total, then compare. For example, 20% of ₹50 lakh (₹10 lakh) is larger than 25% of ₹36 lakh (₹9 lakh), even though 25% is the bigger share.

items.title: Tabular Data Interpretation: Approach and Solved Set
items.description: Solve table-based DI with row and column totals, growth, shares and percentage comparisons, using a quarterly sales table and a department staff table.
items.intro: Tables are the most information-dense DI format and the most common in IBPS PO mains, SBI PO and RBI Grade B, and they also appear in prelims and SSC CGL Tier 2. Unlike graphs, there is no reading error — the numbers are exact — so the challenge is choosing the right rows and columns and avoiding unnecessary arithmetic. Row and column totals are the most reused figures, so compute them once.

concepts.heading: Map the table first
concepts.text: Identify what rows and columns represent and the unit of each cell. Note whether a column is already a total or a percentage. Many questions combine cells from one row (an item across periods) or one column (all items in a period).

concepts.heading: Totals are reusable
concepts.text: Questions like "which model sold the most", "what share of Q2 sales came from S" or "average sales per quarter" all depend on row or column totals. Write totals in the margin as you compute them, so later questions take seconds.

concepts.heading: Shares and percentages
concepts.text: Share of an item in a period = cell ÷ column total × 100. Percentage of women in a department = women ÷ department total × 100. Keep track of which total is the base; questions often switch bases between parts.

concepts.heading: Combining rows and columns
concepts.text: Some questions ask for a cell as a share of the grand total, or for one row’s total compared with one column’s total. Compute the grand total once by adding either the row totals or the column totals, and use the other set as a check: both must give the same figure.

concepts.heading: Comparing ratios across rows
concepts.text: To find which row has the highest proportion of something, compare fractions such as 60/100, 90/240, 80/200 and 40/100. Cross-multiplication or converting to percentages quickly identifies the largest.

shortcuts: Add columns in pairs that make round numbers (120 + 180, 150 + 150) to speed up totals.
If a question asks "approximately", compare fractions to benchmarks like 1/4, 1/3 and 2/5.
Growth of a row from first to last period: (last − first)/first × 100.
Average of a row = row total ÷ number of periods; avoid averaging percentages from different bases.

examples.question: Phone sales (units) of four models: P 120, 150, 180; Q 200, 180, 220; R 90, 110, 100; S 160, 140, 200 for Q1, Q2, Q3. Find total sales in Q3.
examples.solution: Add the Q3 column: 180 + 220 + 100 + 200 = 700 units. Pairing 180 + 220 = 400 and 100 + 200 = 300 makes the addition instant.

examples.question: Which model had the highest total sales over the three quarters?
examples.solution: Row totals: P = 120 + 150 + 180 = 450, Q = 200 + 180 + 220 = 600, R = 90 + 110 + 100 = 300, S = 160 + 140 + 200 = 500. Model Q is highest with 600 units. Keep these totals; later questions on averages or shares reuse them.

examples.question: Find the percentage growth in P’s sales from Q1 to Q3.
What is the average quarterly sale of model R?
Model S’s share of total Q2 sales is about what percent?
examples.solution: Q2 total = 150 + 180 + 110 + 140 = 580. Share = 140/580 × 100 ≈ 24.14%, slightly under one-quarter.

examples.question: Which model showed a decline in sales from Q1 to Q2, and by what percentage?
examples.solution: Q fell from 200 to 180 (10% decline) and S fell from 160 to 140 (12.5% decline). P and R both rose. So two models declined, and S had the sharper fall in percentage terms even though both lost 20 units.

practice: Staff (men, women): HR 40, 60; IT 150, 90; Sales 120, 80; Finance 60, 40. Total employees are:
Department totals are 100, 240, 200 and 100, which add up to 640 employees.
Using the same table, the percentage of women in IT is:
IT has 90 women among 240 staff, and 90/240 = 3/8 = 37.5 percent.
Using the same table, the ratio of men to women in the firm is:
Men total 370 and women total 270, and 370 : 270 simplifies to 37 : 27.
Using the same table, which department has the highest percentage of women?
HR
IT
Sales
Finance
Women shares are HR 60%, IT 37.5%, Sales 40% and Finance 40%, so HR is the highest.
Using the same table, Finance employees form what percentage of the total?
Finance has 100 of 640 employees, and 100/640 × 100 = 15.625 percent of the workforce.
faqs: Why are table DI sets considered time-consuming?

Because they contain more numbers than graphs and questions often need several cells combined. The cure is to compute and note row and column totals once, and to approximate whenever the options allow. With that habit, table sets are often faster than graph sets.
What if a table has missing cells?

Then it is a missing-data DI set. Use the given relationships, such as totals, percentages or differences, to fill the gaps first, and then answer the questions. These sets are common in IBPS PO mains.

items.title: Caselet DI: How to Convert Paragraph Data into a Table
items.description: Caselet data interpretation explained: turn paragraph data into a quick table, handle nested percentages and answer five questions fast, with a worked set.
items.intro: Caselet DI presents data as a paragraph instead of a chart, so the first job is to organise it. IBPS PO mains, SBI PO, RBI Grade B and recent prelims papers include caselets regularly, and CAT’s DI section often starts from text too. The arithmetic is usually simple percentages; what separates fast and slow candidates is how quickly they convert the text into a clean table and how carefully they track which base each percentage refers to.

concepts.heading: Build a table first
concepts.text: Read the whole caselet once, decide the rows and columns (for example, gender × stream), and fill the table as you read the second time. Most questions then become look-ups or one-line calculations. Do not answer questions directly from the text — it is slower and error-prone.

concepts.heading: Nested percentages
concepts.text: Caselets layer percentages: "45% of students are girls; of the girls, 40% chose Science". The second percentage applies to girls, not to all students. Compute each layer in order: girls = 540, girls in Science = 40% of 540 = 216.

concepts.heading: Use "rest" and totals as checks
concepts.text: Phrases like "the rest chose Arts" give the last category by subtraction. Always check that each row adds up to its total; a mismatch reveals a misread percentage before it costs marks.

concepts.heading: Questions often cross categories
concepts.text: Expect questions like "what percentage of Science students are girls?" — the base here is all Science students, not all girls. Re-identify the base for every question.

concepts.heading: Whole-number sanity check
concepts.text: Counts of people, loans or items must be whole numbers. If a calculation gives 189.6 students, you have probably applied a percentage to the wrong base. Exam setters choose numbers so that the correct path gives integers.

shortcuts: Draw the grid before reading the questions; it typically takes under a minute and saves several later.
Write totals in a final row and column so cross-category questions are instant.
When a caselet gives ratios, convert them to actual numbers immediately.
Underline the words "of the", "remaining" and "rest" — they signal a change of base.

examples.question: A school has 1,200 students; 45% are girls. Of the girls, 40% opted for Science, 35% for Commerce and the rest for Arts. Of the boys, 50% chose Science, 30% Commerce and the rest Arts. Tabulate the data.
examples.solution: Girls = 540: Science 216, Commerce 189, Arts 135. Boys = 660: Science 330, Commerce 198, Arts 132. Row totals check: 216 + 189 + 135 = 540 and 330 + 198 + 132 = 660.

examples.question: How many students chose Science in all?
examples.solution: Add the Science column of the table: 216 girls + 330 boys = 546 students, which is 45.5% of the school. Without the table you would have to recompute both layers of percentages here.

examples.question: How many students chose Arts in all?
examples.solution: Arts = 135 girls + 132 boys = 267 students. Check the grand total: Science 546 + Commerce 387 + Arts 267 = 1,200, matching the school strength.

examples.question: Find the ratio of girls to boys in Commerce.
examples.solution: 189 : 198 = 21 : 22 (dividing both by 9).

examples.question: What percentage of Science students are girls?
examples.solution: Base is all Science students (546). 216/546 × 100 ≈ 39.56%. Using girls (540) as the base would wrongly give 40%.

examples.question: How many more girls than boys chose Arts?
examples.solution: 135 − 132 = 3. Even though girls are fewer overall, a larger share of them chose Arts (25% against 20%).

practice: A branch received 800 loan applications: 40% home, 35% vehicle, rest personal. 75% of home, 60% of vehicle and 40% of personal applications were approved. How many were approved in total?
Approved: home 240, vehicle 168 and personal 80, which together make 488 applications.
Using the same data, the overall approval rate is:
488 approved out of 800 applications gives 488/800 × 100 = 61 percent.
Using the same data, how many vehicle loan applications were rejected?
Vehicle applications were 280 and 168 were approved, so 280 − 168 = 112 were rejected.
Using the same data, personal loans form about what percentage of all approved loans?
Personal approvals are 80 of 488 total approvals, and 80/488 × 100 ≈ 16.39 percent.
Using the same data, the ratio of approved home loans to approved vehicle loans is:
240 : 168 simplifies to 10 : 7 when both terms are divided by 24.
faqs: Why are caselets considered harder than graph-based DI?

Because the data are not organised for you. The calculations are usually no harder, but extracting and tabulating the numbers takes time, and misreading a base is easy. Building a table first neutralises most of that difficulty.
Can a caselet have data that cannot be fully determined?

Yes. Some caselets deliberately leave one value unknown and ask which questions can be answered. In such cases, compute what you can and recognise when a question requires the missing piece. These overlap with data sufficiency thinking.

items.title: Missing Data Interpretation: Filling Gaps in DI Tables
items.description: Missing DI sets explained: use totals, percentages and given relations to fill blank cells, then answer questions, with a shop sales and profit example.
items.intro: Missing DI is a table in which some cells are blank and must be worked out from the others before any question can be answered. It is a regular feature of IBPS PO mains, SBI PO mains and RBI Grade B, and it has started appearing in prelims too. These sets test arithmetic relationships — part and whole, percentage and amount, revenue, cost and profit — more than chart reading.

concepts.heading: Know the relationship in each row
concepts.text: Every row hides a formula: total = online + offline; revenue = cost + profit; profit % = profit/cost × 100. Write the formula above the table so you can fill any two-of-three situation immediately.

concepts.heading: Fill the whole table first
concepts.text: Complete every blank before reading the questions. Questions usually need several filled cells, and having the full table avoids recomputation. If one cell cannot be found, note it — a question may ask which value cannot be determined.

concepts.heading: Percent of what?
concepts.text: A blank may be given as "online sales are 30% of total" or "profit is 20% of cost". Identify the base carefully. Profit as a percentage of revenue and as a percentage of cost give different numbers, and setters use both.

concepts.heading: Chains of blanks
concepts.text: Sometimes one blank can only be found after another is filled — for example, a total from one row is needed to compute a percentage in another. Work in the order the information allows, and keep a short note of which cells depend on which, so a single correction can be carried through.

concepts.heading: Cross-check with totals
concepts.text: If the table gives a grand total, add your filled values to confirm. A mismatch means an earlier cell is wrong, and it is cheaper to fix it now than after answering three questions.

shortcuts: From part and percentage: total = part ÷ percentage. 120 being 30% of total gives total 400.
From total and percentage of the complement: if 75% is offline and offline = 360, total = 480.
Profit % on cost p with revenue R gives cost = R × 100/(100 + p).
Write filled values in a different colour or with a mark so you know which were derived.

examples.question: Shop sales: A total 400, online 35%. B online 120, which is 30% of its total. C total 500, offline 300. D offline 360, online 25% of total. Find B’s total and offline sales.
examples.solution: Online sales of 120 are 30% of B’s total, so total = 120 ÷ 0.30 = 400. Offline = 400 − 120 = 280. Dividing by the percentage, not multiplying, is the key step whenever a part and its percentage are given.

examples.question: What percentage of C’s sales were online?
Find D’s total and online sales.
examples.solution: Online is 25%, so offline is the remaining 75% of total. Total = 360 ÷ 0.75 = 480 and online = 480 − 360 = 120. Using the complement percentage is what makes this row solvable.

examples.question: Find the total online sales of all four shops.
Find the ratio of A’s offline sales to D’s offline sales.
Which shop had the highest share of online sales, and which had the lowest?
examples.solution: Online shares: A 35%, B 30%, C 40%, D 25%. C has the highest and D the lowest share. In absolute terms, however, C (200) is also the largest online seller, while B and D tie at 120 units — another reminder that share and amount can rank differently.

practice: Company data (₹ lakh): P revenue 500, cost 400. Q cost 600, profit 20% on cost. R revenue 900, profit 150. S revenue 650, profit 30% on cost. Q’s revenue is:
₹720 lakh
₹750 lakh
₹660 lakh
₹780 lakh
Q’s profit is 20% of 600 = ₹120 lakh, so revenue = 600 + 120 = ₹720 lakh.
Using the same data, R’s profit percentage on cost is:
R’s cost = 900 − 150 = 750, and 150/750 × 100 = 20 percent profit on cost.
Using the same data, S’s cost is:
₹455 lakh
₹500 lakh
₹520 lakh
₹480 lakh
Revenue is 130% of cost, so cost = 650 ÷ 1.3 = ₹500 lakh and profit is ₹150 lakh.
Using the same data, the total profit of all four companies is:
₹520 lakh
₹500 lakh
₹470 lakh
₹550 lakh
Profits are P 100, Q 120, R 150 and S 150, which add up to ₹520 lakh.
Using the same data, which company has the highest profit percentage on cost?
P
Q
S
R
Profit percentages are P 25%, Q 20%, R 20% and S 30%, so company S is the highest.
faqs: Are missing DI sets only in mains exams?

They are most common in IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B mains, but simpler versions have appeared in prelims. Practising them builds the habit of reading relationships between columns, which also helps with ordinary table and caselet sets.
What if a blank cell cannot be found from the given data?
Then the table is intentionally incomplete. A question may ask for that value with an option such as "cannot be determined". Make sure you have used every given relation before choosing that option.

items.title: Mixed Graph DI: Combining Bar and Line Charts
items.description: Solve mixed DI where a bar graph gives totals and a line shows percentages: derive actual values, compare years and avoid unit traps, with examples.
items.intro: Mixed or combined graphs pair two chart types — commonly bars for totals and a line for a percentage — so that useful numbers come only from combining them. IBPS PO mains, SBI PO, RBI Grade B and CAT use this format, and it now appears in prelims as well. The calculations are straightforward multiplications, but each question needs values from both charts, so a small derived table saves a lot of time.

concepts.heading: Two axes, two meanings
concepts.text: The bars usually use the left axis (units, students, ₹ crore) and the line uses the right axis (percentages). Confirm which series belongs to which axis before reading. Reading a percentage off the wrong axis is the most common error in this format.

concepts.heading: Derive the hidden series
concepts.text: The questions rarely ask about the bars or the line alone. If bars show production and the line shows the percentage sold, the key derived values are units sold (= production × % sold) and unsold units (= production − sold). Compute both for every year first.

concepts.heading: Percent of different bases
concepts.text: A higher percentage does not always mean a higher amount. 88% of 75 thousand (66 thousand) exceeds 70% of 80 thousand (56 thousand), but 80% of 50 thousand (40 thousand) is less than 75% of 60 thousand (45 thousand). Always compare actual derived values.

concepts.heading: Weighted overall rates
concepts.text: An overall percentage across years is total derived value ÷ total base, which weights each year by its size. The simple average of yearly percentages ignores those weights and is usually slightly different, so check which one the question wants.

concepts.heading: Growth on derived values
concepts.text: Growth questions on mixed graphs usually refer to the derived series. A rise in pass percentage with a fall in candidates can still reduce the number who pass. Compute the derived values first, then the growth.

shortcuts: Build a four-row table: base value, percentage, derived value, complement — then answer.
Multiplying by a percentage like 75% or 88% is faster as a fraction (3/4) or as (1 − 0.12).
If the question asks for the complement (failures, unsold units), subtract from the base rather than recomputing.
Ratios of derived values can often be simplified before multiplying out.

examples.question: A factory produced 50, 60, 80 and 75 thousand units in 2019–2022, and the line shows that 80%, 75%, 70% and 88% of production was sold. How many units were sold in 2021?
examples.solution: Read the 2021 bar (80 thousand) and the 2021 point on the line (70%). Units sold = 70% of 80 thousand = 56 thousand. Neither chart alone gives this number, which is the essence of a mixed graph.

examples.question: Find the total unsold units over the four years.
examples.solution: Sold: 40, 45, 56, 66 thousand. Unsold: 10, 15, 24, 9 thousand. Total unsold = 58 thousand.

examples.question: In which year were the most units sold?
examples.solution: Compare derived values, not bars: sold units are 40, 45, 56 and 66 thousand. The answer is 2022, with 66 thousand units, although 2021 had the tallest production bar (80 thousand). The high 88% sale rate in 2022 more than made up for lower production.

examples.question: Find the percentage increase in units sold from 2019 to 2022.
Find the average number of units sold per year.
What was the overall percentage of production sold over the four years?
examples.solution: Total produced = 50 + 60 + 80 + 75 = 265 thousand; total sold = 207 thousand. Overall rate = 207/265 × 100 ≈ 78.1%. This is not the simple average of the four percentages (78.25%), because each year’s rate applies to a different base.

practice: Candidates appeared: 800, 900, 1,000, 1,200 in 2020–2023; pass rates 60%, 70%, 72%, 65%. How many passed in 2022?
72% of 1,000 candidates is 720, combining the bar value with the line percentage.
Using the same data, the total number of failures over the four years is:
Failures are 320, 270, 280 and 420, which add up to 1,290 candidates.
Using the same data, the percentage increase in the number passing from 2020 to 2023 is:
Passes rose from 480 to 780, an increase of 300 on 480, which is 62.5 percent.
Using the same data, which year had the most failures?
Failures were 320, 270, 280 and 420, so 2023 had the most despite having the most passes too.
Using the same data, the ratio of passes in 2021 to passes in 2023 is:
Passes were 630 and 780, and dividing both by 30 gives the ratio 21 : 26.
faqs: What is the most common trap in mixed graph DI?

Comparing percentages when the question asks about actual numbers, or vice versa. A year with the highest pass rate need not have the most passes. Always ask whether the question is about the rate or the derived amount before answering.
Do mixed graphs appear in prelims or only mains?
They are more common in mains papers of IBPS PO, SBI PO and RBI Grade B, but simpler bar-plus-line sets have appeared in prelims. Practising both levels is useful because the method is identical.

items.title: DI Calculation Shortcuts: Percentages, Ratios, Fractions
items.description: Speed up data interpretation with fraction benchmarks, cross-multiplication, assumed-mean averages and quick percentage-change methods, with examples.
items.intro: Every DI set in IBPS PO, SBI PO, RBI Grade B, SSC CGL Tier 2 and CAT ultimately reduces to a handful of calculations: percentages, percentage change, ratios, averages and fraction comparison. Candidates who know the concepts but calculate slowly run out of time in the DI section. This page collects the calculation habits that save the most time, each with a worked example on DI-style numbers.

concepts.heading: Fraction benchmarks
concepts.text: Know the percentage values of common fractions: 1/3 = 33.33%, 1/6 = 16.67%, 1/7 ≈ 14.29%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 ≈ 11.11%, 1/11 ≈ 9.09%, 1/12 ≈ 8.33%. Then 16.67% of 7,230 is just 7,230 ÷ 6 = 1,205, and 1,847/6,112 is quickly seen to be a little over 30%.

concepts.heading: Comparing fractions
concepts.text: To decide which of a/b and c/d is larger, compare a × d with c × b. For 347/521 and 412/617: 347 × 617 = 2,14,099 and 412 × 521 = 2,14,652, so 412/617 is slightly larger. When fractions are far apart, compare each with a benchmark like 2/3 instead.

concepts.heading: Percentage change by fractions
concepts.text: An increase of 12.5% means × 9/8, 20% means × 6/5 and 25% means × 5/4. So 6,480 grown by 12.5% is 6,480 + 6,480/8 = 6,480 + 810 = 7,290. For the change between two values, look for a simple ratio: 2,450 → 2,940 is a rise of 490, which is one-fifth of 2,450, i.e. 20%.

concepts.heading: Assumed-mean averages
concepts.text: For numbers close together, pick a convenient middle value, average the deviations and add. For 528, 532, 541, 519 and 530, deviations from 530 are −2, +2, +11, −11, 0, which average 0, so the mean is 530.

concepts.heading: Approximate early, exact late
concepts.text: Round figures to two or three significant digits for a first answer. Only if two options fall within about 2% of each other should you go back and calculate exactly.

shortcuts: Percentage growth comparison: compare increase ÷ base, not raw increases — 240 → 300 (25%) beats 360 → 440 (22.2%).
For ratios like 3,600 : 4,800, cancel common factors first (36 : 48 = 3 : 4).
Multiplying by 1.5 = adding half; by 0.75 = subtracting a quarter; by 1.25 = adding a quarter.
When options differ widely, estimate with one significant figure and pick immediately.

examples.question: Which is larger: 347/521 or 412/617?
examples.solution: Cross-multiply: 347 × 617 = 2,14,099; 412 × 521 = 2,14,652. The second product is larger, so 412/617 > 347/521. Both are close to 2/3, which is why a benchmark alone was not enough here.

examples.question: Approximately what percent of 6,112 is 1,847?
A value of 6,480 grows by 12.5%. Find the new value.
Find the percentage change from 2,450 to 2,940.
examples.solution: Change = 490. Since 2,450 ÷ 5 = 490, the change is one-fifth, i.e. 20%.

examples.question: Which grew faster: A from 240 to 300, or B from 360 to 440?
examples.solution: A: 60/240 = 25%. B: 80/360 ≈ 22.2%. A grew faster even though B’s absolute increase was larger.

examples.question: Find the average of 528, 532, 541, 519 and 530.
examples.solution: Assume 530. Deviations: −2, +2, +11, −11, 0; total 0. Average = 530.

practice: Which is larger: 5/7 or 7/10?
Both are equal
Cannot be determined
Cross-multiplying gives 5 × 10 = 50 and 7 × 7 = 49, so 5/7 is slightly larger than 7/10.
3,600 is what percent of 4,800?
3,600/4,800 simplifies to 3/4 after cancelling 1,200, and three-quarters is 75 percent.
16.67% is one-sixth, and 7,230 ÷ 6 = 1,205, so no long multiplication is needed.
The percentage change from 1,250 to 1,100 is:
12% decrease
15% decrease
12% increase
13.6% decrease
The fall is 150 on a base of 1,250, and 150/1,250 = 0.12, a 12 percent decrease.
The average of 248, 252, 255 and 245 is:
Deviations from 250 are −2, +2, +5 and −5, which sum to zero, so the average is exactly 250.
faqs: Is it worth learning Vedic maths for DI?

A few techniques help — multiplying numbers near a base, squaring numbers ending in 5 — but the biggest gains come from fraction benchmarks and approximation, which apply to nearly every DI question. Learn those first and add other tricks only if they feel natural.
How accurate do DI calculations need to be?

Usually only accurate enough to separate the options. If options are 10% apart, rough estimates work. If two options are within 1–2%, calculate more carefully. Looking at the options before calculating tells you how precise you need to be.

items.topic: Growth Rate and CAGR in DI
items.title: Growth Rate, CAGR and Index Numbers in DI Questions
items.description: Year-on-year growth, overall growth, CAGR, index numbers and percentage-point changes as used in bank and CAT DI sets, with worked numerical examples.
items.intro: Questions on growth appear in almost every DI set: "by what percent did sales grow", "what was the average annual growth" or "which year had the highest growth". RBI Grade B, IBPS PO mains, SBI PO and CAT go further with compound annual growth rate (CAGR), index numbers and market-share changes. Getting these right depends on understanding which base each growth figure uses.

concepts.heading: Year-on-year and overall growth
concepts.text: Year-on-year growth compares each year with the previous one. Overall growth compares the last year with the first. Successive growths combine multiplicatively: 10% followed by 20% is an overall growth of 1.1 × 1.2 − 1 = 32%, not 30%.

concepts.heading: CAGR
concepts.text: The compound annual growth rate is the constant yearly rate that takes the first value to the last: CAGR = (last/first)^(1/n) − 1 over n years. ₹200 crore growing to ₹242 crore in 2 years gives (1.21)^(1/2) − 1 = 10% a year. It differs from the simple average of yearly growth rates.

concepts.heading: Index numbers
concepts.text: An index sets a base year to 100 and expresses other years relative to it. If the 2022 index is 125 with 2020 = 100, the 2022 value is 25% above 2020. With an actual 2020 value of ₹80 crore, the 2022 value is ₹100 crore.

concepts.heading: Percent versus percentage points
concepts.text: If a market share rises from 12% to 15%, it rose by 3 percentage points, which is a 25% increase in the share. Questions use both phrasings; options usually include both numbers.

concepts.heading: Rule of 72 (approximate)
concepts.text: At a steady growth rate of r% a year, a value roughly doubles in 72/r years. At 8% that is about 9 years; at 12%, about 6 years. It is an approximation, useful for quick checks but not for exact answers.

shortcuts: Highest growth year: compare increase ÷ previous value for each year, not raw increases.
A fall of x% followed by a rise of x% leaves the value below the start.
Index-to-value: value = base value × index/100.

examples.question: A company’s revenue grows from ₹200 crore to ₹242 crore in 2 years. Find the CAGR.
examples.solution: Growth factor = 242/200 = 1.21. Since 1.21 = 1.1², the constant yearly factor is 1.1, so CAGR = 10% per year. The overall two-year growth is 21%, not 20%, because the second year grows on a larger base.

examples.question: Revenue was ₹500 crore in 2020, ₹550 crore in 2021 and ₹660 crore in 2022. Find the yearly and overall growth.
With 2020 = 100, a sales index reads 125 in 2022. If 2020 sales were ₹80 crore, what were 2022 sales?
examples.solution: Value = base value × index/100 = 80 × 125/100 = ₹100 crore. The index itself has no unit; it only tells you that 2022 sales were 1.25 times the 2020 level.

examples.question: A bank’s market share rises from 12% to 15%. Describe the change in two ways.
examples.solution: It rose by 3 percentage points; relative to its earlier level, it rose by 3/12 = 25%.

examples.question: What annual growth rate takes a value from 400 to 576 in 2 years?
examples.solution: 576/400 = 1.44 = 1.2², so the required CAGR is 20%.

examples.question: Roughly how long does a value growing at 8% a year take to double?
examples.solution: By the rule of 72, about 72/8 = 9 years. Check: 1.08⁹ ≈ 2.0.

practice: A value grows from 1,000 to 1,210 in 2 years. Its CAGR is:
1,210/1,000 = 1.21 = 1.1², so the compound annual growth rate is 10 percent.
Sales grow by 20% in one year and 25% in the next. The overall growth is:
Overall factor = 1.2 × 1.25 = 1.5, so the overall growth over the two years is 50 percent.
With 2019 = 100, an index is 140 in 2023. If the 2019 value was 250, the 2023 value is:
Value = 250 × 140/100 = 350, i.e. 40 percent above the base-year value.
A firm’s market share rises from 8% to 10%. The percentage increase in its share is:
The share rose 2 percentage points on a base of 8, which is a 25 percent increase.
By the rule of 72, a value growing at 12% a year roughly doubles in about:
8 years
12 years
6 years
4 years
72 ÷ 12 = 6 years, and indeed 1.12⁶ is close to 2, confirming the approximation.
faqs: Is CAGR the same as average growth rate?

No. The simple average of yearly growth rates ignores compounding and the changing base. CAGR is the single constant rate that links the start and end values. For growths of 10% and 20%, the simple average is 15% but the CAGR is about 14.9%.
Why do DI questions use index numbers?

Index numbers make comparisons across years easy without giving actual values, and they let setters combine data from different scales. Convert an index to a value only when the question needs an amount, using the base-year value given elsewhere in the set.

items.title: Data Sufficiency in Quant: Method, Traps and Examples
items.description: Data sufficiency questions explained: the five answer choices, testing each statement alone and together, uniqueness traps and quick quant examples.
items.intro: Data sufficiency (DS) asks whether given statements are enough to answer a question, not for the answer itself. IBPS PO, SBI PO, RBI Grade B and IBPS Clerk mains include DS sets in the quantitative and DI sections, and CAT and CMAT test it in DI and logical reasoning. DS rewards disciplined testing of each statement and punishes the habit of solving completely or assuming facts that are not stated.

concepts.heading: Standard answer choices
concepts.text: The usual choices are: (a) statement I alone is sufficient; (b) statement II alone is sufficient; (c) either statement alone is sufficient; (d) both together are needed; (e) even both together are not sufficient. Some papers add a third statement, but the logic is the same.

concepts.heading: Test in a fixed order
concepts.text: First test statement I alone, forgetting II. Then test II alone, forgetting I. Only if neither is sufficient alone, combine them. Mixing information from the other statement while testing one alone is the most common error.

concepts.heading: Sufficient means a unique answer
concepts.text: A statement is sufficient only if it leads to exactly one value (or a definite yes or no). x² = 16 gives two values, so it is not sufficient for "what is x?" unless another fact rules one out. For yes/no questions, a definite "no" is also sufficient.

concepts.heading: Do not solve fully
concepts.text: You need only to know that an answer can be found. Two independent linear equations in two unknowns are sufficient; you do not have to solve them. This saves time across the set.

concepts.heading: Hidden dependence
concepts.text: Two statements that are really the same information (one equation is a multiple of the other) do not combine into a solution. Check that combined statements add genuinely new information.

shortcuts: Count unknowns and independent equations: n unknowns need n independent equations.
Ratios alone rarely give actual values; you also need one absolute quantity.
For speed questions, you need any two of distance, speed and time.
Yes/no questions: a consistent "no" counts as sufficient.
Never use outside assumptions such as "ages are integers" unless the question says so.

examples.question: What is x? I. 3x + 2y = 12. II. x − y = −1.
examples.solution: I alone has two unknowns — not sufficient. II alone also has two unknowns — not sufficient. Together they give x = 2, y = 3. Answer: both together are needed.

examples.question: Is the integer x even? I. 3x is even. II. x² is even.
examples.solution: I: 3x even means x even (3 is odd) — sufficient. II: x² even means x even — sufficient. Answer: either statement alone is sufficient.

examples.question: What is A’s age? I. A is 5 years older than B. II. B’s age is half of C’s age.
examples.solution: Even together there are three unknowns and only two relations. Answer: not sufficient even together.

examples.question: What is the speed of a train? I. It passes a pole in 12 seconds. II. It is 240 m long.
examples.solution: I gives time only; II gives distance only. Together, speed = 240/12 = 20 m/s. Answer: both together.

examples.question: What is the profit percentage on an item? I. Its cost price is ₹800. II. Its selling price is ₹920.
examples.solution: Each statement alone lacks the other price. Together, profit = ₹120, i.e. 15%. Answer: both together.

examples.question: What is x, given x² = 16? I. x > 0. II. x is an integer.
examples.solution: x = 4 or −4. I rules out −4, so x = 4 — sufficient. II allows both values — not sufficient. Answer: statement I alone.

practice: What is the ratio of the ages of A and B? I. A is twice as old as B. II. The sum of their ages is 45.
Statement I alone is sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed
Either statement alone is sufficient
Statement I fixes the ratio at 2 : 1 directly, while the sum alone cannot give the ratio.
What is the rate of simple interest? I. A sum doubles in 8 years. II. SI on ₹1,000 for 4 years is ₹500.
Statement I alone is sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed
Either statement alone is sufficient
I gives 100/8 = 12.5% and II gives 500/(1,000 × 4) = 12.5%, so each statement works alone.
What is the area of a rectangle? I. Its perimeter is 30 cm. II. Its diagonal is 12 cm.
Statement I alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed
Statement II alone is sufficient
Not sufficient even together
Together l + b = 15 and l² + b² = 144 give lb = (225 − 144)/2 = 40.5, but neither statement alone fixes the area.
Is n divisible by 6? I. n is divisible by 3. II. n is divisible by 2.
Statement I alone is sufficient
Both statements together are needed
Either statement alone is sufficient
Not sufficient even together
Divisibility by 6 needs both 2 and 3; each statement alone leaves the answer open, but together they confirm it.
How many students are in a row? I. Ravi is 12th from the left. II. Ravi is 20th from the right.
Both statements together are needed
Statement I alone is sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient
Either statement alone is sufficient
Together the total is 12 + 20 − 1 = 31 students; each position alone says nothing about the total.
faqs: Do I need to find the actual answer in data sufficiency?

No. You only need to decide whether the statements allow a unique answer. Stopping once sufficiency is clear saves time. Computing fully is useful only when you are unsure whether the solution is unique.
What is the biggest trap in data sufficiency?

Using information from one statement while judging the other alone, and assuming facts not stated, such as values being positive or whole numbers. Treat each statement in isolation first, and rely only on what the question and statements actually say.

items.title: Coordinate Geometry Basics: Distance, Slope and Area
items.description: Distance, mid-point and section formulas, slope and line equations, intercepts and triangle area for SSC CGL and CAT, with verified worked examples.
items.intro: Coordinate geometry is a small but regular topic in SSC CGL and CHSL, usually one or two questions, and it appears in CAT and CMAT within geometry and algebra. Bank exams do not test it. The questions are formula-based: distance between points, the point dividing a segment, the slope of a line, intercepts and areas. Each formula is short, so accuracy with signs is the main challenge.

concepts.heading: Distance and mid-point
concepts.text: The distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]. The mid-point is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Many questions use Pythagorean triples, so distances like 10 or 13 appear often.

concepts.heading: Section formula
concepts.text: The point dividing the segment from A(x₁, y₁) to B(x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m : n is ((m x₂ + n x₁)/(m + n), (m y₂ + n y₁)/(m + n)). The centroid of a triangle is the average of its three vertices.

concepts.heading: Slope and equations of lines
concepts.text: Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). A line with slope m and y-intercept c is y = mx + c. For ax + by + c = 0, the slope is −a/b. Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1.

concepts.heading: Intercepts and area
concepts.text: The line x/a + y/b = 1 cuts the x-axis at a and the y-axis at b, forming a triangle of area |ab|/2 with the axes. The area of a triangle with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃) is ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|. If this area is zero, the points are collinear.
concepts.formula: Area = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|

shortcuts: To find intercepts of ax + by = c, divide by c: 3x + 4y = 12 becomes x/4 + y/3 = 1.
A point on the x-axis has y = 0; on the y-axis, x = 0 — use this to find where lines cut the axes.
Perpendicular slope = −1/m: a line perpendicular to slope 4 has slope −1/4.
Check collinearity quickly by comparing slopes of AB and BC.
Sketch the points roughly; a picture often reveals a right angle or symmetry.

examples.question: Find the distance between (2, 3) and (8, 11).
examples.solution: Differences are 6 and 8, so d = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 units — a 6-8-10 triangle.

examples.question: Find the mid-point of (−4, 6) and (10, −2).
Find the point dividing the segment from (1, 2) to (7, 8) internally in the ratio 1 : 2.
examples.solution: x = (1 × 7 + 2 × 1)/3 = 3; y = (1 × 8 + 2 × 2)/3 = 4. The point is (3, 4), one-third of the way from the first point.

examples.question: Find the slope and equation of the line through (2, 5) and (6, 13).
examples.solution: Slope = (13 − 5)/(6 − 2) = 2. Using y = 2x + c with (2, 5): 5 = 4 + c, so c = 1. Equation: y = 2x + 1.

examples.question: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (4, 5) and (7, 1).
examples.solution: ½|1(5 − 1) + 4(1 − 1) + 7(1 − 5)| = ½|4 + 0 − 28| = 12 square units. Check: base from (1, 1) to (7, 1) is 6 and height is 4, giving 12.

examples.question: Find the area of the triangle formed by 3x + 4y = 12 with the coordinate axes.
examples.solution: Intercepts: x = 4 and y = 3. Area = ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 square units.

practice: The distance between (−1, 2) and (5, 10) is:
Differences are 6 and 8, so the distance is √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 units.
The mid-point of (3, −5) and (7, 9) is:
Average the coordinates: ((3 + 7)/2, (−5 + 9)/2) = (5, 2), the mid-point of the segment.
The slope of the line 2x − 3y + 6 = 0 is:
For ax + by + c = 0 the slope is −a/b = −2/(−3) = 2/3; rewriting gives y = (2/3)x + 2.
The area of the triangle formed by 2x + 5y = 10 and the coordinate axes is:
10 square units
7 square units
2.5 square units
5 square units
The intercepts are x = 5 and y = 2, so the area is ½ × 5 × 2 = 5 square units.
The slope of a line perpendicular to y = 4x − 7 is:
Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1, so the required slope is −1/4 for a line with slope 4.
faqs: Is coordinate geometry important for bank exams?
No, IBPS, SBI and RBI papers do not normally include it. It matters for SSC CGL and CHSL and for MBA entrance exams like CAT and CMAT. Bank aspirants who are not taking SSC can give it low priority.
How do I check whether three points are collinear?
Find the area of the triangle they form; if it is zero, they lie on a line. Alternatively, compute the slopes of AB and BC — equal slopes through a shared point mean the points are collinear.

items.title: Clock Problems: Angle Between Hands and Coinciding Hands
items.description: Angle between clock hands using |30H − 5.5M|, times when hands coincide or are at right angles, and mirror-image times, with worked examples.
items.intro: Clock questions are short arithmetic puzzles that appear in SSC CGL and CHSL, occasionally in CAT, CMAT and MAT, and in the reasoning sections of some bank papers. They rely on one relative-speed idea: the minute hand gains 5.5° on the hour hand every minute. With that and one formula for the angle, nearly every clock question can be solved in under a minute.

concepts.heading: Speeds of the hands
concepts.text: The minute hand moves 360° in 60 minutes, i.e. 6° per minute. The hour hand moves 30° per hour, i.e. 0.5° per minute. So the minute hand gains 5.5° per minute on the hour hand, and it gains 60 minute-spaces in 65 5/11 minutes.

concepts.heading: Angle between the hands
concepts.text: At H hours and M minutes, the angle is |30H − 5.5M| degrees. If the result exceeds 180°, subtract it from 360° to get the smaller angle. At 3:40 the angle is |90 − 220| = 130°.

concepts.heading: Coinciding and right-angle times
concepts.text: Between H and H + 1 o’clock, the hands coincide when 30H = 5.5M, i.e. M = 60H/11 minutes past H. For a right angle, set |30H − 5.5M| = 90; for opposite hands, 180. The hands coincide 11 times in 12 hours (22 times a day) and are at right angles 22 times in 12 hours (44 times a day).

concepts.heading: Mirror images
concepts.text: The time seen in a vertical mirror is 11:60 minus the actual time (or 12:00 minus it when the minutes are zero). A clock showing 3:40 appears as 8:20 in the mirror.

shortcuts: Hands coincide every 65 5/11 minutes, not every 60 minutes.
At exactly H o’clock, the angle is 30H (or 360 − 30H if larger than 180).
Between 5 and 6 or 6 and 7, check both sides of the hour hand for right angles — two answers usually exist.
Mirror time trick: subtract from 11:60, so 4:25 becomes 7:35.
A clock that gains or loses time: compare clock minutes with real minutes as a ratio and scale.

examples.question: Find the angle between the hands at 3:40.
examples.solution: θ = |30 × 3 − 5.5 × 40| = |90 − 220| = 130°. Intuitively, the minute hand is at 240° (the 8) and the hour hand has moved two-thirds of the way from the 3 towards the 4, i.e. to 110°; the gap is 130°.

examples.question: Find the angle between the hands at 7:20.
examples.solution: θ = |30 × 7 − 5.5 × 20| = |210 − 110| = 100°. Since 100° is less than 180°, it is already the smaller angle.

examples.question: At what time between 4 and 5 o’clock do the hands coincide?
examples.solution: At 4:00 the minute hand is 20 minute-spaces (120°) behind. It gains 5.5° a minute, so it needs 120/5.5 = 240/11 = 21 9/11 minutes. The hands coincide at 21 9/11 minutes past 4, not at 4:20, because the hour hand keeps moving.

examples.question: At what time between 2 and 3 o’clock are the hands at right angles (after the minute hand passes the hour hand)?
examples.solution: |60 − 5.5M| = 90 with the minute hand ahead: 5.5M = 150, so M = 300/11 = 27 3/11 minutes past 2.

examples.question: A clock reads 3:40. What time does its mirror image show?
examples.solution: Subtract from 11:60: 11:60 − 3:40 = 8:20. You can verify by noting that 3:40 + 8:20 = 12:00, which holds for every mirror pair.

examples.question: How many times do the hands of a clock coincide in a day?
examples.solution: 11 times every 12 hours, so 22 times in 24 hours. The coincidence near 12 o’clock is shared between two 12-hour periods, which is why it is not 24.

practice: The angle between the hands of a clock at 5:30 is:
θ = |30 × 5 − 5.5 × 30| = |150 − 165| = 15 degrees, as the hour hand is halfway past 5.
The smaller angle between the hands at 9:15 is:
|270 − 82.5| = 187.5°, which exceeds 180°, so the smaller angle is 360 − 187.5 = 172.5°.
Between 2 and 3 o’clock, the hands coincide at:
10 minutes past 2
10 10/11 minutes past 2
11 minutes past 2
10 5/11 minutes past 2
M = 60 × 2/11 = 120/11 = 10 10/11 minutes past 2, using the coincidence formula.
How many times are the hands of a clock at right angles in 12 hours?
They are at right angles twice in most hours, but only 22 times in 12 hours because some instances are shared.
A clock shows 4:25. Its mirror image shows:
Subtract from 11:60: 11:60 − 4:25 = 7:35, which is the time seen in a vertical mirror.
faqs: Why do the hands coincide only 11 times in 12 hours?

Because the minute hand laps the hour hand once every 65 5/11 minutes, slightly more than an hour. In 720 minutes it completes 720 ÷ (720/11) = 11 laps. The coincidence at 12 o’clock counts once, not twice.
Is the angle formula valid for any time?

Yes. |30H − 5.5M| gives the angle between the hands for any hour H from 1 to 12 and minute M from 0 to 59. If the result is more than 180°, subtract it from 360° when the question asks for the smaller angle.
